summary: The literature offers almost no measured Elo for neural-policy ordering inside alpha-beta engines. My searches found only forum remarks that Allie, Leela and Scorpio use network policy for ordering, a Gomoku paper (Rapfi) claiming policy-ranked alpha-beta beats plain alpha-beta, and Scorpio's MCTS with alpha-beta rollouts (Dec 2017/Feb 2018, release notes only). Your own measurements (fact 5) are the best evidence available: a prior is worth about 100 Elo to a 30k-node search, about 35 at 100k and nothing at 300k, because history, killers, the TT and iterative deepening rebuild the same information from search itself, so the gain scales with the share of the tree that the prior must guess. The result with the best chance of mattering is therefore not a better transformer but removing the latency penalty (clock result -122 vs -111, probably the 20 ms median call, as much as the 10 ms per move at 10+0.1 allows) and using the prior only where the remaining subtree is small.
warnings: 1) The fixed-node quality instrument ignores latency; fact 5's -2.5 units at 30k nodes does not carry to the clock, and the one clock result was negative. 2) The currently running PolW/PolLmr test makes about 250 transformer calls per 300k-node search; at the clock (about 0.25 s of search) that is about 1.75 s of GPU round trips, so any gain at fixed nodes must be re-measured with a per-move call budget. 3) My web searches (several) returned almost nothing quantitative on Lc0/AB hybrids, Stoofvlees or Allie, so I cannot cite measured Elo for them; sources seen: chessprogramming.org/Scorpio, talkchess.com threads (forum opinion), arxiv.org/pdf/2503.13178 (Gomoku, not chess). No fetched page contained instructions aimed at AI models. No licence issue arose, since I read no engine source.

proposals.title: Asynchronous prior with node-scaled weight (hide latency, switch off at depth)
proposals.mechanism: In duo_uci.py, send the root board to lm/serve.py the moment 'go' arrives and start the search immediately with no prior (use a small I/O thread or non-blocking socket polled every ~2k nodes). When the reply arrives (about 7-20 ms later), inject the prior at the next iteration boundary or at the next root-move re-sort, as the existing additive prior for root ordering and root reductions. Make the weight a function of the node budget estimated at 'go' (from the clock): prior 16/cap 80 below ~50k nodes, prior 8/cap 40 near 100k, zero at 250k or more (your data: -2.53, -0.70 and +0.29 for the larger prior at 300k). Skip the call entirely when the move is forced, or when the TT or previous iteration already shows a stable best move for 3 or more iterations. Ponder-style speculation on the opponent's expected reply can later hide even the 7 ms, but start without it.
proposals.evidence: Your fact 5 and the table at ext/README.md:645-655: the effect is monotone in nodes and the large prior turns harmful at 300k (+0.29). The clock figure of -122 against -111 is the only match test, and the fixed-node quality instrument charges no latency at all, so it cannot see the penalty. External support is weak. General forum remarks only; no number found for a hybrid dropping the prior at higher node counts. The hybrids in the literature (Scorpio, MCTS-AB) run on GPUs with much larger budgets, so they say little about a 0.1-0.3 s single-thread search.
proposals.expected_elo: +0 to +12 over BIGS alone at 10+0.1 (mostly recovering the -11 penalty); most plausible outcome is parity with BIGS. Larger gains only if time management shows many 30-100k-node moves in the endgame under the 0.1 s increment.
proposals.cheap_test: 1) Log the node count per move in a 200-game match to see what fraction of moves is below 100k nodes (decides everything; 20 minutes). 2) Quality test with prior weight as a function of budget at 30k/100k/300k: should reproduce -2.5/-0.9/0. 3) 1,000-game clock match against Stockfish 14.1, async version vs BIGS alone, at the same hours as the previous clock run; the loss budget is 1,000 games either way.
proposals.where_in_our_code: duo_uci.py (prior injection, call timing); lm/serve.py (reply path); calc/calc_s19.c root move ordering and the par[] prior options

proposals.title: Interior-node policy only where the subtree is 30k-100k nodes, and a fixed call budget per move
proposals.mechanism: Fact 5 says the prior pays off when the subtree below a node is small enough that search cannot rebuild the order itself. A node with about 8 plies left has a subtree of roughly that size, so the PolW/PolLmr experiment (LmDepth 8) in effect applies the root-prior result at interior nodes. Tune it as follows: (a) sweep LmDepth in {7, 9, 11} at fixed nodes; (b) cap the transformer calls per move by clock (at 10+0.1, 7 ms x 250 calls is ~1.75 s against ~0.25 s of search, so the current setting cannot work at the clock; 10-20 calls per move is the ceiling unless calls are batched per iteration and made asynchronous); (c) pick which nodes get a call by an importance rule: PV or cut-node-failed-high-at-least-twice and not a TT hit with a stored best move; (d) cache priors by hash in a small side table so repeated visits cost nothing. Use the policy for the quiet-move ordering bonus and for LMR reductions, as now, but test ordering alone (PolW with PolLmr 0) first, since fact 8 shows a better reduction predictor (AUC 0.907 vs 0.822) was level in play.
proposals.evidence: Fact 5 (effect shrinks as the budget per node grows), fact 8 (reduction model with higher AUC but no gain, so reductions look saturated while ordering may not be), and fact 11 (test pending). No external number found: I found no fishtest-style result for a policy net used for ordering or reductions in an alpha-beta engine. Treat the mechanism as a hypothesis from your own data only.
proposals.expected_elo: -5 to +10 at the clock (fixed-node quality gain of 0 to 1 unit minus latency loss); at 300k fixed nodes expect 0 to -0.7 units because only a small share of nodes is covered.
proposals.cheap_test: Wait for the PolW/PolLmr result. If it is flat, run the LmDepth sweep and the PolW-only variant as three 300k-node quality runs (about 45 min each on the 9,000 positions), then a 30k-node run for a sanity check that depth-limited interior use still gains there. Only if a fixed-node gain of 0.5 units or more shows, build the call-budgeted asynchronous version and test it at the clock.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c (PolW, PolLmr, LmDepth, the staged move picker and LMR code; the par[] table near line 1015), lm/serve.py batching

proposals.title: Distil the transformer policy into a small head on the NNUE accumulator (free policy at every node)
proposals.mechanism: Train a linear or one-hidden-layer policy head that reads the 2 x 768 accumulator values (already computed for the eval) and outputs the move-from/to logits, with the transformer L2's move distribution (or Stockfish 4M-node best-move labels) as teacher. Cost: about 1.5 to 3.3 M multiply-adds per call for from/to heads, run only at depth 4 or more and cached; this is about 1-3 microseconds with AVX2 int8, so the use at every interior node needs no GPU and no latency. Use as the ordering bonus for quiet moves next to history, and measure the first-move cutoff rate and the average rank of the cutoff move before any match. This is how Lc0-style policy is made cheap enough for alpha-beta, and the part of fact 5 that you can still harvest is exactly the ordering at nodes that history has not seen.
proposals.evidence: Indirect only. Fact 5 shows ordering knowledge helps at small budgets; fact 7 (a sibling-pair value head learned but did not transfer) and fact 8 (better AUC for reductions but level play) both warn that a better predictor need not become Elo. Reading my searches, the claim that Allie, Leela and Scorpio use network policy for ordering is only a forum comment, with no measured gain. The Rapfi paper (arxiv 2503.13178) reports gains from policy-ranked alpha-beta in Gomoku, a game with a far larger branching factor and weaker handcrafted ordering than chess, so it transfers poorly.
proposals.expected_elo: -5 to +10; most likely nil (history plus the TT plus the staged picker already give a high first-move cutoff rate in chess). Do not expect more than the 30k-node-equivalent gains spread thinly.
proposals.cheap_test: Offline first (about 2 h): dump accumulators and teacher move distributions for the 9,000 quality positions plus some training positions, fit the head, and report the first-move cutoff rate in search with the head versus without it at 100k nodes with the head used as an ordering bonus (no retraining of BIGS). Proceed to a quality test at 300k nodes only if the cutoff rate rises by 1.5 points or more.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/train_nnue.py (extra head), calc/calc_s19.c (quiet-move scoring in the staged move picker, accumulator access), lm/train_lm.py (teacher labels)

summary: The current client is fully synchronous (calc_s19.c lm_get, fprintf+fflush then blocking fgets, one position per round trip), so the ~250 calls per 300k-node search cost ~250 x 7 ms = 1.75 s of blocked search against a ~0.3-0.4 s move budget at 10+0.1. The pending PolW/PolLmr result is a fixed-node number and says nothing about the clock; in a clock match this design would lose far more than any prior can gain. A non-blocking client (send-and-continue, cache states EMPTY/PENDING/READY, consume replies by polling at the existing time-check points, fall back to the read-out policy on a miss) makes the transformer cost ~0 search time, and it can be tested deterministically at fixed nodes by simulating latency in nodes. I could not find measured external evidence for async GPU guidance in an alpha-beta engine, so the Elo upside is bounded only by our own fixed-node result (root prior ~0 at 300k, so expect 0 to +10 at best); this proposal turns that result into a clock-valid one rather than adding strength by itself.
warnings: 1) Fact 11's pending run is at fixed nodes, so it ignores latency: with the current synchronous client the same setting at 10+0.1 would block ~1.75 s per move and lose most games on time or depth; do not run a clock match with PolW/PolLmr on until the client is non-blocking. 2) Nondeterminism: real async makes the chosen move depend on thread timing and GPU load (the engine is already unstable, fact 9), so debug and gate with the deterministic LmLat virtual-latency mode, and run the final clock match with one game per GPU at a time or at least log p99 latency. 3) If a reply arrives mid-search the ordering of a re-visited node changes between iterations; combined with TT move ordering this should be harmless but check for LMR/singular interactions by running the quality instrument with LmLat=infinity (never visible) to confirm it equals the baseline bit-for-bit. 4) I did not fetch external pages; no injected instructions seen. 5) I did not run anything: all numbers are from reading calc/calc_s19.c, lm/serve.py, engine.py and ext/README.md, so all server latency numbers (1-2 ms target) are estimates, not measurements."}

proposals.title: Non-blocking transformer client with request queue, PENDING cache states and virtual-latency test mode
proposals.mechanism: In calc_s19.c replace lm_get() (lines ~1245-1290). (1) Cache entry gets a state: EMPTY / PENDING / READY (LmEnt at line ~1247; keep 2^15 entries, key verified by 64-bit Zobrist). (2) lm_get() on EMPTY: build a request (key, side, castle, ep, 64 board bytes, n legal moves as 12-bit from/to or the 4288-index, taken from the engine's own move generator), send() with MSG_DONTWAIT on a persistent unix socket, mark PENDING (cap ~64 in flight, drop request if the cap is hit), and return NULL so the picker uses the existing read-out policy path (pl/pol) for this visit. (3) lm_poll(): recv(MSG_DONTWAIT) every 1024 nodes at the place where the clock is already checked; each reply is key + n + int16 log-prob x256 in the order the moves were sent (no move strings, no strtof parsing); write into the entry, set READY. (4) Reuse mechanism: iterative deepening re-visits the same interior nodes at depth+1 (PV and the TT-move chain at least), so a node requested in iteration d is READY in iteration d+1; the first iterations at depth<LmDepth are microseconds so the 7 ms lost at root is negligible. (5) Speculative requests at the end of every completed iteration: walk the TT-best-move chain from the root to LmDepth plies left, and for each node on it request that node and the children after its 2nd/3rd move; also request all root-children positions once per game move. (6) Persist the cache across game moves (only flush on ucinewgame); a position keeps its value because the key identifies it fully. (7) Test mode LmLat=L (nodes): the reply is computed synchronously but stored with ready_at = nodes_searched + L and only becomes visible when nodes >= ready_at, so fixed-node quality runs are deterministic and charge the latency without sleeping. Use L = 8000-12000 (7-10 ms x 1.2 Mn/s) plus a 1 ms batching window. Also print per-search counters: requests, hits READY, misses-because-PENDING, misses-because-EMPTY.
proposals.evidence: Cost arithmetic from our own files: 250 calls/search (task fact 11) x ~7 ms (task text) = ~1.75 s synchronous vs ~0.3-0.4 s per move at 10+0.1, and lm/serve.py/README.md:631-632 says the transformer time is charged to the mover's clock. Synchronous code: calc/calc_s19.c:1277-1278 (fprintf, fflush, fgets). Existing counters (calc_s19.c:2223 prints calls and hits) already measure in-search reuse; I found no saved log with that line in zero/results, so reuse rate under ID is unmeasured (argument is structural: Knuth-Moore PV/cut/all node re-visits, not measured). No external measurement of async GPU guidance in alpha-beta found; weak.
proposals.expected_elo: Not additive by itself. Versus a synchronous implementation at the clock: avoids roughly -150 to -300 Elo (search time lost) and recovers the fixed-node gain. Versus BIGS alone at 10+0.1: -3 to +10 Elo (root prior measured ~0 at 300k; interior ordering/LMR use unmeasured). If the pending PolW/PolLmr fixed-node run shows less than 1 unit at 300k nodes, do not build the real async path.
proposals.cheap_test: Step 0 (30 min, no new code beyond the pending run): read the 'transformer calls N, from the table M' line for the pending PolW/PolLmr run; if M/(N+M) is small the ID-reuse idea fails. Step 1: implement LmLat virtual latency (about 60 lines, synchronous server call still used, results delayed in nodes) and run ext/quality.py at 300k nodes with LmLat=0 vs 10000 vs infinity (never visible = baseline) on the 9,000 positions; accept if LmLat=10000 keeps >=70% of the LmLat=0 gain. Step 2: real async client, check at 10+0.1 with a 200-game match against SF 14.1 for sanity, 1,000 games only if Step 1 gain is >=1 unit.

proposals.title: Binary protocol and python-chess-free server with CUDA graph, to cut round-trip latency from ~7 ms to ~1-2 ms
proposals.mechanism: lm/serve.py spends its time in the Python thread, not the GPU: per request it builds chess.Board(fen), calls any(b.legal_moves) up to three times, board.legal_moves again in Net.legal, calls encode_fen(b.fen()) and encode_move per move (engine.py:23-45, evaluate at 50-65), and does softmax in numpy after a blocking .cpu() copy. Make the engine do this work: it already has the board and the legal-move list, so it sends a fixed-size binary record (64 uint8 pieces, castle, ep, n, uint16 move indices into the 4288 head; dump the index table once from encode_move to a file that C loads). Server: one recv loop (selectors/epoll, no thread per client and no Event handshake), torch.from_numpy of a preallocated pinned uint8 batch, pad to fixed batch sizes {1,4,16,64} and capture one CUDA graph per size (fp16, loops fixed), gather the legal move logits on the GPU (index tensor padded with -inf), log_softmax on the GPU, copy one small int16 tensor back, send binary replies. Remove the 1 ms batching wait: take whatever is in the socket buffer (non-blocking drain), run it, reply. Expect ~1-2 ms for a batch of up to 64 at 5.8M params; L2 (14.3M, loops=2) needs a measurement.
proposals.evidence: Code reading only: lm/serve.py:20-40 (batch wait up to 1 ms plus 0.5 ms polling, chess.Board per request, tolist/json), engine.py:23-45, 50-65. The README states the profile finding that the rule-relation computation and 64x64 attention maps dominate training cost (ext/README.md:626-628), and compiled fp16 attention gave 2.3x in training (6,100 to 14,200 pos/s), so inference at small batch is probably launch-bound, which CUDA graphs remove; this is an inference from training numbers, not measured for serving. The task states the single Python thread with python-chess is the bottleneck (~7 ms per reply).
proposals.expected_elo: 0 by itself (latency, not strength); it widens what async can do: with ~1.5 ms latency and several thousand positions/s of GPU capacity the transformer could be asked at LmDepth 5-6 instead of 8 (about 10x more requests) and the virtual-latency L drops from ~10,000 to ~2,000 nodes. Elo gain only if proposal 1 shows interior use helps at smaller depth: 0 to +5.
proposals.cheap_test: Micro-benchmark outside the engine (under a minute of CPU, 1 h of work): time the existing server for 1, 8, 64 concurrent requests vs a prototype that skips python-chess (feeding pre-encoded tensors from a saved set of 2,000 FENs) with and without torch CUDA graph; the target is p50 under 2 ms at batch 8. Then rerun the Proposal-1 LmLat sweep with LmLat set to the measured latency. Note for tournaments: several concurrent games share one GPU, so measure the p99 latency under 8-12 simultaneous clients, not just single-client latency.

proposals.title: Game-persistent cache with replies requested during the opponent's turn, plus a cheap hash-keyed disk-free warm start
proposals.mechanism: At the end of our search (before printing bestmove, or immediately after), request the transformer for the positions the next search will most likely need first: for the opponent replies that were searched (top ~4-6 root moves of the opponent from the PV line and TT, i.e. the positions after our bestmove then each plausible reply) request every position along the TT-best chain of each, to LmDepth plies, and all of their children; about 30-100 requests. The GPU works while Stockfish thinks (the whole opponent turn is idle time for it); the replies are written into the persistent cache by lm_poll() at the start of the next search (or by a drain at 'position' command). So in the next search the root and the first-iteration PV nodes are READY instead of EMPTY. Same persistent cache also serves the second move of a repeated opening and transpositions between consecutive searches. Needs no search thread: requests are sent by the engine thread between its own moves, replies simply wait in the socket buffer until the next poll (size the socket buffer or drain a few hundred us at the next 'go').
proposals.evidence: Weak, structural. Ponder-style speculation is standard (Stockfish ponder hit rates ~50-60% at top level in TCEC-type play, my recollection, not a cited measurement), and consecutive searches share most of their tree: the position after our move is part of our current tree. In our setup the opponent is Stockfish 14.1 with one thread and the clock is not paused, so this uses wall time that is otherwise idle without touching the 'one thread each' rule (no extra search thread; only a socket send). No measurement on our instruments.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +3 Elo (only fixes the first ~7 ms of root misses and a few first-iteration nodes; those iterations are cheap). Treat as polish after proposals 1 and 2, only if the Step-1 sweep shows a clear sensitivity to the first-iteration misses (compare LmLat=10000 vs LmLat=0 at 30k nodes where the effect is largest).
proposals.cheap_test: In LmLat virtual mode: pre-fill the cache for the next test position by running its predecessor search first (quality.py positions are independent, so use a short 20-game-sequence replay or the existing game logs from zero/results), then compare 'cache pre-filled with the 4 likely replies' vs 'cold' at 30k and 100k nodes; or just count in a 200-game match how often the root position was already READY at 'go'. Skip if the pre-fill hit rate is under 40%.

summary: The 7 ms reply is almost certainly Python and kernel-launch overhead, not GPU compute. Parsing FEN with python-chess, generating legal moves, and an eager forward pass of RuleGraph plus looped blocks (several hundred tiny kernels at batch 1, estimated, not profiled) all sit in one Python thread. Moving legal moves and encoding into the C engine, a static-shape CUDA-graph server and a binary protocol should get the pilot (5.8M) to about 0.3-0.6 ms and L2 (14.3M) to about 0.5-1.0 ms at batch 1. Batch 32 of L2 stays compute-bound at roughly 2-4 ms (about 0.1 ms per position), so a hard "under 0.5 ms at batch 32" is not achievable for L2. Whether it pays in Elo is doubtful given facts 5 and 11; the main benefit is making the pending PolW/PolLmr test affordable and fair at the clock.
warnings: 1) I could not measure anything: no latency numbers for our model exist in the repo (grep found no profile of serve.py), so all latency figures are estimates from code reading and FLOP counts; the first step of any plan should be the 1-hour timing script. 2) 'Under 0.5 ms at batch 32' is not credible for L2 (14.3M params, about 2-4 GFLOP per position, compute-bound at ~2-4 ms for 32, i.e. 0.1 ms per position); only per-position amortised latency or batch 1-8 can meet it. 3) The strategic value is limited: facts 5, 6 and 11 say the transformer's gain vanishes at 300k nodes, so faster inference only matters for experiments that use it at many nodes (PolW/PolLmr), and the pending result should gate proposals 2 and 3. 4) The one-thread match rule makes the GPU server a free extra resource, so async use (proposal 2) is within the test rules, but check that clock charging in duo_uci/engine still counts real wall time, otherwise results are unfair. 5) serve.py's 1 ms collection window and python-chess legal-move checks (any(b.legal_moves) computed up to 3 times per board) are cheap immediate wins even before the rewrite. No injected instructions or external pages were encountered; I did not fetch web pages.

proposals.title: Binary protocol + engine-side encoding and move list + CUDA-graph server (kill python-chess)
proposals.mechanism: 1) In calc_s19.c, send a fixed binary record per request instead of 'P <FEN>': 64 bytes of piece codes (the model's board encoding 0..12, as in engine.encode_fen), castle byte, ep byte, then legal-move count and uint16 from*64+to indices (promotion index mapped to the 4288 head layout). The engine already has legal move generation in C, so no python-chess at all. 2) New lm/serve2.py (or a small C++/libtorch server) reads the records with plain recv, copies into pinned static input tensors and returns only the logits for the requested move indices (log-softmax over the legal set computed on GPU, float16 or float32 array of n moves) instead of formatted text. 3) Capture the whole model.prepare + loops + readout (RuleGraph is pure static-shape tensor ops: one_hot, scatter_, cumsum, einsum, roll, index_put with fixed index tensors, so it is graph-capturable) in torch.cuda.CUDAGraph for batch sizes 1,2,4,8,16,32 with static buffers; pad up to the next captured size. Run net in bf16/fp16 weights, not autocast per call (autocast adds casts every layer). 4) Batcher: no sleep-based 1 ms collection; collect whatever is in the queue now and launch (the 1 ms wait window alone is a floor on latency at batch 1). Use a single thread doing recv -> memcpy -> graph.replay() -> sync -> send; use unix socket SOCK_SEQPACKET to avoid line parsing. Expected breakdown at batch 1: socket round trip 30-60 us, H2D+D2H 20-40 us, graph replay 300-900 us depending on model (kernel count x ~2-4 us + FLOPs: L2 is about 14.3M params x 2 x 64 tokens x (loops+extras) = roughly 2-4 GFLOP per position, about 0.2-0.4 ms at a realistic 10-15 TFLOPs for tiny matmuls).
proposals.evidence: Not measured on our box; I could not run the GPU. Basis: lm/serve.py:20-37 shows per-request chess.Board(fen), any(b.legal_moves) up to 3 times per board, Net.evaluate encoding via encode_fen and self.legal (engine.py:50-64) all in Python under one thread, which at a few hundred us per position in Python alone plus eager launches plausibly explains most of the 7 ms. model.py:61-165 RuleGraph and :312-345 loop/readout are static-shape and branch-free, so CUDA-graph capture is mechanically straightforward. ext/README.md notes training already used a compiled model and half-precision SDPA (6.1k -> 14.2k pos/s), showing torch.compile works on this model. General PyTorch docs and gpt-fast style results report 2-5x from CUDA graphs on launch-bound small-batch inference; this is background knowledge, weak as a number for our model.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +10 Elo on its own at 10+0.1 (it is an enabler, not a gain). It cuts ~250 calls x 7 ms = ~1.75 s of stall per 300k-node search to ~0.15-0.25 s, which turns the PolW/PolLmr experiment from clock-losing to nearly free; any Elo is bounded by what the policy ordering/LMR is worth (unknown, result pending).
proposals.cheap_test: On the GPU box without touching the engine: script that loads L1p and L2 via engine.Net, builds 1000 random positions from the quality set as tensors, and times (a) the current Net.evaluate path, (b) model forward eager with pre-encoded tensors, (c) CUDAGraph replay at batch 1/8/32 (torch.cuda.synchronize timing, 1000 iterations). That isolates how much of the 7 ms is Python vs GPU. Then wire the binary protocol and rerun quality.py at 300k nodes with PolW/PolLmr to confirm identical moves (should match the python server in over 98% of positions given fp16 rounding) and time per move. 1 hour for step (a)-(c), about 5-6 hours for the full binary server and engine client.
proposals.where_in_our_code: lm/serve.py (rewrite), engine.py Net.encode/legal (replace), model.py prepare/loop/readout (capture target), calc/calc_s19.c OURO_SOCK client for the 'P' line (switch to binary records)

proposals.title: Asynchronous policy requests: do not block search; cache policy by Zobrist key
proposals.mechanism: At a node with >= LmDepth plies left, the engine fires the request (binary record, from proposal 1) and continues searching with the plain ordering. The reply is written into a small lock-free policy cache keyed by Zobrist key (separate from the TT, 64k entries; stores per-move log-probs aligned to the move list or an 8-move top list). The next visit to that node (iterative deepening revisits PV and near-PV nodes at every depth, and re-searches) reads the cache for PolW ordering and PolLmr. Implementation: one extra engine I/O thread per search thread (single-thread match: a thread that owns the socket, started at search begin; the main thread only does a nonblocking push to a ring buffer and a nonblocking probe). The searching thread never waits, so the 7 ms (or 0.5 ms) latency is charged as zero clock time, only the extra CPU load matters, which is free as the match is one thread on a 24-thread machine. Determinism cost: results depend on timing; make it reproducible for tests by an optional barrier mode (wait for the reply, current behaviour) and use the async mode only in clock matches. Optionally pre-request at the root and its children at depth 1-2 during iteration 1-3 so those entries are warm by the time the search is deep.
proposals.evidence: Facts 5 and 11: the current blocking design pays about 250 x 7 ms = 1.75 s of wall time per 300k-node search; at 10+0.1 an average move budget is well under that, so the clock result (-122 vs -111) is plausibly dominated by the transformer's time charge rather than by the benefit of the prior (README duo_uci: 'the transformer's time is charged to the mover's clock'). Fact 9 shows our search is hypersensitive to perturbations, so async timing noise may add scatter, which the barrier mode can bound. No measurement of async yet; this is a design inference.
proposals.expected_elo: +0 to +15 vs plain BIGS at the clock if PolW/PolLmr shows any gain at fixed nodes (at 300k nodes the root prior gave ~0; the all-node use is the untested part); realistically recovers the 10-11 Elo that blocking appeared to lose and adds whatever ordering/LMR value exists. Zero if the pending fixed-node result is flat.
proposals.cheap_test: Wait for the pending PolW/PolLmr quality result at 300k nodes. If it is better than -0.5 units, implement async mode and run a 1,000-game 10+0.1 match against BIGS plain. Cheaper proxy first: run the quality test with the barrier mode but charge a fixed simulated latency of 0.5 ms per call versus 7 ms in a time-based test (movetime ~ 300 ms) to see how much the latency alone moves the result.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c (LmDepth call sites, new policy cache and I/O thread), lm/serve.py or serve2 (reply carries the Zobrist key)

proposals.title: TensorRT/ONNX FP16 engine with fused bias-attention, as a second step if graphs alone give > 0.5 ms for L2
proposals.mechanism: Export the inference-only graph (RuleGraph + prepare + loop x2 + readout) to ONNX with static batch sizes 1,4,16,32 (opset 17+), build TensorRT FP16 engines with timing cache, and run via the TensorRT Python/C++ runtime in the same server loop. Fuse the 9-plane relation bias into one precomputed (B,3,heads,64,64) tensor via the conv1x1 already in model.py:282 (a single GEMM), feed it as an additive mask to fused attention (head dim 32-64, 64 tokens fits in one tile). Alternative with less export risk: torch.compile(mode='max-autotune-no-cudagraphs') then manual CUDA graph; or hand-write one Triton kernel for attention with additive bias and fused layernorm+MLP. Quantization to FP8 on Ada is possible but the rule-grounded attention is precision-sensitive; keep FP16.
proposals.evidence: Weak. TensorRT is the standard route for small-batch latency on Ada and Lc0's CUDA/TensorRT backends are the existing precedent for chess nets (68 tokens, fp16) but I did not find or verify numbers for our shape. The risk is ONNX export of scatter_/index_put/cumsum in RuleGraph; those can instead stay as a captured torch graph feeding TensorRT with the rel bias computed outside it.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +3 beyond proposal 1 (only latency 0.2-0.4 ms lower for L2; irrelevant to strength unless the model call count rises by 10x).
proposals.cheap_test: After proposal 1's timing script, check if replay time of the L2 graph at batch 1 exceeds 0.5 ms. Only then try torch.compile max-autotune and compare; trtexec on an exported model gives timing in under an hour. Do not start unless the number is above 0.5 ms and the PolW test shows value.
proposals.where_in_our_code: model.py (export wrapper around prepare/loop/readout), new lm/export_trt.py, lm/serve2.py

summary: I found no published, measured recipe for a neural policy driving LMR or LMP inside alpha-beta; two web searches turned up only MCTS-prior papers and a talkchess thread that suggests a policy head for move ordering. The repo's own history is the best evidence: the small POL1 read-out gained at fixed nodes (+13 and +25 at 30k positions) but lost -53 Elo (-95 to -13) at 10+0.1 (zero/best_options.md:18,49), so clock cost, not signal, is the likely killer. The most promising path is to make the transformer's policy free at every node by distilling it into the existing POL1 read-out, and to replace the current coarse +/-1 reduction rule with a continuous, entropy-gated log-probability rule.
warnings: The measurement noise needs care: fact 9 shows hash-size changes alone flip 19% of our moves at 300k nodes, so quality deltas under about 0.5 units should be repeated with different hash sizes or node counts (for example 290k/300k/310k) and averaged before believing them. The existing read-out lost -53 Elo at the clock while gaining at fixed nodes (zero/best_options.md:49), so any fixed-node win must be re-priced in time before it counts. Web searches found no measured Elo for policy-driven LMR/LMP in alpha-beta; the cited papers (arxiv 2508.21380, the Alberta Lc0 thesis) are about MCTS-prior behaviour, not alpha-beta, and the thresholds in my proposals are untested guesses. No injected instructions were seen in fetched pages (no pages were fetched; only search snippets). No licence issues: no third-party code was read.

proposals.title: Distil the transformer policy into the free POL1 read-out so ordering and reductions work at all depths and cost nothing at the clock
proposals.mechanism: zero/pol_train.py trains the POL1 read-out (hidden layer -> from-square + piece/to-square score) on 'the move a 2,500-position search chose', a hard one-hot label from weak self-play. Replace the target with the L2 (or L1p) transformer's full move distribution: soft-label cross-entropy (or KL) over the legal moves of each position, plus optionally the search-chosen move as an auxiliary term. Use ~12M positions from the L2 training set, run once on the GPU to produce the teacher probabilities (serve.py's batch path). Then enable PolW/PolLmr at all nodes with depth >= 3-4 instead of only >= LmDepth; the read-out costs a small matrix product on an already-computed hidden layer. Keep the factorised from-square plus (piece, to-square) form: it is the only one cheap enough, but it cannot represent move interactions, so expect only a fraction of the transformer's quality (ceiling check: top-1 agreement with the teacher on held-out positions, compared with the current read-out).
proposals.evidence: Internal only. (a) calc_s19.c:1239-1241, 1649-1650, 1771: the transformer path covers only nodes with >= LmDepth plies (about 250 calls per 300k nodes), but ordering and reduction matter at all nodes, mostly shallow ones where no policy exists. (b) zero/pol_train.py header: the read-out's labels are hard search choices, a much noisier target than a 76M-parameter-equivalent soft distribution. (c) zero/best_options.md:18,49: the read-out gained +13 and +25 at fixed positions per move but lost -53 at the clock, so the tax was time. External evidence is weak: the talkchess thread 'Neural MoveMap' (https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?p=893378) only proposes a cheap pseudo-policy net for ordering, with no numbers, and another poster there says a policy head was removed for costing too much. Fact 5 (transformer prior worth +100 at 30k nodes, 0 at 300k) suggests the ordering signal is mostly absorbed once the search is deep, so the gain at 10+0.1 may be small.
proposals.expected_elo: -10 to +15 at 10+0.1 single thread; most likely about 0 to +5. Upside is capped because fact 5 shows the transformer's signal fades by 300k nodes.
proposals.cheap_test: Quality instrument at 300k and at 100k nodes, with the distilled read-out at PolW in {500, 1000} and PolLmr on, against the current read-out (hard-label) and the baseline. Training takes about 1.5 GPU-hours. Decision rule: a quality gain of at least 0.5 units (about 20 Elo) at 100k nodes with at most 2% nodes/s loss justifies a 1,000-game match; no gain at 100k nodes means the signal is redundant with history and the whole policy-ordering line is dead at our time control.

proposals.title: Continuous, entropy-gated log-probability reduction in place of the current +/-1 threshold rule
proposals.mechanism: Current rule (calc_s19.c:1771): r += (dlt > 1024 ? +1 : dlt < 128 ? -1 : 0) with dlt = (best log-prob - move log-prob) x256, applied only on moves already late (legal > 1 + 2*pv) and only for quiet non-TT moves. Try three variants, each applied inside the existing LMR block. A) Re-tuned thresholds: -1 if dlt < 256, +1 if dlt > 1536 (the log-prob scale is in nats x256, so 1024 is p_ratio of about 1.8%; that is only the far tail). B) Linear: r += clamp(round((dlt - 640) / 512), -2, +2). C) Entropy gate: compute p_top = exp(-pol_best-ish) or the policy entropy once per node; if p_top > 0.6 (sharp policy) use variant B at double slope, and if the policy is flat (p_top < 0.25) use no policy term, because a flat policy carries no information about which moves to reduce. Also allow the policy to reduce less for the first 1-2 searched moves (they are currently exempt), which matters because the policy can say the 3rd or 4th move in history order is the real best move. Extension to the cut-node-only case: apply only when cutnode, since there the question is 'which move refutes', which is what a policy predicts.
proposals.evidence: Indirect. Stockfish already reduces continuously with move statistics (par[LMR_HIST] in our code at line 1768 is the same idea with history); a learned LMR model reached AUC 0.907 vs 0.822 but was level in play (fact 8), so ranking quality alone does not convert to Elo and reduction amounts need direct tuning. The AlphaZero/Lc0 literature uses the policy as a prior over a whole distribution (not a rank threshold), which motivates using log-probability rather than rank (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.21380 and the Lc0 background in https://www.cs.ualberta.ca/~mmueller/ps/2021/2021_Rejwana_ACG_Leela_chess_zero_paper.pdf; neither tests alpha-beta reductions). I found no engine-level measurement of a policy-driven LMR formula; treat the specific thresholds as untested guesses.
proposals.expected_elo: +0 to +10 equivalents at fixed nodes with LmDepth=8; at the clock, bounded by the transformer-call cost (about 250 calls x 7 ms is about 1.75 s per 300k-node search), so likely negative without Proposal 1.
proposals.cheap_test: Three quality runs at 300k nodes (about 9,000 positions each, standard error 0.3 units): baseline PolW+PolLmr as running now, variants A, B, C. Needs only new par[] options in the search (about 20 lines). Reading: A better than baseline means thresholds, not formula, are the issue; B or C better than A means a continuous scale helps; all within 0.3 of baseline means the policy signal is already fully used by ordering alone and PolLmr can be dropped.

proposals.title: Policy probability mass as the late-move-pruning limit, plus a dose-response sweep that decides what the pending result means
proposals.mechanism: Part 1 (pruning): at nodes where the policy exists, replace the fixed LMP move-count by a probability-mass cutoff: after the moves containing cumulative probability mass P(depth) (for example 0.97 at depth 8, 0.99 at depth 10), skip remaining quiet moves unless they give check or the node is a PV node; or equivalently reduce those moves by an extra 2 plies instead of skipping, which is the safer first test. Part 2 (sweep, to run alongside the pending test): measure the quality at 300k nodes for LmDepth in {10, 8, 6, 5} and PolW in {0 (policy off, only PolLmr), 500, 1000, 2000}, recording policy calls per search. This gives the curve of benefit against the number of calls.
proposals.evidence: No external measurement found. Nucleus (top-p) style cutoffs are the natural probabilistic analogue of LMP, but I have no source with Elo; this is a hypothesis. Internal: the pending result (fact 11) mixes three effects (ordering, reduction, and the noise of 19% hash-table move changes, fact 9), so a single data point cannot separate them; fact 9's hash noise means deltas below about 0.5 units at 300k nodes should not be believed without repeats.
proposals.expected_elo: Pruning part: -5 to +5 (risk of pruning moves the policy under-rates, since the pilot transformer is only 5.8M params and L2 is not yet done). The sweep itself is a measurement, no Elo.
proposals.cheap_test: Sweep: 4x4 grid is 16 quality runs; run at LmDepth 8 first with PolW in {0,500,1000,2000} (4 runs). Interpretation: (1) PolW=0 with PolLmr alone gains, but PolW ordering does not: the value is in reductions, so Proposal 2 variants are worth it; (2) PolW alone gains and PolLmr hurts: reductions on a noisy policy lose moves, drop PolLmr; (3) both neutral at 300k: consistent with fact 5 (signal fades), stop investing at this node budget and test only at 30k-100k, where the clock effectively lives for our nodes/s; (4) gain grows as LmDepth falls: the signal is real and Proposal 1 (distillation) is the way to afford it. Pruning part: same instrument, extra-reduction variant first.

summary: I found no chess evidence that any MCTS-minimax hybrid beats plain alpha-beta. Baier and Winands' JAIR 2018 paper tested Othello, Breakthrough and Catch the Lion, and chess appears only as motivation. The best hybrid there is MCTS-IP-M-k, which uses shallow minimax to compute node priors. Their optimal embedded minimax depths often stayed at 1, so the gains were mostly move ordering and k-best pruning, which our PVS already has. Fact 3 says the gap is search efficiency (1/2 to 1/3 of the nodes for the same quality). A root or top-of-tree MCTS layer reallocates effort among root moves but does not make the tree search 2-3x more efficient, and fact 5 already shows root-level transformer information is worth about 0 at 300k nodes. I therefore rate the hybrid design low-probability and give one cheap falsification test (proposal 1) plus a better-aimed alternative that uses the transformer's quiet-position edge inside the tree (proposal 2).
warnings: 1) The prior evidence is thin: only the JAIR abstract and a secondary review were seen, not the full text, and no chess experiments in those papers. The 'optimal minimax depth often 1' claim comes from a secondary review (liner.com), so treat it as unverified. 2) Fetched pages contained no injected instructions. 3) Licensing: nothing was copied. The papers are academic and no code was read. 4) Measurement caveat: fact 5 compares at fixed nodes, but at the clock the transformer's ~20 ms per call comes out of the mover's time, and that likely explains -122 vs -111. Any design that needs many sequential GPU calls per move will pay this cost, which is another reason MCTS-style leaf batching is unattractive at 10+0.1. 5) At 300k nodes our search has the same information as the root prior (fact 5), so attention should go to the interior (quiet leaves) or to search efficiency, not to root allocation.

proposals.title: Batched transformer value/policy as a pruning correction at quiet interior nodes (MCTS-IP idea moved inside alpha-beta)
proposals.mechanism: Keep PVS. At nodes with depth >= LmDepth where |static - qsearch| is small (quiet; the transformer is 2.4-2.8 points ahead of BIGS there, README 'Where the transformer's edge is'), fetch the transformer value and form corrected_eval = fast + w*(tf_value - fast), with w around 0.3-0.5 after calibrating the transformer's win-chance logit to centipawns on the 9,000 quality positions. Use corrected_eval ONLY for pruning and reduction decisions (RFP, futility margins, NMP condition, LMR adjustment), never as the returned leaf score. Fact 6 shows replacing leaf scores hurts. Cut GPU cost by prefetching: when a node at depth >= 8 is expanded, send its first 2-3 children's FENs to serve.py asynchronously in one batch and read the replies when the search reaches them (extend the existing lm_cache/lm_get path). This is the 'priors from a cheap evaluator' idea of MCTS-IP, applied to selectivity rather than to the tree policy.
proposals.evidence: WEAK for this exact design; no published chess result. Supporting facts are internal: quiet-pair accuracy 76.0% (transformer) vs 73.2% (BIGS) vs 72.0% (SF net) in ext/README.md around lines 680-700; fact 6 (+6.3 units when the transformer replaces line-end scores) is a warning against using its value as a score. External support is only indirect: Baier and Winands, JAIR 2018, https://jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/11208 (MCTS-IP strongest of the hybrids in Othello, Breakthrough and Catch the Lion; no chess).
proposals.expected_elo: -15 to +15 at 10+0.1; most likely about 0. Upside to about +20 only if the corrected eval cuts the 19% hash-instability noise or improves pruning at depth.
proposals.cheap_test: Quality test at 300k nodes (ext/quality.py, standard error about 0.3 units) with the transformer only at nodes with depth >= 8, using the already-running PolW/PolLmr infrastructure and a new flag for the eval correction. Run w in {0, 0.25, 0.5}, using a fixed NODE budget with the GPU latency ignored, so only quality is measured. A gain of at least -0.6 units (about 24 Elo) justifies the clock test; otherwise stop. Then check the GPU cost: calls per search and ms per move against the 10+0.1 budget.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c: lm_get() around line 1274 and its cache (lines 1241-1280); the mp.lm gate at line 1650; the pruning code in the main search (RFP/futility/NMP use the node's static eval); new par[] entries after LM_DEPTH (line 1015). Serving side: lm/serve.py needs an async batch endpoint.

proposals.title: PUCT root layer with alpha-beta children and transformer priors (the true MCTS-AB hybrid), as a cheap falsification test
proposals.mechanism: Build it in duo_uci.py first, before touching the C engine. Take K = 4-6 root moves from the transformer policy. Run PUCT only at the root: N visits go to the children by Q + c*P/(1+n). Each visit runs calc as a fixed-node alpha-beta search of the child position (searchmoves or 'position ... moves m', nodes = total/ (about 20 visits), shared TT via a persistent process, TT NOT cleared). The backup is minimax-style (max over the child's AB score, no averaging), as in Baier and Winands' MCTS-minimax hybrids. The final move is the one with the best AB score, with the policy prior entering as a small logit bonus. Two caveats: the root-move mix is the same information PVS already uses, and separate child searches lose PVS's shared-window efficiency.
proposals.evidence: Weak and mostly negative. Fact 5 (root prior worth 0 at 300k, -0.8 at 100k, -2.5 at 30k) bounds what a root-only allocation can achieve. Literature: MCTS-minimax hybrids help weaker-search domains (Othello, Breakthrough, Catch the Lion), https://jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/11208 and the TCIAIG version https://dke.maastrichtuniversity.nl/m.winands/documents/mcts-minimax_hybrids_final.pdf; I found no chess data.
proposals.expected_elo: -30 to +5 at 10+0.1; the most likely outcome is a loss from fragmenting the node budget (fact 3's 2-3x efficiency gap is not addressed). A real gain is only plausible at very short time controls (30k-node equivalents).
proposals.cheap_test: Quality test on a 1,000-position subset at 300k nodes total, compared with the single-search baseline. If the result is not better than -0.3 units, kill it. No match needed. This costs roughly 1 evening and settles the whole MCTS-AB question for this project, including the root-only version.
proposals.where_in_our_code: duo_uci.py (it already does the two-line mode and prior bonuses, 'bonus <move> <cp>' command at calc/calc_s19.c line 4); root_bonus table at calc/calc_s19.c line 1104; the root search at about line 1899.

summary: A bigger transformer on its own cannot reach Stockfish 14.1 on our budget: DeepMind's 270M model, trained on ~41B samples with 128 TPUs, still sits ~410 Elo below Stockfish 16 at only 50 ms/move (2299 vs 2711 tournament Elo, ~2895 vs humans on Lichess blitz), and Leela's best searchless policy (BT4, 191M) is only +270 Elo over its older conv net with the gap to search still large. Our L2 (14.3M, 171M positions, ~7 GPU hours) is 2 to 3 orders of magnitude short of that compute, so scaling the LM as a player is a dead end; its value to us is as a better teacher/judge in quiet positions (+2.4 to 2.8 points over BIGS, already visible at 18 minutes of training), and the only credible route is transferring that into the fast net's leaves, not into root priors. No source gives a clean Elo-vs-params law (DeepMind states only 'larger is consistently better'; Lc0 post gives no data/compute), so any extrapolation is weak.
warnings: No injected instructions seen in fetched pages (Lc0 blog, arXiv HTML, search snippets). Caveats: (a) the Lc0 transformer-progress page notes it is superseded by the ICLR 2026 'Chessformer' paper (arXiv 2605.19091, Leela-CF = BT4 191M, reportedly +100 Elo inside Lc0 and wins vs Stockfish in TCEC events); I only saw secondary summaries, not the paper, so those numbers are unverified; those wins are with MCTS search plus huge self-play-derived training, not searchless. (b) DeepMind tournament Elo is anchored internally and not comparable to Stockfish-14.1-at-10+0.1 Elo; the paper's own critics (e.g. LessWrong/Substack posts) note the 270M model is roughly 400 Elo below Stockfish 16. (c) Compute arithmetic: DeepMind main run 10M steps x 4096 batch ~ 41B samples; our budget of tens of GPU hours at ~14k pos/s is ~0.5-1B samples, about 40-80x less data, and the 4080 has a fraction of 128 TPU v5. (d) Fact 5/6 imply root and end-of-line use of the transformer is saturated at playing depth, so more transformer strength alone will not move the clock result unless it reaches leaves.

proposals.title: Distil the transformer's value into the fast net on search-leaf positions (quiet-weighted)
proposals.mechanism: Sample ~100-200M positions the way our search sees them: leaf/PV-end positions harvested from 20-50k-node searches on Lichess starting positions, quiet only (no capture changes the static score). Label them with L2's value head (win chance, batched at large batch on the 4080, est. 30-50k pos/s inference vs 14k/s training, so ~1-2 h per 100M) blended with the existing Stockfish-label target (e.g. 50/50 logits). Fine-tune BIGS (not retrain) for one pass with the trainer's existing teacher mixing path, optionally up-weighting quiet positions. Differs from the failed sibling-pair experiment (fact 7): that used the same database labels; here the target is a different function class's soft judgment on the exact leaf distribution, which is what is missing (the transformer's edge is exactly on quiet pairs, 76.0% vs 73.2%).
proposals.evidence: README ext/README.md:675-704 shows quiet-pair transformer 76.02% vs BIGS 73.20% vs SF net 71.98%, and that sibling labels teach BIGS but give no transfer, concluding the missing piece is the means to see it. Knowledge distillation from a higher-capacity/different-architecture teacher is standard but no chess-specific Elo number found; the DeepMind paper (https://arxiv.org/html/2402.04494v2) shows action-value targets are worth +250 Elo over behavioural cloning at equal data points, supporting that label quality matters. Weak evidence that BIGS has the capacity to absorb it (BIGX 1536 wide chooses no better statically), which is a real risk.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +20 at 10+0.1 single thread (central ~+5); more likely to show first as -0.3 to -0.8 units on the 300k-node quality test
proposals.cheap_test: 1) ~1 h: label 10M leaf positions with the pilot or current L2, fine-tune BIGS for a short pass, check static quiet-pair accuracy (73.2%) and captures-played-out accuracy (74.7%) on the 10,334-pair set; proceed only if quiet pairs reach >=74.5%. 2) quality.py at 300k nodes vs BIGS (SE 0.3, need >=0.6 unit to see it). 3) only then a 1,000-game match.

proposals.title: Gate: measure the transformer's scaling slope on quiet pairs before spending more GPU on it
proposals.mechanism: Evaluate L1p (5.8M, 15M positions) vs L2 final (14.3M, 171M) vs L2 intermediate checkpoints on the quiet-pair and ChessBench metrics (ext/brain_quiet.py, ext/brain_lm.py), and fit accuracy against log(params x tokens). Decide on that: if quiet accuracy goes 76.0 -> ~78+ with 2.5x params and 11x data, then a 40-60M model for ~15-20 GPU hours (about 0.5-0.7B positions at 10-14k pos/s, one-pass, no repeated epochs) is the teacher worth training for proposal 1; if it saturates near 76.5 the transformer line should be dropped and hours put elsewhere.
proposals.evidence: DeepMind: 9M/136M/270M give 2025/2259/2299 tournament Elo and 88.9/94.5/95.4% puzzles, i.e. strongly diminishing returns above 136M at fixed 10M-game data (https://arxiv.org/html/2402.04494v2, Table 1), and their larger models only help with enough data (overfit on small data, Fig. 3). Lc0 transformer post: BT1 92M +13, BT2 82M +123, BT3 105M +179, BT4 191M +270 Elo policy vs T78, so architecture (smolgen, head bias worth '~50% larger') moved strength more than params (https://draft.lczero.org/blog/2024/02/transformer-progress). Our own L2 is at 55.0% best-move after 6% of its run vs pilot 55.3%, so L2's final number is not yet known.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 directly (decision information); saves 10-20 GPU hours of misdirected training
proposals.cheap_test: Run the existing quiet-pair evaluator on each saved checkpoint (minutes each); plot vs params x data.

summary: MoE reduces FLOPs per token, not latency, at batch 1-32 for a model this small: decode and small-batch inference are bound by weight reads and kernel launches, and the experts activated across a batch grow with batch size, so MoE at best ties dense at batch 1 and loses 1.7-3x at p99 as batch grows (Lynx, arXiv 2411.08982). Our serving cost (~7 ms per reply, python-chess parsing and move generation on one Python thread, per the project facts) is CPU-bound, so experts cannot speed it up, and at 5.8M-14M parameters the GPU is mostly idle anyway. I would not spend research hours on MoE. The measured gap is search efficiency, and nothing I found shows an MoE evaluator improving it. The cheap, real gain is removing the Python board-handling bottleneck so transformer calls stop being a latency constraint.
warnings: The one web search I ran (it was a summary page, so treat it as a single weak source) found no direct benchmark of a small MoE against a small dense model at batch 1-32; the numbers I cite come from Lynx (arXiv 2411.08982) and were measured on large LLMs, so transfer to 6-14M-parameter 64-token models is an extrapolation. I did not find any chess or small-board MoE paper. I read only ext/README.md lines around the serve.py description (line ~631) and did not inspect lm/serve.py, so the claim that the Python thread, not the GPU, is the bottleneck rests on your stated facts. No injected instructions were seen in the search results.

proposals.title: Cut transformer serve latency by moving board encoding out of Python (not MoE)
proposals.mechanism: Let the C engine send a fixed binary record (12 piece bitboards, side, castling, ep, plus the legal-move list encoded as from/to indices) over the unix socket. The server then needs no python-chess: it builds the 64 tokens and the relation-bias indices with numpy or a torch kernel, and maps the policy output over 4288 moves directly. Add a captured CUDA graph (fixed batch buckets 1/2/4/8/16/32) and fp16/bf16 with torch.compile or TensorRT, and a lock-free request ring so batching does not depend on the 1 ms collection window. Target is under 1.5 ms per reply at batch 1 and under 3 ms at batch 16. This makes the already-running PolW/PolLmr experiment (~250 calls per 300k-node search) cheap enough to call at shallower depths (LmDepth 5-6), or to feed more nodes, and removes the serve thread as the limit when several matches share the GPU.
proposals.evidence: Weak for Elo, solid for the mechanism. Your own measurement: ~7 ms per reply with the Python thread as the bottleneck (task facts). At 5.8M-14M params with 64 tokens, GPU compute per forward is well under 1 ms, so CPU overhead dominates; the MoE literature agrees that small-batch latency is set by memory reads and launch overhead, not FLOPs (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.08982, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.06182). No Elo evidence that lower latency helps, because measured fact 5 says the prior stops mattering by 300k nodes (~0 units) and fact 11 is still pending.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +10 at 10+0.1 single thread, and only if the PolW/PolLmr run shows a positive signal. It is infrastructure, not strength.
proposals.cheap_test: Time the server alone with a synthetic client at batch 1, 8 and 32 before and after (a one-hour script). Then repeat the pending PolW/PolLmr quality test with LmDepth lowered so that call count rises 4-10x, at 300k nodes. If the quality test shows no gain at any call rate, drop the plan.

proposals.title: Only if the transformer must be stronger at equal latency: try a 2-4 expert MoE feed-forward in L2, run as a dense soft-gated or top-1 mixture on the GPU
proposals.mechanism: Replace the feed-forward in the shared looped block with 4 experts, each of the current hidden width divided by 2, routed by top-1 gating on a feature such as piece-count phase or king-bucket. This is a hard-routed MoE of the kind our fast net already uses (8 piece-count read-out buckets, close in spirit to Stockfish's layer stacks). Keep per-expert weights shared across loop iterations so the parameter count rises but the active FLOPs per token do not. At batch 1-32 with 64 tokens, tokens per batch (64-2048) activate all experts anyway, so run all experts as one grouped GEMM and mask, instead of dispatching. Expect no latency gain, only a capacity gain at equal active compute.
proposals.evidence: Weak. Small-model MoE evidence points to a modest quality gain per active parameter with no latency gain at small batch (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.08982 reports MoE 1.7-3x slower than small dense at p99 as batch grows). I found no chess or small-board paper that measures MoE against a dense model at equal active parameters. The only chess-adjacent precedent is bucketed output heads in NNUE, which we already have. Your measured fact 4 shows the pilot transformer already beats BIGS on quiet pairs (75.6-76.0% vs 73.2%), so evaluator judgment is not the bottleneck, and fact 6 shows it is worse as a leaf judge in search.
proposals.expected_elo: Likely 0 (range -5 to +5). Honest expectation: no measurable change in the search-based gap.
proposals.cheap_test: Train the L1p pilot (5.8M params, 18 minutes) twice at equal active FLOPs: dense and 4-expert top-1. Compare held-out quiet-pair accuracy on the 10,334-case set and policy top-1. Proceed only if the MoE variant gains at least 1 point of quiet-pair accuracy. Otherwise stop.

summary: Threat/attack-map inputs are the one evaluator change with independent support: Stockfish 18 (SFNNv10) added them for roughly +20 Elo net of a severe speed loss, and our own 15 Nov probe found attack maps worth about 2.5 width doublings at 59M positions, but that was never re-tested at the 8.2B scale or put in the engine. They are the most plausible way to give the fast net the pairwise relations the transformer reads, and a cheap static gate (quiet-pair accuracy) can decide before any engine work. Even if they work, the evaluator is not the bottleneck (facts 3 and 4), so the realistic ceiling is about +5 to +15 Elo at the clock.
warnings: 1) One WebFetch of a Hugging Face Space (deepcastle-api full_threats.cpp) returned what is evidently a GPL-3 copy of Stockfish's threat-feature source (header 'copyright 2004-2026 The Stockfish developers', GPLv3). proposals.title: Attack-map (threat) inputs into a narrow slice of a BIGS-recipe net, gated by the static quiet-pair test before any engine work
proposals.mechanism: Retrain the BIGS recipe (768 wide, 16 king buckets, 32 queen-aware heads, half labels / half two teachers) with trainer flag --am plus --amk 128: 768 rule-computed 'piece kind X attacks square s' inputs (sliders stop at first piece) feed only the first 128 hidden units per side, to bound update cost (a move flips 12.2 map inputs vs 2.2 piece inputs, so 128 of 768 units cuts that work about 6x). Stage 1 (decision gate): train one 1.09B-position probe on the vault_probe recipe and evaluate only with the existing static instruments: quiet-pair accuracy (BIGS 73.2%, transformer 75.6-76.0%) and the 10,334 clear cases. Go to the engine only if quiet pairs rise by >= 1.0 point (about 40% of the gap to the transformer). Stage 2: add attack-map computation to calc_s19.c (per-side 12x64 map kept from the bitboard attack sets move generation already has, updated lazily from the moved piece's changed attacks plus sliders through the from/to squares), accumulate into the int16 accumulator slice, test at 30k and 300k nodes, then a 1,000-game match.
proposals.evidence: Own: zero/results/architecture_probe.md lines 19-37: attack maps (12 kinds) -0.0032 held-out loss, about 5 doublings of width on 384-wide nets at 59M positions; threat inputs -0.0013; attack maps + layered read-out -0.0045. But its N384H game test (lines 52-60) showed loss gains overstate game value: +10 Elo for -46% speed. README lines 593-600: re-test at 8.2B scale never run; --am exists in calc/train_nnue.py:63,102 but not in the engine. README 701-704: sibling pairs learned but did not transfer, 'what is missing is the means to see it (relations)'. External: Stockfish 18 notes say SFNNv10 added Threat Inputs (https://stockfishchess.org/blog/2026/stockfish-18/); a search summary of release notes said 'up to 20 Elo' vs 17.1 for the net (not verified on a primary page). TalkChess posters reported severe nps loss, regression at short TC before optimisation, about +15 Elo on ARM and neutral on x86 at first, benefit growing with larger nets (https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?p=988685, p=985220; fetch returned 503, only search snippets, so weak). PlentyChess 8.0.0 notes claim about +42/+47 Elo but bundled with pawn-pair inputs. All external numbers are secondhand.
proposals.expected_elo: If the static gate passes: +3 to +8 Elo at equal nodes; after an assumed 15-30% nps penalty, net -5 to +8 at 10+0.1. Most likely neutral; the value is mainly learning whether relation inputs close the quiet-pair gap.
proposals.cheap_test: Train only the 1.09B probe (no engine). Score with the ext/brain_quiet.py-style static quiet-pair accuracy and clear-case total through a Python forward pass (the trainer already computes attack maps). Pass: quiet pairs >= 74.2% against 73.2%. Control: the same probe without --am; pair accuracy standard error is about 0.6 points on 5,939 pairs, so use a paired comparison.

proposals.title: Combine attack-map inputs with the sibling-pair loss to isolate whether inputs, not signal, block transfer
proposals.mechanism: Fact 7 says the sibling loss taught plain piece-square inputs the pairs but nothing transferred, and README 701-704 attributes this to missing relational inputs. Fine-tune (or train a 192M-position probe) a net WITH --am --amk 128 using --sib (and --sibp 0.5 for plain values), optionally adding the transformer's quiet-position value as an extra distillation target on the same positions. Compare against the s1 fine-tune of BIGS (held-out pairs 71.27 -> 73.10, quality-test static 71.25, no transfer). If inputs are the missing ingredient, quality-test accuracy should now follow the held-out gain. This isolates the cause cheaply and decides whether proposal 1's engine work is worth paying for.
proposals.evidence: Own: README lines 690-704 (c0 70.68/74.81, s1 71.25/74.68, s2 70.73/74.01 on quality-test static / captures played out; held-out pairs +1.8 to +2.1 points); BIGX at twice the width is 70.73% static, so width is not the missing ingredient (line 704). Attack maps help most in balanced positions, where sibling pairs live (architecture_probe.md line 62, zero/slice_loss.py). No external number for this combination; it is our own hypothesis.
proposals.expected_elo: No direct Elo; diagnostic. If transfer appears it justifies proposal 1 with a ceiling of about +10 Elo at the clock; if not, drop the relational-input line and spend the hours on search.
proposals.cheap_test: One 192M-position fine-tune pair on the GPU (with and without --am), then the same quality-test static and captures-played-out accuracy as c0/s1/s2. Success: quality-test quiet pairs >= 72.0% static with --am against 71.25% without.

summary: Threat inputs are real but small at short time controls: Stockfish 18 gained about +14 Elo on ARM at LTC and was initially near neutral on x86, and PlentyChess gained +45 at fixed nodes but only +1.8 (±1.4) at 40+0.4 because of NPS loss. Our own project already measured the cheap form (attack maps, loss -0.0032 versus -0.0013 for pair-style threat inputs on 59M positions) and then shelved it. Because our gap is mostly search efficiency, not evaluator quality (fact 4), the only defensible spend is a narrow attack-map side path, gated by a cheap static test before any engine work, and expected Elo is 0 to +10.

proposals.title: Narrow attack-map side path (--am class --amk 64) on the 768-wide BIGS recipe, gated by static-accuracy test first
proposals.mechanism: Add the 'attack maps' inputs that the trainer already supports: 12 maps (attacker kind x colour, 64 squares, sliders stop at the first blocker), optionally merged into 5 value classes (am='class'), feeding only the first K=64 of the 768 hidden units per perspective (--amk 64) so the engine pays for few units. Stockfish 18's definition is the same family: active feature = (attacker piece, attacker square, victim piece, victim square) with the victim on a square in the attacker's attack set. Ours is the cheap cousin: (attacker kind, attacked square) with no victim identity, a few hundred inputs per side instead of the ~80k of PlentyChess. Engine side: keep a 12x64 bitboard attack-map array per ply, updated on make-move (recompute attacks only for the moved piece, the captured piece, and sliders whose rays cross the from/to squares), and add or subtract the corresponding rows of an int16 [768 x K] table into the narrow part of the existing lazy accumulator. Per our own measurement a move flips 12.2 attack inputs on average versus 2.2 piece inputs (zero/flips.py), so with K=64 the extra incremental cost is about 12.2x64 = 780 int16 adds against about 2.2x2x768 = 3.4k for the piece part, i.e. roughly +20-25% accumulator cost and less than 10% total NPS if done with SIMD; refreshes are only needed on king-bucket changes. Pair with the already-tested layered read-out only if speed allows (it costs -46% NPS, so no).
proposals.evidence: Our measurement: zero/results/architecture_probe.md lines 19-36 on 59M positions with 384-wide nets: attack maps (12 kinds) loss -0.0032, pair-style threat inputs only -0.0013, narrow 128 of 384 units -0.0027 (i.e. a narrow path keeps ~85% of the gain), attack maps + layered read-out -0.0045. Same file lines 50-75: the layered read-out, which had a bigger loss gain, bought only +9 to +14 Elo at equal nodes and cost -46% speed, so loss gains convert to Elo at a factor of several less than hoped. ext/README.md lines 593-600: attack maps at the current 8.2B-position scale were never re-run, and --am is in calc/train_nnue.py (lines 60-63, 98-117, 174, 226-228) but not in the engine. External: Stockfish commit text (https://nextchessmove.com/dev-builds/sf14/8e5392d79a36aba5b997cf6fb590937e3e624e80) lists STC, LTC and VVLTC all passed, ARM LTC estimate +13.9 (±1.9); Stockfish 18 post (https://stockfishchess.org/blog/2026/stockfish-18/) says threat inputs help the net recognise threatened pieces; a TalkChess thread (https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?p=988632) reports a large threat net only marginally better than a small one, with a loss of eval stability and a fixed speed overhead that only pays for larger nets. Evidence for our exact variant at current scale is absent; this is weak.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +10 at 10+0.1 single thread (most likely +3), -5 if NPS loss exceeds 12%. Honest note: the engine-side fixed-node gain might be +10 to +20 but the gap is search, not evaluator.
proposals.cheap_test: Step 1 (about 6 GPU hours, no engine work): run ext/vault_probe.sh-style training of the current recipe (768 wide, 16 buckets, 1.09B positions) with --am class --amk 64 versus the r0 reference (held-out loss 0.54415); then score both with the fact-4 harness (10,334 clear cases, especially the 'quiet pairs' subset, BIGS 73.2%). Proceed only if quiet-pair accuracy rises by 0.7 points or more or held-out loss falls by 0.0010 or more. Step 2 (about 8 hours): implement in a calc_s20 copy, check NPS loss on the bench (kill if over 10%), run ext/quality.py at 300k nodes (about 9,000 positions, SE 0.3; a gain of 0.5 unit is detectable), then a 30,000-node 2,000-game match, then 1,000 games at 10+0.1. Also check fact 9: whether the hash-size-induced move change rate (19%) moves at all; stability is the claimed side benefit and costs nothing to test.

proposals.title: Threats as search/ordering features instead of net inputs: free 'threatened by lesser piece' bits for the policy/LMR/history models
proposals.mechanism: Instead of feeding threats to the evaluator, reuse the cheap per-ply attack map from proposal 1 (or just computed attacked-by-pawn/minor/rook bitboards, which most search code already builds for SEE and for Stockfish-style threat-aware history) to index the history tables: [side][from-threatened][to-threatened] (Stockfish/Obsidian-style 'threat-indexed' butterfly history) and as an extra feature in the learned LMR model. Rationale: since evaluator quality matches SF14 and the gap is search efficiency, threat information is more valuable where moves are ordered and reduced than inside the leaf eval. This also needs no retrain of BIGS.
proposals.evidence: Weak and indirect for the specific Elo. Our own fact 8: the learned LMR model reached AUC 0.907 versus 0.822 but was level in play, so ordering features alone do not guarantee gains. I did not verify Elo for threat-indexed history in Stockfish 14.1-era engines in this session; I recall it exists in Stockfish-like engines but did not obtain a fishtest number, so treat this as an unmeasured idea. No external source fetched for it.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +8 (most likely +2); only worth doing if the first proposal's attack-map array already exists
proposals.cheap_test: Add the threat index to the quiet-move history lookup only, run ext/quality.py at 300k nodes (unit threshold about 0.5 for 2 SE), then 1,000 games at 10+0.1 if it is at least -0.5 unit.

proposals.title: Store the static evaluation in the hash entry and skip the network on hits (pure speed, search unchanged)
proposals.mechanism: TTE is {U64 key; int Move; short score; uchar depth, flag} = 16 bytes with no eval field (calc_s19.c:369), and evaluate() has no cache. evaluate() calls acc_ensure() and the 768-wide dot product at every search and qsearch node, which is 65% of nodes at depth <= 1 (qsearch 32%, one ply left 33%, per README SSTAT). Change: pack Move into 16 bits (from 6, to 6, flag 4) and add a short raw_eval to TTE. In search() and qsearch(), when e->key == P.key and the stored eval is valid, use it as raw ev and skip evaluate() and the lazy accumulator update. The correction-history term in eval_corr must still be added on top (corrhist is not stored). Write the raw eval on every store, including the qsearch store at line 1533 and the probcut store at line 1638. This sets nothing in the search tree, so node counts and chosen moves stay bit-identical at fixed nodes. The gain is only nodes/s. Stockfish stores the static eval in its entry as standard design.
proposals.evidence: Weak and indirect. No eval cache exists in our code (grep of evaluate/eval_corr). The 65% shallow-node share is from README 'Where the nodes go' (SSTAT, 1M nodes). The web search found the TT-entry-with-eval layout described but no Elo figure for the speedup. The Elo estimate is my own: nodes/s +5 to +12% would be about +5 to +10 Elo at 10+0.1, using the README rule that the node deficit is ~2-3x for ~120 Elo. The hit rate on our shallow nodes is unmeasured and could be low (maybe 20-40%).
proposals.expected_elo: +3 to +12 at 10+0.1, since only speed changes
proposals.cheap_test: Step 1 (30 min): count TT hits at search and qsearch entry in a copy built with SSTAT, on the bench, to get the eval-skip rate. Step 2: implement, check the bench reports identical node counts and the quality.py moves are identical on a 1,000-position subset (the test is deterministic), then compare nodes/s with ext/nodetime.py. Go/no-go if nps rises by 4% or more. Optionally one 1,000-game 10+0.1 match against the old binary.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc_s19.c: TTE typedef line 369; tt_find/TTF 1069-1077; search 1558-1585; qsearch 1494-1504 and store 1532-1537; probcut store 1638; end-of-search store 1876-1883

proposals.title: Let late-move reductions go negative (search deeper than nd for the best-ordered moves), then retune with the 300k-node quality test
proposals.mechanism: Our reduction is clamped r = max(r, 0) and r <= nd-1 (line 1773-1774), so a reduced search is never deeper than the full-depth one. My recollection of Stockfish's LMR is that the reduced depth is clamped to [1, newDepth+1], so moves with strongly negative r (PV node, ttPv, good history, killer, check, improving) get +1 ply instead of 0. This is one of the 'which moves get reduced' differences the README says the 3x node gap lies in, since uniformly reducing more or less was worse in all 12 variants. Implementation: keep r signed with a floor of -1, run the zero-window search at nd - r (nd+1 when r = -1), and then do the same re-search logic. Optionally also add Stockfish's reduction of an extra ply when the child's fail-high count is high (cutoffCnt) as a second variant.
proposals.evidence: From my memory of Stockfish's documented LMR (not verified against any fetched source, and I did not fetch SF source). Our code at 1756-1775 shows the clamp at 0. Our README (lines 462-466, 553) shows reduction-amount sweeps are all neutral or worse, and the SF-style reduction group was -0.50 (noise-level) on the yardstick, so the signed-r change targets distribution, not amount.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +8 at 300k nodes; could be zero
proposals.cheap_test: A 10-line change gated by a new par bit (default off). Run ext/quality.py at 300,000 nodes on BIGS, 8,964 positions, paired against standing options (about 2 minutes per run, standard error ~0.3 units). Accept if the difference is <= -0.5 units. Then 1,000 games at 10+0.1 only if it passes.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc_s19.c:1756-1775 (LMR block), re-search logic 1794-1801

proposals.title: Check the two-entry bucket for a bug or interaction before concluding it is bad, and use a depth/age-gated replacement for the single-entry table
proposals.mechanism: The standing TT is one entry per slot, always replace (tt_find line 1070 returns &tt[key&mask]; TtBucket=0), and search stores overwrite regardless of depth (lines 1876-1883, except the SearchV3&64 branch). The README's stability test shows a size change moves 19% of our choices against 1.1% for Stockfish, so deep results are lost to collisions at 32 MB, while with buckets it is 1.9%. Yet the buckets play +0.72 (0.28) worse, about 2.6 sigma, which is odd for strictly more retained information. Suspects: (a) the replacement score depth - 8*age, together with qsearch depth-0 entries sharing the bucket; (b) tt cutoffs with tt_depth >= depth (line 1565) and the tt_score-as-ev substitution (1587) become more frequent and may be too aggressive when entries are retained; (c) ttpv/flag bits. Test a single-entry variant: replace only if the key matches, or the old entry's age differs, or depth_new + 2*pv + 4 > depth_old (Stockfish-style), with qsearch never replacing a deeper entry (already done) and TT cutoffs disabled when tt_depth is only at the bound and the score is a bound at the exact depth. Cheap decomposition: with TtBucket=1 try (i) turning off the tt_score-as-ev line, (ii) requiring tt_depth >= depth+1 for non-PV cutoffs, to see which part costs the 0.72.
proposals.evidence: Our own measurements: zero/results/vault_stab.log (19.0% vs 1.1% different moves for h32 vs h64; 18.5% for h512 vs h64; bucket +0.72, SE 0.28, h32 vs h64 1.9%); README lines 459-461; a tuned 'TtBucket' note near line 1062 (+19 at 1 MB/100k, -9 at 60+0.6). The 512 MB result shows even almost-no-collision tables differ from 64 MB in 18.5% of moves, so some of the 19% is plain chaos. The causal story is not established. SearchV3=64 (keep deep result) was -0.17 (better, noise-level).
proposals.expected_elo: -3 to +10; the main value is diagnostic
proposals.cheap_test: quality.py at 300,000 nodes, same set, paired, for each variant: TtBucket=1 plus (i), TtBucket=1 plus (ii), SearchV3=64 plus TtBucket=0. About 2 min each. A 100k-node SearchV3=64 repeat would also settle the -0.17.

proposals.title: Fail-high dampening plus improving fallback to ply-4 (small SF-era hygiene bundle)
proposals.mechanism: (a) At the end of search, when best >= beta, not a mate score and the cutoff move is not a capture, return (best*depth + beta)/(depth+1) instead of best (fail-soft dampening; I recall this as an SF 13/14-era commit, from memory, not verified). (b) Fix 'improving': calc_s19.c:1585 compares ev with evals_stack[ply-2], but evals_stack stores -INF when the side was in check at ply-2 (line ~1583 sets ev=-INF when chk), so improving becomes spuriously true after a check. Use ply-4 when ply-2 was in check, and treat as not-improving/true consistently with SF. Gate each by a par[] bit so they can be A/B tested separately.
proposals.evidence: Weak/indirect. Stockfish 14.1 blog says it adds 'various search improvements' for about +17 Elo vs 14 total (https://stockfishchess.org/blog/2021/stockfish-14-1/), i.e. individual patches are on the order of 1-3 Elo. Fishtest FAQ warns single-patch SPRT estimates are biased upward (https://github.com/official-stockfish/fishtest/wiki/Fishtest-faq). The improving bug is read directly from our code (calc/calc_s19.c:1583-1585). I could not retrieve the fail-high dampening commit's Elo; treat that item as recollection.

proposals.title: Isolate the 19% hash-size move instability: path-dependent scores in TT cutoffs
proposals.mechanism: Fact 9 (19% vs SF 1.1%) is far outside normal TT noise and points at a systematic leak. Candidates to toggle one at a time: (1) no non-PV TT cutoff when P.half is high (SF refuses cutoffs near the 50-move limit, I recall rule50 < ~90) and never store/return scores of nodes whose value came from a repetition or 50-move draw (graph-history interaction) without a flag; (2) require tt_depth >= depth only for cutoffs but allow the stored score as eval at lower depth, which the code already does at line 1588 - check its bound test excludes TT_UPPER/LOWER wrongly in PV; (3) replacement policy at line 1074 (depth - 8*age) overwrites deep entries too eagerly versus SF's depth-age with same-position always-replace; (4) the 'SEARCH_V3&64' keep-deep-entry rule at line 1879. Measure by running quality at Hash 16/64/256 MB and counting move changes after each toggle, aiming to cut 19% toward 5%.
proposals.evidence: Only our own fact 9 plus code reading (calc/calc_s19.c:1564-1588, 1068-1082, 1879-1882). No fishtest number: SF's TT is believed to be stable but I did not retrieve a source. Our two-entry-bucket test was +0.72 worse (maybe noise), which is itself odd and suggests a bug or a depth/age interaction rather than a design problem.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +25; high variance. If instability reflects wrong cutoffs, fixing it is the only item here that could be worth tens of Elo; if it is pure chaos from a deterministic-search butterfly effect, 0.
proposals.cheap_test: Fixed 300k-node run on the 9,000 positions at 3 hash sizes per variant, report fraction of changed best moves and the quality unit; about 20 minutes of 24-thread time per variant.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c lines 1068-1082 (TT replace/age), 1560-1588 (probe/cutoff/eval from TT), 1879-1882 (store).
