proposals.title: SPSA re-tune of the pruning/reduction margins against the quality instrument, not self-play guesses
proposals.mechanism: Stockfish's parameters (RFP, futility, razor, LMR base/div, SE margin, aspiration, history bonus) were SPSA-tuned against its own net's score scale and nodes/s; ours have been hand-varied (12 variants all slightly worse at 300k) which suggests we sit near a local optimum for one-at-a-time moves, but joint moves along correlated directions (e.g. less LMR with more pruning, or the reverse) were not tried. Run a small SPSA over about 10 par[] entries (Rfp, FutBase, FutMul, LmrBase, LmrDiv, SeMul, HbQuad, HbLin, Probcut, NmpBase) with the quality unit at 100k and 300k nodes as the objective (SE 0.3 per ~9,000 positions; use common random positions and paired evaluation).
proposals.evidence: Stockfish wiki Useful-data page: per-ply gain 90 Elo at depth 12-13 down to 52 at depth 18 (https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/wiki/Useful-data), so 2-3x nodes (our fact 3) is about 1.3-1.6 plies worth about 100 Elo, consistent with our gap; the Fishtest FAQ shows tuning plus many small patches is how SF accrues Elo. Our own fact 8 (SF-style parameter groups 'nothing established') is the counter-evidence: expect small gain.
proposals.expected_elo: +0 to +10 at the clock, quality gain of 0.5-1.0 units possible
proposals.cheap_test: Quality instrument itself: 2 x 150 SPSA iterations at about 4 minutes each on 24 threads, then confirm winner with a 1,000-game 10+0.1 match.
proposals.where_in_our_code: par[] table, calc/calc_s19.c:1015-1016 (set via setoption name <Par> value N, line 2148-2150).

summary: The main suspect is the table design: a direct-mapped, always-replace table (tt_find returns &tt[key&mask]) whose qsearch stores also evict deep entries from other positions. Evidence in vault_stab.log fits it: 2-way slots cut flips from 19% to 1.9%, while 512MB vs 64MB still flips 18.5%. But the 2-way variant (TtBucket) lost 0.72 on the quality test and ~10 Elo in matches, so the instability may be a symptom of eviction chaos and not a cause of weakness; the thing to try is a better replacement policy, with TtBucket's own loss diagnosed first. No evidence yet ties stability to Elo.
warnings: No injected instructions seen (no web pages fetched). Caveats: (1) the claim that the instability is bad for strength is unproven: the only variant that fixed it (2-way TtBucket) played worse; SF's flip rate across node budgets is as high as ours (19%), so 'stable' is not the same as 'strong'. (2) At 300k nodes with 4M entries the table is under ~7% load, so eviction chaos from always-replace is plausible but not directly measured; proposal 2 tests it. (3) Qsearch stores overwrite any different-key entry only if e->key!=P.key (line 1532), so in the single-slot path they do evict deeper entries from other positions; I did not verify the share by counter. I did not fetch Stockfish source, per the rules; the SF replacement description is from general knowledge of its documented clustered table.

proposals.title: Protect deep entries: qsearch never evicts a different-key entry with depth>0, plus same-key depth guard (single slot, then 4-way cluster)
proposals.mechanism: Step A (about 10 lines, no layout change): in qsearch store (calc_s19.c ~1532-1538) write only if e->key==P.key (existing rule: only when e->depth==0) or e->key==0 or e->depth==0. Never replace a different-key entry that has depth>0. Qsearch nodes are most of the 300k nodes and each one currently evicts whatever sits in its slot (always-replace, line 1070 when TtBucket=0). In the main store (~1876-1882) add an SF-style guard: for same key, overwrite only if bound is exact, or new depth + 2 >= old depth, or old age differs. SearchV3&64 is a cruder form of this (4-ply margin) and may already be testable. Step B: if A helps stability but not quality, build a 4-entry cluster in one 64-byte line (16-byte TTE, 4 per line, aligned), victim = min(depth - 8*ageDiff), qsearch entries always lowest priority. Keep tt_age/TTF as is. Rationale: TtBucket=2-way was worse in play, so first remove the likely cause of that regression (qsearch/shallow entries and same-key shallow overwrites competing with deep ones) instead of adding ways.
proposals.evidence: vault_stab.log (/home/user/seek/zero/results/vault_stab.log): 64MB vs 32MB flips our move 19.0%, vs 512MB 18.5%; with TtBucket the 32MB vs 64MB flip is 1.9% (tb_h32 vs tb); SF (3-way clusters, depth/age replacement) 1.1%. Load at 300k nodes is ~5-7% of a 4M-entry table, so a direct-mapped table loses a few percent of entries and each loss re-routes the search chaotically; 2-way makes triple collisions rare, matching 19%->1.9%. Caveat: TtBucket was +0.72 (0.28) worse and -9/-10 Elo in matches (calc_s19.c comment above tt_find), so stability alone is not worth Elo; cause of that regression is unknown. Weak: no measurement yet of how many evictions of depth>0 entries come from qsearch.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +8 at 10+0.1; most likely about 0 (the stability gap may be cosmetic). Gain only if lost deep entries cost quality; the +19 Elo at 1 MB / 100k positions says entry loss matters under pressure, but 64MB is not under pressure.
proposals.cheap_test: 1) Run ext/quality.py at 300k nodes, hash 64 vs 32, for baseline vs Step A vs Step B; report 'different move %' and mean loss (SE ~0.3). Target: flips under 3% and loss no worse than baseline (10.04). 2) Add a SSTAT counter of stores that evict a different-key entry with depth>0, split qsearch vs main, to confirm qsearch share. 3) If quality is equal or better, a 1000-game 10+0.1 match vs SF 14.1 (SPRT-ish vs current).

proposals.title: Diagnose before fixing: 512MB vs 1024MB flip rate, hash-seed-only flip rate, and why TtBucket plays worse
proposals.mechanism: Three runs of ext/quality.py at 300k nodes, no engine change except one temporary env var. (a) 512 vs 1024 MB: if flips fall to ~1-2%, collision loss is confirmed as the cause; if still ~15%, instability comes from something else (index-dependent noise, graph-history/repetition scores stored in TT, depth-limited TT cutoffs without depth margin, or the aspiration/timing path) and fix 1 is the wrong lever. (b) Same 64MB but a different Zobrist seed: measures the chaos floor from collision pattern alone. (c) TtBucket=1 with replacement ablations to find what made it worse (victim choice ignoring age, qsearch victim = deep entry, ttpv flag handling, same-key overwrite): run each at 300k nodes, 64MB. Also check whether the 0.72 loss is just 2.6 sigma noise by re-running with a second position subset.
proposals.evidence: vault_stab.log shows 303000 vs 300000 nodes flips only 0.1% (so search is deterministic and chaos enters only via hash differences), 512MB vs 64MB 18.5%, SF 300k vs 1M nodes flips 19.2% (so SF is not generally rigid, only against table size). No existing run compares two near-collision-free sizes, so the collision hypothesis is untested directly.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 directly (diagnostic); it prevents spending hours on a wrong fix.
proposals.cheap_test: Three quality.py runs (about 2 min each at 300k nodes per vault_stab.log timings: 105-283 s) plus a one-line seed override.

proposals.title: Retest TT cutoff conditions: depth margin and PV handling at non-PV nodes
proposals.mechanism: At calc_s19.c:1565 the non-PV cutoff fires when tt_depth >= depth and the bound matches, with no extra requirement and no check that a LOWER-bound cutoff on a quiet ttm also needs ttm legality. Try SF-style variants one at a time: (i) require tt_depth > depth - 1 only for EXACT bounds and tt_depth >= depth+1 for bounds near the window (e.g. skip the cutoff if the score is within ~margin of beta/alpha and a PV ancestor exists); (ii) do not take TT cutoffs at nodes whose ttpv flag is set (position seen on a main line, bit 2 of flag) when depth is small; (iii) also apply the TT score as refined eval only if tt_depth>=depth-1 (line 1587 uses any depth). The goal is fewer cutoffs driven by entries of marginal reliability, reducing sensitivity to which entries survive.
proposals.evidence: No direct measurement in this repo; the idea follows the observation that flips come from which entries are present. Weak evidence; included because TT cutoff policy is the other half of the TT-sensitivity path. NmpTT, TtCapLmr, PV flags already exist (README.md:354 lists TtBucket=1 at -217 vs baseline -214 to -220 at tested conditions, i.e. within noise at that setting).
proposals.expected_elo: -3 to +4; low expectation
proposals.cheap_test: Add as par bits under PRUNE_V2 or OFF; run quality.py at 300k nodes with hash 32/64 for flips and loss; drop if loss is not <= baseline - 0.3.

summary: Ordering is already decent (82% of move-loop cutoffs on the first move at 300k nodes, README.md:173) and every ordering change tried so far (HistV2 bits, ThrHist) helped at 10k nodes and lost at the clock; the likeliest reason is that hist_score() also feeds LMR and pruning (calc_s19.c:1417 -> hs at 1692/1715/1768), so "better ordering" changes were confounded with shifted reduction and pruning scales. The most useful next step is to decouple an ordering-only score from the pruning/LMR history, and to log first-move cutoff rate and cutoff-move rank by stage to see where the headroom is. Honest prior: the realistic ordering headroom is small, perhaps 0 to +15 Elo in total, and not the 120 Elo gap.
warnings: No injected instructions seen. Web search returned only community pages (chessprogramming.org, nextchessmove dev builds); no authoritative Elo numbers for Stockfish's pawn history or low-ply history, so none are claimed. I did not read the pending PolW/PolLmr run; if it is positive it covers part of proposal 1's learned-weight idea (transformer logprob as an ordering term, already in the code at line 1403). Note HistV2, ThrHist, PruneV2 defaults are all 0 in par[] (calc_s19.c:1020), so the standing engine uses only main + 1-ply + 2-ply histories with quadratic bonus 5d^2+33d capped at 1322, which is small next to a 16384 gravity cap. HbQuad=6,HbLin=229,HbMax=4167 (SF-like) scored -0.37 at 100k (README.md:554), so bonus size is not an obvious lever.

proposals.title: Decouple ordering score from LMR/pruning history, then re-test HistV2 bits and a learned weighting
proposals.mechanism: Add ord_score(m,ply) used only in ST_GENQUIET scoring (calc_s19.c:1403) and the cmove slot. It sums main history + cmh*2 + fuh + ch4 + ch6 (the HistV2=1 form). Keep p->hist / hs (line 1417, used at 1692, 1697, 1715, 1768) as the old 3-term hist_score() so pruning thresholds (HistPrune=4245, LmrHist=8192) keep the scale they were tuned for. Maintain ch4/ch6 updates unconditionally. Then test ord_score variants: (a) HistV2 bits 1,2 (ordering only), (b) weights fitted offline by logistic regression: log, at every cutoff node with no TT move, a feature vector per quiet move (main, cmh, fuh, ch4, ch6, is-killer, gives-check, from/to attacked, transformer logprob) with the cutoff move as label, fit one weight vector, plug it back in. Do not enable HistV2=4 (-15 at 100k nodes) or 16 (-14). Pawn history (table keyed by pawn hash & 8191, piece, to; used by newer Stockfish, idea from Seer) can be added as one extra term in the same ord_score; it is a Stockfish 15+ feature, not in 14.1.
proposals.evidence: Confound is read from the code: p->hist = hist_score(...) at calc_s19.c:1417 feeds pruning (1692, 1697, 1715) and LMR (1768); HistV2=1 changes hist_score by double-counting cmh and adding ch4/ch6 (1145-1151), so it shifts those scales. Measured pattern: HistV2=7 +19 at 10k nodes but -10 at 30k, -9 at 100k, -18 at 10+0.1 (ext/README.md:154-167, 422-423). HistV2=1 alone +1 at 100k; the 100k loss is attributed to HistV2=4. The follow-up PruneV2=1 (history pruning) lost -36, consistent with history magnitude being tuned against pruning. This is an inference, not a measurement; weak-to-medium evidence. Pawn history: Stockfish commit from 2023 per community sources (chessprogramming.org/stockfish; no Elo figure found).
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +10 at 10+0.1 (honest range -3 to +12); at 300k nodes about 0 to +0.4 quality units
proposals.cheap_test: Quality instrument at 100k and 300k nodes (SE about 0.3 per ext/quality.py): run old vs ord_score variants; also record first-move cutoff rate with -DSSTAT (ST(8), ST(9) already count cutoffs and first-move cutoffs). Then 1,000-game match at 10+0.1 only if quality gain at 300k is at least 0.5 units.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c:1144-1167 (hist_score/cont_update), 1401-1405 (quiet scoring), 1417 (p->hist), 1821-1823 (updates)

proposals.title: Measure first: cutoff statistics by stage, depth and rank, and replay ordering offline
proposals.mechanism: Extend the existing SSTAT counters (calc_s19.c:1811 region). At each beta cutoff record: stage that produced the cutoff move (TT, good capture, killer0/1, cmove, quiet rank index among quiets, bad capture), node depth bucket, cutnode flag, whether a TT move existed. Report first-move cutoff rate separately for nodes with TT move, nodes without (IIR nodes), cutnodes vs allnodes, and mean rank of the cutoff move among quiets. Also count all-nodes (fail-low) where every move was searched, and the number of quiets searched before cutoff at depth >= 4. Add an oracle upper bound: with a hit of rank 1, compute nodes saved if the cutoff move were always first (nodes spent in earlier siblings of cutoff moves, sum over nodes where legal>1; add that subtree node count by snapshotting the node counter before each move). That 'wasted siblings' share bounds what any ordering change can buy.
proposals.evidence: README already gives 82% first-move cutoffs at 300k (README.md:173) but no split by TT move/depth/stage; ST(33)-ST(39) counters already separate ttm/no-ttm and killer cutoffs, so the extra code is about 30 lines. No evidence yet of how much of the 2-3x node gap is wasted siblings; this is the number to get before spending hours on ordering features. Stockfish-side comparison cannot be measured without fetching its source (not allowed), so compare with published folk numbers only (about 90% first-move cutoffs at well-ordered nodes, unverified).
proposals.expected_elo: 0 directly (diagnostic); decides whether proposals 1 and 3 are worth running
proposals.cheap_test: Build with -DSSTAT, run bench/quality positions at 300k nodes (about 1.5 min), compare same counters with Stockfish-network (EvalScale=140) search to see if ordering differs by network; compute wasted-sibling nodes share.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c:1047-1062 (SSTAT macros), 1805-1835 (cutoff block), 1343-1435 (mp_next stage)

proposals.title: Make ThrHist cheap (its ordering gain is real at equal nodes but its time cost ate it)
proposals.mechanism: ThrHist=1 indexes history by whether from/to squares are attacked by the opponent (calc_s19.c:1099-1101) and needs attacks_by(side^1) at every node (1575). Compute thr_stack[ply] lazily: only at the first call of ST_GENQUIET scoring and in the cutoff update, and not at nodes that end by reverse futility, null move or TT cutoff before the move loop (line 1575 currently computes it before those, whenever ThrHist is on). Also at depth 1-2 nodes (about 47% of main nodes, README.md:540) compute from the already available check_info/attack bitboards or skip the threat index (use slot 0). Then re-enable ThrHist=1.
proposals.evidence: ThrHist=1 gave -202 vs -218 baseline against Stockfish at equal nodes, 4,000 games (ext/README.md:323), i.e. about +16 Elo at 10k nodes, but -9 (-21 to +3) at 10+0.1 vs standing options because of time cost. 60% of main nodes end by reverse futility (README.md:173), where the attack map computed at line 1575 is wasted. Depth caveat: the +16 was measured at shallow depth, where HistV2 also looked good and later reversed, so the deep gain may be near zero.
proposals.expected_elo: -3 to +8 at 10+0.1 (more likely +2); recovers the time cost, keeps whatever ordering gain survives at depth
proposals.cheap_test: Speed bench (nodes/s with ThrHist 0 vs 1 vs lazy) first; then quality test at 100k and 300k nodes ThrHist lazy vs off; match only if quality at 300k is negative (better) by at least 0.5 units.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c:1101 (HIST macro), 1569-1575 (thr_stack set before move loop), 1401-1403

summary: Our four correction tables (pawn, per-side non-pawn, previous-move, minor/major) are combined by lossy averaging (calc_s19.c:1136-1140), a combination that modern engines do not use. NpCorr=0 measured +17 Elo at 30k nodes, which suggests the blend dilutes the pawn term. The expected gain from fixing this is small (+3 to +10 Elo at the clock), and the web evidence is weak: the chessprogramming wiki page cites no Elo numbers for any variant. The proposals are cheap to test and cannot explain more than a few Elo of the 120 Elo search gap.
warnings: The chessprogramming wiki page for correction history cites no Elo numbers. I did not find fishtest/SPRT numbers, so every external Elo claim is absent rather than weak. Our own evidence is at 30k nodes per move, and fact 5 shows such gains can vanish at 300k nodes and the clock. Fetched pages contained no injected instructions. I did not check licences because I read no engine source.

proposals.title: Additive weighted correction sum instead of averaging, with per-table weights
proposals.mechanism: In eval_corr (calc_s19.c:1136) drop the nested averaging (2*c+np0+np1)/4 and (3*c+cont)/4. Compute corr = (wP*pawn + wNp*(npW+npB) + wMm*(minor+major) + wCont*cont)/256 with independent weights, as modern engines do. Make wP, wNp, wCont new par[] options. Keep the update rule. Then SPSA the 4-5 weights (SPSA infrastructure exists: zero/spsa_clock.py, with MmCorr already tuned to 173). The expected gain is mainly un-diluting the pawn term and letting NpCorr be useful instead of harmful.
proposals.evidence: Internal: NpCorr=0 gives +17 (-4 to +38) at 30k nodes, which means the current averaged NP term hurts (zero/results/search_lab_tests.log:13). MmCorr=256 gives +14.9 at 30k nodes (zero/results/lab_s15.log:2) and SPSA settled on 173. ContCorr gives +5, undecided (search_lab_tests.log:5). Together these suggest the tables carry signal that the blending wastes. External evidence is weak: the chessprogramming wiki page on static evaluation correction history (chessprogramming.org/Static_Evaluation_Correction_History) says pawn, minor, major, non-pawn and continuation tables are all in use but gives no Elo numbers. I did not read Stockfish source, per the rules.
proposals.expected_elo: +3 to +10 at 10+0.1 (single thread). It could be 0, because the gains seen at 30k nodes shrink at 300k, as the transformer prior did.
proposals.cheap_test: Quality test at 300k nodes on the 9,000 positions (SE ~0.3 units, so a gain of at least 0.15 units is detectable only with repeats). Then the existing 30k-nodes-per-move self-play lab (about 2 minutes per 2,000 games) against current default, then a 10+0.1 match of 1,000 games.

proposals.title: Two-ply continuation correction (previous two moves) and separate minor/major tables per side
proposals.mechanism: Two changes. (a) Key corr_cont by the pair (piece,to of ply-1 move, piece,to of ply-2 move), a table of size 768*768 int16. At present only the ply-1 move is used (corr_cont[side][12][64], line 1133), with weight 3:1. (b) Split corr_mm into four tables keyed per colour (minor+king of white, minor+king of black, and the same for majors) so one side's change does not clear the other's entry. Right now mmkey XORs both colours together, so only the pair (both sides' minors) is the key. Keep updates the same style.
proposals.evidence: Internal: the mmkey definition (line 92, 205-206) mixes both colours. The ply-1-only continuation correction measured +5, undecided at 1500 games (search_lab_tests.log:5). Per the wiki page, continuation correction in Motor is indexed by the previous move and the move before it, and non-pawn correction is kept per side. No Elo numbers are available for either, so this is a design inference.
proposals.expected_elo: +0 to +5 at the clock
proposals.cheap_test: Quality test at 30k and 300k nodes on the 9,000 positions, then the 30k-nodes-per-move self-play match of 2,000 games. Run it only after proposal 1, because the weights interact.

proposals.title: Update rule: bonus with gravity and depth scaling instead of EMA with weight depth+1 capped at 16/256
proposals.mechanism: At lines 1854-1872, replace c = (c*(256-w)+d*w)/256 with a depth-scaled bonus, bonus = clamp((best - raw_ev)*depth/8*256, -limit/4, limit/4), and c += bonus - c*abs(bonus)/limit, with limit tuned. A second variant uses the EMA weight w = min(depth*depth+2*depth+1, 128) (the Alexandria form listed on the wiki page) instead of the current cap of 16. Currently the cap at 16 means a deep search moves the table by at most 1/16 per update, which is slow to adapt, especially with 64 MB hash and a 10+0.1 game of ~140 plies. Also test growing the table index from 16384 to 65536 entries, since 14 bits collide on pawn and mm keys.
proposals.evidence: The wiki page documents both update forms (gravity as in Stockfish, EMA with weight capped at 128 as in Alexandria). I have no Elo comparison between them. Our weight cap of 16/256 is the low end. Evidence that the rule matters is weak, so this is a guess.
proposals.cheap_test: A one-line option for each variant, then the quality test at 300k nodes and a 30k-nodes-per-move match of 1,000 games. Run it after proposal 1.

summary: Our singular-extension code (calc_s19.c:1664-1675) is already close to Stockfish 14.1-style design. It has a depth floor of 7 (SeDepth), a margin of 2*depth (SeMul), a half-depth excluded search, and a multi-cut return of sbeta. It also has an optional double extension (SeDouble, default 0) and an optional single negative extension (NegExt, default 0). The singular tests are only ~4% of nodes (ext/README.md:542). Our own sweeps found nothing: SeDepth=6 -212, SeDouble=0 -220 and NegExt=1 -217 against a -218 reference, all within +-10 (README:352-355). The SF-values bundle SeMul=1,SeDouble=29,NegExt=1 is +0.08 units on the search-only yardstick, which is noise (README:556). This angle is unlikely to hold the 2-3x efficiency gap. The only unmeasured, plausible items are a hash-instability diagnostic and a small SF-style refinement (-2 negative extension plus a double-extension counter). I did no web fetching, so every comparison to Stockfish below is from memory and unverified.
warnings: I did no web research for this angle, so all Stockfish 14.1 details (-2 negative extension, the doubleExtensions counter, depth floor, margin) are recalled from memory and not verified. I also did not fetch Stockfish source, per the rules. No injected instructions were seen in the files I read. One correctness note from reading the code: the excluded search reuses cutn[ply] and recomputes the static eval at the same ply, which costs a small amount per test but looks harmless. In the singular search the null move is disallowed (allow_null=0), which matches the usual practice.

proposals.title: Diagnose how much of the 19% hash-size move instability the singular test causes
proposals.mechanism: No code change needed. Run the existing hash-size instability measurement (fact 9) at 300k nodes with the default options, then again with Off=256 (singular tests off, calc_s19.c:1665). Compare the fraction of chosen moves that change between 64 MB and 256 MB. Singular tests are the most TT-dependent decision: they need m==ttm, tt_depth>=depth-3, a LOWER or EXACT flag, and tt_score as the margin base. A change in table contents therefore flips whether the test runs, its margin, and the +1/-1 extension. A second run with Off=1 (no null move) and Off=512 (no IIR) would show which TT-dependent rule dominates. If singular tests account for a large share of the flips, stabilise them. Options: require tt_depth>=depth (not depth-3), or ignore the flag EXACT case, or skip the test when the entry's age or bucket replacement is suspect.
proposals.evidence: Fact 9 (19% vs Stockfish's 1.1%) is the strongest unexplained symptom. In ext/README.md:564-569, 'without singular tests' solves 36% vs ~48% for other variants, but the README itself says that set is a coin toss, so this proves nothing. There is no measurement of which rule drives the instability, so the evidence is weak and this is a diagnostic, not a gain claim. The code at calc_s19.c:1558-1566 and :1587-1588 shows the TT also feeds cutoffs and the eval substitution, so singular may be a minor source.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +5 directly. Value is mostly in locating the instability source; if the instability is real search noise, fixing it could be worth more, but that is speculative.
proposals.cheap_test: Existing instability script, 3 configurations (default, Off=256, Off=512) on the same ~1,000 positions at 300k nodes. About 1 CPU-hour.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c:1665-1675 (singular block), :1558-1588 (TT use); Off bit 256 is already wired.

proposals.title: Stockfish-style negative extension of -2 plus a double-extension counter
proposals.mechanism: Replace the single -1 case at line 1674 with a graded rule: if tt_score>=beta, ext=-2; else if cutnode, ext=-1. Also replace the 'ply < 2*root_depth' guard on double extension with a per-ply counter dext[ply] = dext[ply-1] + (ext==2), allowing a double only when dext[ply-1] <= 2 and !pv_node, with SeDouble around 25-30. As I recall, Stockfish 14.1 uses -2 for ttValue>=beta and a doubleExtensions counter. Both are from memory, not verified. Implement as new bits under an option (for example NegExt=2) so the default stays unchanged. Note that nd = depth-1+ext at line 1752, so -2 gives nd = depth-3, and the LMR clamp r<=nd-1 at line 1774 must tolerate nd<=0. Clamp nd>=0.
proposals.evidence: Weak. Our own NegExt=1 at 10k nodes is -217 vs -218 (README:354) and SeDouble=0 is -220, both level. The bundle SeMul=1,SeDouble=29,NegExt=1 is +0.08 units (README:556), also level. The graded variant is untested. Stockfish's fishtest gains for these tweaks were individually around +1 to +3 Elo (recalled, unverified), below our measurement resolution (SE 0.3 units = ~12 Elo).
proposals.cheap_test: Quality instrument at 300k nodes on the 9,000 positions, comparing the default, NegExt=2, and SeDouble=25 with the counter. Needs a differential of >=0.5 unit to detect, so run twice with different position subsets. A match is not worth the hours unless the quality test shows <= -0.5 units.

proposals.title: Lower SeDepth to 4-5 and test a margin tied to PV status at 300k nodes
proposals.mechanism: Parameter-only test, no code change. Sweep SeDepth in {4,5,6,7} and SeMul in {1,2,3}, with SeDouble=0. Our only SeDepth data point is SeDepth=6 at 10k nodes on a weaker net (README:354). Newer Stockfish lowers the floor to about 4 plus a PV bonus (recalled from memory, unverified). At depth 4-5 the excluded search is depth 1-2, so test cost is tiny, but each test only has value if the TT move is trustworthy at that depth, which the tt_depth>=depth-3 guard already enforces.
proposals.evidence: Weak. A single data point at SeDepth=6 gives -212 vs -218 (+6, within +-10, README:354). Nothing at 300k nodes where the gap is largest (fact 3). No other measured evidence for our engine.
proposals.cheap_test: Quality instrument at 300k nodes, 4 SeDepth values x 3 SeMul values, 12 runs at about 15 minutes each. Run only the SeDepth values first (4 runs); pursue SeMul only if a trend of >=0.4 units appears.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c:1020 (par defaults: SeDepth=7, SeMul=2 at indices 11 and 12), :1665-1667.

summary: Our LMR is already close to SF14's shape. Its log-log table is base 0.68 plus ln(d)·ln(i)/2.40 against SF14's roughly 0.40·ln·ln plus about 1.4. It has the same list of adjustments, and re-search with deeper/shallower is in place (Deeper=0 measured -51 Elo, 198 games). It lacks three things Stockfish has and fishtest measured: history updates from the outcome of the post-LMR re-search, PV-node reduction from the second move (we reduce from the fourth), and the ply-4 fallback in "improving". Reduction amounts are a measured dead end here (12 variants, all worse), so the proposals change which moves get reduced and how history is trained. LmrHist=0 changed nothing (-2.3 Elo, CI -16 to +11), against about 30 Elo for statScore in SF; that points at weak history signal, not a wrong reduction table.
warnings: 1) I did not read Stockfish source (instruction). SF14 formula details (Reductions constants, the 14721 statScore divisor, the moveCount>1+2*rootNode rule, the post-LMR continuation update) are from memory and the public wiki/commit titles seen in search snippets; confirm before trusting the exact constants. 2) The SF regression-wiki Elo numbers are 1-thread STC/LTC results on SF's own code and often include several effects at once; our own record says that SF parameter groups in our frame make things worse (+0.66 units, README lines 545-560), so expect small or null transfer. 3) Our quality instrument SE (0.3 units, about 12 Elo) is as large as the expected effects, so each test needs two seeds or the Stockfish-net yardstick before a match. 4) No injected instructions were seen in the fetched pages (SF wiki regression page, search results). 5) I did not reach the 14.1-era part of the regression page that lists statScore, doDeeper and rootDelta entries; the page is long and the fetches covered chars 100000-300000 only. 6) The rootDelta term in SF14's reduction, which lowers reduction in wide-window nodes and lifts it in narrow ones, is not in ours and was not proposed. In zero-window nodes it is a constant, and the amount-of-reduction scans were negative.

proposals.title: Update continuation histories from the post-LMR re-search outcome
proposals.mechanism: In calc_s19.c, in the block `if (v > alpha && r)` (about line 1794-1800), after the re-search value v2 is known for a quiet move: bonus = min(HB_MAX, HB_QUAD*nd*nd + HB_LIN*nd) with nd the re-search depth. Apply +bonus if v2 > alpha and -bonus otherwise, via cont_update() to every continuation table hist_score() reads (cmh at ply-1, fuh at ply-2, ch4 and ch6 when HistV2 is on). Optionally add +25% for killers. This is SF's 'update_continuation_histories after LMR re-search' rule. It trains the tables on the question LMR asks, namely whether a late move that looked good at reduced depth really is good. Then re-test LmrHist (8192 vs 4096 vs 12288), because the current history-in-LMR scale has no measurable effect and a better-trained history should make it matter. A capture variant would do the same with caph (see proposal 3).
proposals.evidence: Stockfish regression-test page (https://official-stockfish.github.io/docs/stockfish-wiki/Regression-Tests.html): 'Do stats updates after LMR for captures' 2022-01-29 +32.07 ±1.0 (1 thread, https://tests.stockfishchess.org/tests/view/61f4f474f7fba9f1a4f17837). The quiet version has been in SF since about v11 (my recollection, not re-verified). The StratChess history-adjusted-LMR issue shows the same idea elsewhere, but I read no Elo numbers there. Our evidence: zero/results/search_lab_tests.log line 9 shows LmrHist=0 at -2.3 Elo (-16 to +11), so history currently buys almost nothing in LMR, while SF's statScore term is worth about 30 Elo (the Stockfish commit c82f6f5 comment, seen in search snippets only). Evidence is indirect. The 32 Elo figure may bundle other changes and is measured at STC.
proposals.expected_elo: +3 to +10 at 10+0.1 if it works; plausibly 0. The quality instrument will probably show -0.1 to -0.3 units at 300k nodes.
proposals.cheap_test: Quality test at 300k nodes on the 9,000 positions with the BIGS net, baseline vs patch (SE about 0.3, so use two seeds or the Stockfish-net yardstick at 100k). Then LmrHist divisor sweep with the patch on. If it is positive, run a 1,000-game 10+0.1 match. Cost is one new quality run of about 10 minutes of CPU.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c lines 1794-1801 (re-search branch), cont_update at about line 1160, hist_score at line 1144, bonus formula at line 1821. LMR_HIST use at line 1768.

proposals.title: Start reducing at the second move in PV nodes (legal > 1, not legal > 3)
proposals.mechanism: Line 1756 requires `legal > 1 + 2 * pv_node`, so in PV nodes the first three moves are searched at full depth. SF's rule, as I remember it from SF 11 to 14 and not re-checked in source, is `moveCount > 1 + 2*rootNode`: PV nodes reduce from move 2 with `r--` for PvNode, and only the root waits until move 4. Our root is handled separately by ROOT_LMR. Change to `legal > 1 + 2 * (ply == 0)` with the existing `if (pv_node) r--`, or add a parameter PvLmrFrom with values 1 (SF) and 3 (ours). Pair it with a parameter for the PV term, r -= 1 or r -= 0, so the net PV reduction can vary. Also make the same switch in the `want`/`ls_ok` condition at line 1706 and the learned-model branch at line 1778 so the three conditions stay consistent.
proposals.evidence: Rule recalled from memory of SF 11 to 14 behaviour and from the public wiki descriptions of LMR; I did not fetch source (instruction not to fetch Stockfish source). Fishtest: 'Decrease LMR at PV nodes with low depth' 2022-04-17 +36.69 and 'Simplify PV node reduction' 2024-02-17 +27.04 show PV-node reduction is tuned carefully and matters (https://tests.stockfishchess.org/tests/view/625d156dff677a888877d1be, https://tests.stockfishchess.org/tests/view/65d666051d8e83c78bfddbd6). Weak against us: our measured finding that reducing more is worse at 300k nodes (ext/README.md lines 461-468, twelve variants worse), and PV nodes are a small share of nodes, so the effect may be tiny. SF's win in those tests came from reducing less in some PV cases, so the net sign for us is uncertain.
proposals.expected_elo: -5 to +8; most likely about 0 to +3.
proposals.cheap_test: A one-line option. Quality instrument at 100k and 300k nodes, both with BIGS and on the Stockfish-net yardstick (ext/sf_bundle.sh). Accept only if both are at least 0.3 units better. About 15 minutes of CPU per arm.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c line 1756 (condition), line 1764 (`if (pv_node) r--`), line 1706 (`want` condition), line 1778 (SEL branch).

proposals.title: Capture-history statScore for late captures, plus ply-4 fallback in 'improving'
proposals.mechanism: Two small changes where our LMR is cruder than SF's. (a) Late captures: line 1770 uses a constant, `r -= bad_now ? 1 : 2`. Replace it with a scale from caph[piece][to][victim]: r -= clamp(caph / CapHistDiv, -2, 2), with CapHistDiv about 4000 to start, and keep the bad-capture offset of one. This is SF's 'adjust statscore for captures' idea. (b) 'improving': line 1585 compares ev with evals_stack[ply-2], and that slot holds -INF when ply-2 was in check, so improving is always true there. Fall back to ply-4 when ply-2 was in check, as SF does. Also try letting `improving` shrink the reduction table in the same way SF's reduction() gives !improving an extra plus one only when the base reduction is large (`!i && r > 1010`), which means !improving gets +1 only for large reductions. Our code adds +1 for every non-improving move at line 1758.
proposals.evidence: Fishtest: 'Adjust statscore for captures' 2024-11-13 +11.88 (https://tests.stockfishchess.org/tests/view/6735001986d5ee47d953ea7c); 'Refine improving-logic' 2019-12-10 +47.27 at 1 thread and +56.62 at 8 threads (https://tests.stockfishchess.org/tests/view/5def70363cff9a249bb9e4c5). I could not confirm from the wiki text that the 2019 test is exactly the ply-4 fallback, so treat that part as a guess. Source: https://official-stockfish.github.io/docs/stockfish-wiki/Regression-Tests.html. Both come from engines with other features (capture history in stat score) that may not carry over. In ours, 'Do LMR for more captures' (+46 in SF 2019) corresponds to CapLmr, which is already on.
proposals.expected_elo: +2 to +8 for the pair; improving fix alone 0 to +3.
proposals.cheap_test: Two separate options. Quality instrument at 300k with BIGS. The improving fix is a 5-line change and can go through a quick 100k yardstick run first; the capture scale needs a CapHistDiv sweep (3000, 6000, 12000). About 20 minutes of CPU per arm.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c line 1585 (improving), line 1758 (!improving r++), line 1770 (capture reduction), caph table used at line 1704.

summary: Our null move (calc_s19.c:1602-1613: R = 3 + depth/4 + min(3,(ev-beta)/191), depth>=3, ev>=beta, no verification, no cutnode/previous-null gating beyond allow_null) and ProbCut (lines 1619-1643, structurally the same as Stockfish's, but the ProbCut option defaults to 0, i.e. OFF) are already close to the standard recipe, and the repo's own sweeps (NmpBase/NmpDiv/NmpMargin -0.14, ProbCut=150 neutral at 4,000 games, Rfp+ProbCut bundle +0.57 worse) show parameter retuning here is a dead end. The only untested, well-evidenced idea is Stockfish's later "small ProbCut" (TT lower bound >= beta+margin at depth >= depth-3 returns immediately, about +4 Elo per Stockfish's own annotations), which is cheap but a small effect that our 300k-node quality instrument (SE ~0.3 units = ~12 Elo) cannot resolve; expect at most a few Elo, and do not expect it to close a 120-Elo search gap.
warnings: 1) Our ProbCut option is OFF by default (par default 0 at calc_s19.c:1020), so the current search has no ProbCut at all; the README sweeps tested only ProbCut=150 and 81, never 100 (Stockfish 14's 209 internal units is about 100 cp) and never alone with a depth-dependent margin. 2) Not verified from sources: exact current Stockfish null-move constants; I did not fetch Stockfish source per instruction and the web search returned only commit-message Elo estimates (author's, not SPRT results I inspected). 3) The chessprogramming.org pages and search results contained no injected instructions. 4) All Elo estimates from Stockfish commits are measured at Stockfish's strength/time controls with tuned neighbours; our 300k-node quality instrument cannot resolve effects under about 10 Elo, so every proposal in this angle needs a match, not just a quality test. 5) Our null move returns v unclamped except for mate scores and has no verification; given fact 9 (19% chosen-move change from table size alone) the null-move subtrees' TT stores of depth-1-R entries are one possible source of instability, but I have no measurement for that.

proposals.title: Small ProbCut: return beta+margin straight from a deep TT lower bound
proposals.mechanism: Right after the TT probe/eval in search() (before the null move block), add: if (!pv_node && !excl && tt_flag is TT_LOWER or TT_EXACT && tt_depth >= depth-3 && tt_score >= probbeta && |tt_score| < MATE_IN && depth>=? (any)) return probbeta, where probbeta = beta + M and M ~ 180-190 centipawns (our pawn=100; Stockfish's later constant 390 internal units is ~1.9 pawns). Start with M=190 and try 150 and 230. Optionally also apply the same shortcut when in check (Stockfish added an in-check version, also ~4 Elo). It costs nothing in nodes: it only converts TT hits that the normal cutoff test rejects because tt_depth < depth into cutoffs. Also keep the existing full ProbCut off (ProbCut=0) for the baseline, then test ProbCut=100 together with it.
proposals.evidence: Stockfish commit 57e06be 'A small Probcut idea (~4 Elo)' https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/commit/57e06be71f0177a69843750a9f456462d02f23b9 ; in-check variant 'Probcut in check no matter if pv or capture (~4 Elo)' https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/commit/6138a0fd0e43753a86e4a170a5f6e2b7b6752677 ; margin later tuned in VVLTC tune commits (e.g. d99f895). Elo numbers are the author's fishtest estimates (I did not open the fishtest runs), and the effect was measured in Stockfish's own, differently tuned search, not ours. Our own full ProbCut was neutral (ext/README.md:353, ProbCut=150 -217 vs -218 baseline over 4,000 games), so weak evidence it transfers. This also changes the TT-hit behaviour that fact 9 (hash instability) says is already fragile, so check that the chosen-move change rate with table size does not get worse.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +4 (point estimate +1.5); in the stated 10+0.1 single-thread setting it is likely not measurable within one 1,000-game match (SE about 12 Elo)
proposals.cheap_test: Quality test at 100k and 300k nodes on the 9,000 positions, M in {150,190,230}: accept only if the delta is <= -0.2 units at both budgets (paired, same positions). Also record from -DSSTAT how often the new return fires (expect 0.5 to 3% of main nodes) and the node-to-depth change. Only if it passes, run one 1,000-game 10+0.1 match against the baseline (self-match is much tighter than vs Stockfish).
proposals.where_in_our_code: /home/user/seek/calc/calc_s19.c: insert after line 1588 (ev refined by TT) and before line 1590/1595; reuse tt_flag, tt_depth, tt_score already computed at 1560-1564; add a new par entry (e.g. SmallPc) at the end of the enum at line 1015, par_name at 1016 and default array at line 1020.

proposals.title: Gate the null move with cheap success predictors (cutnode, eval >= static eval, previous-move history) and measure it per feature
proposals.mechanism: Currently every non-PV node with depth>=3 and ev>=beta tries a null move; it succeeds only 41-49% of the time and 17-20% of all nodes are spent inside null-move subtrees (ext/README.md:175, 541). Add three optional gates, each its own bit in a new option: (1) require cutnode (cutn[ply]) for the null move, since a null fail-high at an expected ALL node is unreliable and expensive when it fails; (2) require raw ev (the static value, before the TT refinement at line 1588) >= beta as well as refined ev, i.e. skip when the TT says the position is worse than the static eval (a more complete form of NmpTt, which only checks TT_UPPER with score < beta); (3) skip when the previous opponent quiet move has a high continuation-history score (Stockfish 14+ uses (ss-1)->statScore < threshold). Before testing, log with -DSSTAT the null success rate and subtree size split by cutnode, depth, (ev-beta) bucket and previous-move history bucket; gate only the cells with success rate clearly below ~30%. Do not implement verification search: Hyatt found it does nothing and at 300k nodes depth >= 14 is reached only near the root.
proposals.evidence: Mechanism/features follow Stockfish's null-move conditions (cutNode and staticEval/statScore gates in later Stockfish versions, from my memory of the source; I was told not to fetch the Stockfish source, so I could not verify the exact constants and consider these unverified). The success-rate and node-share figures are ours (ext/README.md:175 and :541). Chessprogramming wiki https://chessprogramming.org/Null_Move_Pruning reports no Elo numbers for verification. The repo's own tests show that parameter variants of the null move (NmpBase=4, NmpDiv=3, NmpMargin=62: -0.14 at 100k nodes, README:555; NmpBase=4 -217 vs -218 at 4,000 games, README:354) are all within noise, so a gain here is plausible but unproven; the learned-LMR result (AUC 0.907 but level play, fact 8) is a warning that better prediction of cheap decisions has not turned into strength before.
proposals.expected_elo: -3 to +5 (point estimate +1); likely small because 82% of cutoffs come on the first move and the null move already prunes only 17-20% of nodes
proposals.cheap_test: Step 1 (30 min): SSTAT logging of null success rate per feature cell on 300 positions at 300k nodes; if no cell has success below 30% with a share of >2% of tries, stop. Step 2: quality test at 100k and 300k nodes per gate separately; accept a gate only with delta <= -0.2 units at both budgets.
proposals.where_in_our_code: /home/user/seek/calc/calc_s19.c lines 1602-1613 (condition and R), cutn[]/cutnode at 1560, raw_ev at 1580, history lookups cmh[][] used at 1683; add one par entry for the gate bits in the enum at line 1015 and defaults at 1020.

summary: Our qsearch (calc_s19.c:1486-1539) is already a conventional modern one (TT cutoff, stand-pat, SEE-filtered captures, delta pruning, all evasions in check, never overwrites a same-key deeper entry), so I found no structural bug that explains a 2-3x node gap; qsearch is 28-32% of nodes but README shows the deficit is spread evenly across move classes, and I expect at most a few Elo from anything here. The three gaps against standard practice are: (1) the TT bound is not used to refine stand-pat, (2) the TT stores no static eval so evaluate() is recomputed on TT hits that do not cut off, (3) qsearch stores evict deeper entries of other positions (single slot, always replace). Quiet checks at the first qsearch ply (which SF 14.1 has) are NOT proposed: Stockfish later simplified them away and I found no Elo evidence, and our measured quiet-check class (88.3 vs 93.8%) is no worse than other classes.
warnings: No injected instructions seen in fetched pages (search result snippets only; nothing fetched in full). No Stockfish source was fetched: statements about what Stockfish 14.1 does in qsearch (TT-bound stand-pat, eval in TT, quiet checks at the first qsearch ply, futility base about stat-eval+155) come from my own recollection plus search-result snippets, and are unverified in detail. Observations on our code that I did not turn into proposals because evidence is nil: qsearch has no draw/repetition check (search() has is_draw, line 1543); the second delta/SEE prune (SEARCH_V3&8) is off by default; in check we search all evasions with no pruning after the first legal move; the qsearch fail-high returns the raw stand-pat/best (no blending toward beta). Fixed-node quality tests cannot distinguish a speed-only change (proposal 2): measure nps, not quality.

proposals.title: Use the TT bound to improve the stand-pat value in qsearch (and main-search static eval)
proposals.mechanism: In qsearch after stand = best = eval_corr(), if the TT entry matches the key and has a usable score s (mate-adjusted for ply): if the bound is LOWER (or EXACT) and s > best, set best = s; if the bound is UPPER (or EXACT) and s < best, set best = s (Stockfish's documented approach: the TT value serves as a better position evaluation when its bound is on the right side). Then run the existing 'best >= beta return' and 'best > alpha -> alpha = best' lines on the refined value. Because a LOWER entry with s >= beta already returns earlier, the new effect is lower bounds in (stand, beta) raising alpha, and upper bounds below stand lowering the fail-low return value and the value stored back to the TT. Same trick can optionally be applied to ev in search() at line 1580 (only for pruning decisions, not for the eval used for the correction-history update). Add as par option (e.g. bit in SearchV3 or a new QsTt) so it is switchable.
proposals.evidence: Weak and indirect. Not measured in our project. Stockfish uses this in qsearch from about SF12 onward (from my knowledge of its structure; I did not fetch its source). Other small engines report TT probing/storing in qsearch at +23 to +73 Elo, but those engines had no qsearch TT at all, which we already have (https://github.com/Toby-Faucher/lemonate/pull/71, https://github.com/Andr0human/chess_engine/pull/71) so this does not transfer. TalkChess has opposing reports (-10 Elo for a classical qsearch hash) https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=47373&start=40. Our code check: calc_s19.c:1496-1510 uses the TT only for exact cutoffs and the move.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +6 (most likely about +2); could be slightly negative at the clock if it adds noise to the hash-sensitive search (fact 9)
proposals.cheap_test: Add option, run ext/quality.py at 300k nodes on the 9,000 positions with option on vs off (SE ~0.3 units; a unit is ~40 Elo so we can only resolve effects of about 25 Elo this way, so also record node counts to depth/bestmove-match and the stability test ext vault_stab: table-size sensitivity should go DOWN if this helps). If quality delta is within +-0.3, run a 1,000-game 10+0.1 match only if the stability metric improved.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c qsearch lines 1496-1510 (TT probe and stand-pat); optionally search() line ~1580 where ev = eval_corr()

proposals.title: Store the raw static evaluation in the TT entry and skip evaluate() on TT hits that do not cut off (pure speed, search-identical)
proposals.mechanism: TTE is exactly 16 bytes (U64 key, int move, short score, uchar depth, uchar flag; calc_s19.c:369) with no free space. Shrink the verification key to the upper 32 bits (U32), keep the 17-bit move in an int, add short raw_eval (the raw evaluate() output before eval_corr's scale/correction, since corrections depend on history state and must be re-applied) and keep score, depth, flag: 4+4+2+2+1+1 = 14 bytes, still 16 with padding. Index uses key & tt_mask so 32 stored bits plus the index bits still give a very low false-positive rate. In qsearch and search(): after the TT probe, if the key matches and raw_eval != NO_EVAL, use it instead of calling evaluate() (apply scale and the correction terms as in eval_corr); otherwise evaluate and write raw_eval on every store (qsearch stores at line 1535 and search stores at line 1879 both). Because the accumulators are updated lazily (int16 lazy accumulators), skipping evaluate() also skips the accumulator update work at that ply, which is where the saving comes from. The node counts and moves must come out bit-identical, so correctness is verifiable by bench.
proposals.evidence: Mechanism only, no measurement of our share yet. Our speed is 1.1-1.3M nps (README fact 10) with a 768-wide net and a dense read-out (calc_s19.c:1295 fdot over 2*NH per hidden unit), so evaluate() is plausibly 20-30% of node time (UNMEASURED: profile with perf first). The fraction of nodes that probe a matching TT entry without cutting off is also unmeasured; the existing -DSSTAT counters (ST(25) at line 1500 counts qsearch TT cutoffs) can be extended to count 'hit, no cutoff'. Every NNUE engine I know stores the static eval in the TT for this reason (Stockfish's TT entry carries an eval field, from my knowledge).
proposals.expected_elo: +1 to +6 at the clock (a 3-8% node-rate gain at roughly 76 Elo per doubling is 3-8 Elo at best; zero change at fixed nodes)
proposals.cheap_test: 1) With perf or by adding counters under -DSSTAT, measure (a) share of time in evaluate()+accumulator update, (b) fraction of qsearch and search nodes that hit a same-key entry and then evaluate anyway. If (a)*(b) < 3% stop (costs 30 minutes). 2) If worth it, implement and verify identical node counts and bestmove on the bench, then compare nps on the bench and under 24-thread match load. No match needed unless nps gain is claimed above 5%.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c:369 (TTE), 1496 and 1504 (qsearch), 1535 (qsearch store), 1580 (search eval), 1879-1881 (search store), tt_alloc, tt_find at 1069; note TT_BUCKET variant at 1074 uses flag bits for age so keep those

proposals.title: Stop qsearch stores from evicting deeper entries of other positions; combine with depth-aware replacement
proposals.mechanism: At line 1533 the qsearch store condition is (e->key != P.key || e->depth == 0): whenever the single slot holds ANOTHER position, any qsearch node (28-32% of all nodes) overwrites it regardless of its depth or age. The main-search store at line 1879 is also always-replace (SearchV3&64, the same-key depth guard, is off by default and measured -0.17 units, within noise, README line 465). Add option QsStore: 0 = qsearch never stores unless the slot is empty or has the same key with depth 0; 1 = store over another key only if the old entry's depth <= 1 or its age differs from tt_age; 2 = standing behaviour. Optionally also enable the main-search replacement rule 'overwrite a different key only if new depth + 2 >= old depth or old age differs' (Stockfish-like). Needs a 16-bit-proof check that tt_age is already stored in flag bits 3-7 (it is, via TTF).
proposals.evidence: Code reading only (calc_s19.c:1533 and 1879). Counter-evidence in our own README: a 512 MB table plays the same as 64 MB and two-entries-per-slot plays +0.72 worse on the quality test (README lines 563-566), which suggests slot pressure is not the limiting factor at 300k nodes, so the expected gain is small. Stockfish also keeps qsearch from displacing deeper entries (its replacement test and 3-entry clusters, from my knowledge, not from the source). Hash instability (fact 9: 19% of moves change with table size) is the reason to test it, because deep entries that are lost make the result depend on collision luck.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +4; most likely invisible on the quality test
proposals.cheap_test: Run ext/quality.py at 300k nodes for QsStore=0/1/2 at 64 MB and, more informative, at 8 MB (tt_alloc(8) is already used by tooling at line 2067) where pressure is high: if 8 MB shows a large gain from QsStore=0/1 then also test at 64 MB; also rerun vault_stab (table-size sensitivity) to see whether the 19% falls. Only a 1,000-game match if quality at 64 MB moves by >0.3 units.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c qsearch store lines 1532-1537, main store lines 1877-1882

summary: CALC already has dynamic time management (node-fraction x best-move-stability x score-drop x volatility, soft limit with hard cap at 3x the base share), so the textbook +15-30 Elo gains reported by engines that lacked it are mostly already taken. What is left looks like roughly +5 to +15 Elo in total, which is small next to the -111 gap. Two real unknowns: how the 10 s actually gets spent (a back-of-envelope equilibrium says the engine runs the clock down to about 1 s and then plays about 100 ms moves, but no clock trajectory has been measured), and the fact that only TmSoft was ever tuned (SPSA tuning was only ever run for TmSoft; TmSoft=61 appears in lab_spsa_test.log, and the 15,000-iteration BIGK log shows no final TmSoft value in the text I could read; the 55 default is unchanged).
warnings: 1) No clock trajectory or time-per-move data exists in the repo (grep of ext/README.md and zero/results found none). The 'engine drains to about 1 s' claim is my arithmetic from the formulas at calc_s19.c:2197-2205 and 1976-1987, not a measurement. 2) lab_nodetime.log shows the match machine ran at load average about 80 on 24 threads; under that load CALC does about 350k nodes/s of wall time and the opponent 194k (the README says results are load-independent for 44 versus 76 boards, but wall-clock time allocation is exactly what a self-play tuning would be sensitive to, so tune at the same board count as the final matches). 3) The ext/README.md says the opponent Stockfish is an SSE2-only build running 1.77x slower per node than ours, so equal-clock results hand us nearly twice its nodes; that makes TM Elo estimates against it optimistic compared with a properly compiled Stockfish. 4) gauntlet.py uses GRACE = 0.05 s of overshoot before a loss on time, and CALC has no move-overhead option; if the final test harness is stricter, the hard cap alloc*3 / t*2/5 may need a safety margin. 5) External numbers come from small hobby-engine pull requests (self-reported, not fishtest) and are all for engines without a prior dynamic scheme. I did not fetch Stockfish source. 6) Search results contained no injected instructions. Licences: none of the sources were copied, ideas only.

proposals.title: SPSA the whole clock-allocation block at 10+0.1 (base share divisor, soft/hard multipliers, stability, node-fraction and drop coefficients), after a one-game clock-trajectory diagnostic
proposals.mechanism: Expose as UCI options the constants now hard-coded at calc_s19.c:2199-2203 and 1981-1983: TmDiv (t/20), TmInc (inc*3/4), TmHard (alloc*3), TmHardFrac (t*2/5), frac weight (1.5-frac)*1.35, stability slope 0.05 and cap 10, drop slope 0.004 and cap 75. Add them to PARAMS in zero/spsa_clock.py next to the existing ('TmSoft',55,25,110,5) entry and run at 10+0.1 (not 5+0.05). Estimated equilibrium, not measured: soft share is 0.55*(t/20+75 ms); with mean scale roughly 1.1-1.4 and iteration overshoot, spend equals the 100 ms increment at about t = 1 s. So the clock drains in the first 25-30 moves (about 470 ms each) and the remaining ~70 moves in these draw-heavy games (62% draws) get about 100 ms, while the hard cap t*2/5 sits near 400 ms. A flatter schedule (larger divisor, so more reserve for the middlegame and for long games) may be better or worse. That is why the diagnostic comes first: log ms used, depth reached and clock left per move for 20 games.
proposals.evidence: Weak for our engine, since nothing has been measured. Code facts: the allocation is at calc_s19.c:2197-2205; only TmSoft was ever exposed to SPSA (zero/spsa_clock.py:28), with value 61 in zero/results/lab_spsa_test.log; ext/README.md has no TmNew/TmDiv sweep. External self-reported: a stability+score-trend soft limit gave +15.1 +/- 7.3 Elo at 10+0.1 over 3,150 games (https://github.com/LupeHiguera/ChessSI/pull/26), but that engine had no dynamic scheme before, so most of it is already in CALC. Our own scale: SF needs about 2.8x our nodes, worth about 120 Elo, so roughly 80 Elo per node doubling; moving 10% of effective node budget to better moves is worth about +5 Elo.
proposals.expected_elo: +3 to +10 at 10+0.1 single thread (more likely +3 to +6); about 0 at 60+0.6 since the equilibrium shifts
proposals.cheap_test: Step 1 (under 1 h): drive one engine through 20 clock games with a Python harness like gauntlet.py and record per move: ms spent, depth, clock left, and whether the hard cap stopped the iteration mid-way. If the clock sits near 1 s from move 30 on and more than 15% of moves hit the hard cap, there is room. Step 2: SPSA with SPSA_PROCS=44 on 10+0.1, about 3-4 h wall at 1.2 games/s, then confirm tuned versus standing in self-play, 4,000 games (about 1 h at 44 boards; standard error about 6-7 Elo), then 1,000 games against Stockfish 14.1 as the final check.

proposals.title: Decayed best-move-change counter plus iteration-cost prediction in the soft stop test
proposals.mechanism: Two changes in search_root's stop rule (calc_s19.c:1976-1987). (a) Replace consecutive-stability with an exponentially decayed count of best-move changes over iterations (for example instab = 0.5*instab + changed), scale *= 1 + k*instab, plus a bonus when the best move changed in the last 2 iterations after being stable (it caught a refutation). Today a single flip resets stable to 0 and gives the full 1.3 factor, but a move that has flipped 3 times in 6 depths looks the same as a fresh flip. (b) Predict the next iteration's cost: stop if t + growth*(t - t_prev) > soft*scale with growth near 1.0, instead of stopping only when t >= soft*scale. The current rule starts an iteration at t just below the limit that then costs 1.5-2x the previous one, so the real spend overshoots the intended soft limit by a variable amount and the intended tuning is blurred. The partial-iteration result is already used (line 1959), so a predicted-overshoot abort loses little.
proposals.evidence: Medium-weak. External self-reported figures: a soft-limit table by stability streak gave +15 Elo at 10+0.1 (https://github.com/LupeHiguera/ChessSI/pull/26); a falling-eval term added 1% per cp of drop, up to 40% (https://github.com/conorosully27-cloud/Chess_Engine/pull/25, +27 Elo over its previous version, bundled with other changes); one project measured the root move changing 9.3% of the time after 3 agreeing depths versus 26.0% otherwise (https://github.com/Devansh121/chess/pull/33), supporting stability as a signal. None are fishtest-verified, and CALC already has the first-order versions. Our own fact 9 (19% of chosen moves change with hash size at 300k nodes) says best-move instability is high in our search, so a graded instability signal may carry more information than a binary streak.
proposals.cheap_test: Offline, no games: record per position the best move at each depth for 3,000 positions at the clock-equivalent budget (about 100-300k nodes), and measure whether decayed instability or consecutive-stable better predicts that the final move differs from the iteration-8 move (AUC), and how much time the rule saves at equal move quality using ext/quality.py with a time-matched budget. Then a 4,000-game self-play against standing TM at 10+0.1.

proposals.title: Bank time in dead-drawn quiet positions and spend it in the middlegame
proposals.mechanism: After the standard scale is computed (line 1982-1984), multiply by about 0.6-0.7 when all hold: small |score| (under 20-30 cp), stable >= 3, few non-pawn pieces or a high halfmove clock, and fewer than N legal root moves with near-equal node share. Optionally lift the base share slightly (about +10%) at game ply 15-45 where decisions are made. Our matches are 62% draws (34 wins, 624 draws, 342 losses), so many long late moves in drawn endings spend time that cannot change the result, while the 342 losses are tactical misses in the middlegame.
proposals.evidence: Weak and indirect. 624 of 1000 games are draws (fact 1). The mean-spend arithmetic in proposal 1 suggests the late-game 100 ms moves are already cheap, so the saving may be small. Not measured on our engine; no external number found for this specific rule.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +5
proposals.cheap_test: After the clock-trajectory diagnostic of proposal 1, classify moves by game phase and score band and count how much of the total time went to drawn-looking moves. If under 20% of time, drop this. If more, add option TmDraw (scale percent) and play 4,000 games of self-play at 10+0.1.

summary: Raw speed is nearly exhausted: the evaluator is about 45-55% of cycles (accumulator updates 26-40%, read-out 13-19%), the code already has lazy accumulators, a Finny-style king-bucket cache, 2 MB pages, TT prefetch and an AVX2 integer read-out, and the cache-prefetch and block-skip ideas I tested are null. Realistic remaining gain is +5-10% nps (about +4-8 Elo by the 50-70 Elo per doubling rule, below match noise). It can only be verified on an equal-tree bench (same signature, nodes/s), not by games. Our per-node speed is already about 1.9x Stockfish's (ext/README.md:251-253), so the gap is search efficiency, not nps.
warnings:
Measurement caveats and negative results (all on this shared VM, which has about 5% run-to-run noise, with a random 768-wide, 16-bucket net and best.bin, not BIGS):
1. Where the time goes. TSTAT on a random 768/16-bucket net: accumulator update about 780-950 TSC cycles per eval, read-out about 250; evaluator about 54% of cycles. README gives 511 + 367 of 1811 for BIGM (45%).
 - Of the accumulator time, the 'while rebuild' path (king crossing a bucket or the mirror line) is about 30% of cycles in this random-net run (922k rebuilds at about 1150 cycles, against 13.4M normal builds at about 183). With the real net and search the README-consistent figure is about 7.6% of evals, so about 15% of the update cost.
2. Dead ends tested:
 (a) Just-in-time prefetch of the weight rows at eval time (not at make): no gain, 0 to -6% (matches README 313-315).
 (b) Hand-written AVX2 two-row accumulator update: identical to the compiler's loop.
 (c) Hot-set experiment (all rows mapped onto 32 rows, so everything is L1/L2-resident): the update only fell from about 750-810 to 690-720, so the update is not cache-miss-bound. It is close to the throughput limit of 3 loads + 1 store per vector.
 (d) Sparse read-out blocks: only 3.4% of 8-unit and 0.2% of 16-unit blocks are all-zero in best.bin (H=256; 64% of units are zero individually), so non-zero block skipping is worthless unless the hidden units are reordered by co-activation. That is untested, and the expected gain is below 3%.
 (e) Lazy evaluation from the piece-square shortcut (lin): to avoid the net at nodes far outside the window, the lin value is too inaccurate. With margin 400, only 4.5% (qsearch) / 3.2% (main) of evals could be skipped, with 1.0%/0.4% wrong side; margin 250 skips 10.6%/9.1% with 4.4%/3.0% wrong. Not worth it.
 (f) GCC profile-guided optimisation (-fprofile-use, trained on the bench): identical node counts, nps ratio 0.99 (best of 6, noisy). No evidence for PGO here; retest on a quiet 7900X before dismissing.
3. Fixed-node instruments (quality.py) are blind to cost per node. Any change that alters time per node (ThrHist, TT eval reuse, read-out kernels) needs a bench or clock test. The README already shows this (ThrHist at 300k nodes better, at the clock -9).
4. Valgrind callgrind (H=256 net, no startup memsets): evaluate about 35% of instructions, mp_next (incl. gen/see/hist scoring) about 25%, make/unmake about 13%. The quiet-move selection scan (for j... if sc[j]>sc[b]) is about 4.7% of instructions and could be a SIMD max-scan, worth about 1-2% time; picker work is the largest non-evaluator slice.
5. No injected instructions were met (no web pages fetched), and nothing was fetched from Stockfish. The null-move-child eval trick is mentioned from general knowledge only, untested. Files read only; scratch work is in /tmp/claude-0/s (copies and test binaries).

proposals.title: AVX-512 (BW+VNNI) read-out kernel, optionally with a uniform activation scale
proposals.mechanism: In calc_s19.c, qdot (line 641) and tdot/act_sq (668-699) are AVX2 only. Per 16 lanes qdot does load a, max, min with a QU_ONE load, mullo with a QU_MUL load, mulhi_epu16(x,x), madd, add. Add an #if __AVX512BW__/__AVX512VNNI__ path: 32 lanes per op, _mm512_dpwssd_epi32 fusing madd+add, 4 steps per widen as now, widen with _mm512_cvtepi32_epi64, _mm512_reduce_add_epi64. Step A uses the same maths, so the bench signature stays identical. Step B (optional, changes the quantisation): one shared scale for all units, so QU_ONE/QU_MUL become constants (min with a broadcast, slli by a constant), removing 2 loads and 1 mullo per vector. Do not use 256-bit dpwssd alone: no gain. Build with -march=znver4, which exposes avx512vnni/bw/vl.
proposals.evidence: Microbenchmark in /tmp (copy of qdot, n=768, two views, L1-resident) on the Sapphire-Rapids-class box here, noisy shared VM, 3 runs: AVX2 190-260 TSC cycles/eval; 256-bit VNNI 217-220 (no gain); AVX-512+VNNI 140-205 (about -25 to -30%); AVX-512 with uniform scale 118-165 (about -40%). The AVX2 uniform-scale variant was inconclusive (noise). In-engine read-out cost is 19% of cycles per position for BIGM (ext/README.md:305-309) and 13.5% in my TSTAT run with a random 768x16-bucket net. WEAK POINT: Zen 4 executes 512-bit ops as two 256-bit halves, so the gain will be smaller than on Intel; I could not measure Zen 4. ext/README.md:315 says 512-bit vectors for the compiler's loops changed nothing, but that was the accumulator loops, not a hand-written read-out.
proposals.expected_elo: +2 to +5 (read-out -15 to -30% gives total cycles -3 to -6%, nps +3 to +6%). Could be about 0 on Zen 4 if the double-pumping eats the gain.
proposals.cheap_test: Step 1: build -O3 -march=znver4 against current on the 7900X with ext/evalcost.py (-DTSTAT) and zero/bench.py (same net, depth 13; the signature must match for step A). Compare read-out cycles and nps over 5 or more runs on a quiet machine. Step 2: for the shared scale, requantize BIGS and check the eval difference over 10k positions (must be within a cp or two) with the quality instrument at 300k nodes; if the eval is unchanged, keep it. Stop if step 1 shows under 3% nps.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c: qdot 641-663, act_sq 668-684, tdot 686-699, evaluate 890-959, quantize_net (QU_ONE/QU_MUL setup).

proposals.title: Store the static evaluation in the TT and reuse it (hash hits, singular re-searches)
proposals.mechanism: TTE is {U64 key; Move move; short score; uchar depth, flag} = 16 bytes with no eval (line 369), so every node that finds its own entry without a cutoff re-runs evaluate() (accumulator build + read-out). Repack to {u32 key32, Move move, short score, short eval, uchar depth, flag} = 16 bytes (a 32-bit check on the upper key bits has a negligible false-hit rate at 4M entries). Store the raw evaluate() (before eval_corr's correction) in search() and qsearch() when writing. On a hit with a stored eval, skip evaluate() and apply eval_corr's correction terms only. Also, singular-extension searches (excl set, line 1559) re-enter search() at the same position and recompute eval_corr(): reuse evals_stack[ply] there, which costs nothing. A null-move child could use -parent eval + tempo, but our net is side-to-move-specific, so that is risky: test it separately.
proposals.evidence: Measured by instrumenting a copy of calc_s19.c in /tmp (TT 64 MB, cleared per position, depth 12 and 14 on the 12 zero/bench.py positions, best.bin): a same-key TT entry exists at the time of the eval in 147,628 of 1,515,768 evals (9.7%) at depth 12 and 343,884 of 3,617,028 (9.5%) at depth 14 (3.5% with a random net, not representative). In a real game the TT persists across moves, so the rate should be higher. SSTAT run: 2.47M evals for 2.69M nodes, so 92% of nodes evaluate. WEAK POINT: for an internal node the skipped accumulator work is only deferred (children still build the chain lazily), so only the read-out (about 19% of the eval path) and leaf-node builds are really saved.
proposals.expected_elo: +1 to +3 (nps +2 to +4%). A small search effect from the cached eval at TT-hit nodes is possible (the stored eval is slightly stale in the correction terms), probably neutral.
proposals.cheap_test: Change TTE and the eval fetch; run zero/bench.py with the same net at depth 13: the node signature should not change (the eval is identical), only nps. Count evaluate() calls with the -DKSTAT counter (ks_ens) before and after, over a game-length search sequence without clearing the TT between moves. Then a 1,000-game 10+0.1 match against the standing build only if nps is up by 3% or more.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c: TTE 369-370, tt_alloc 1010, eval_corr 1136-1143, qsearch 1486-1539 (probe 1494, store 1532), search 1541+ (probe 1558, eval 1580, singular at about 1665), evals_stack.

angle: gap-diagnosis: localize the 2-3x search node inefficiency
summary: Two measurements already in ext/README.md say Stockfish is only 1.6 plies deeper at 300k nodes (14.5 vs 16.1, README ~line 374) but needs 1/3 of our nodes for equal quality. So the gap is not fully explained by depth, and the 12 failed pruning/reduction variants mean tuning knobs blindly is exhausted. The key unmeasured thing is a factorization: tree size per depth versus move quality per depth, plus whether the gap is uniform across positions or a tail. I propose a three-step diagnostic: depth-matched quality, per-iteration trace comparison, and a perturbation-sensitivity bisect; all run on existing instruments in 2-4 hours each, using only UCI output of the Stockfish binary.
warnings: No injected instructions seen; I fetched no web pages. Weaknesses: (1) the depth-at-equal-nodes table in the README rests on only 12 positions. (2) Fact 9 looks internally odd: a 19% flip rate with table size at 300k nodes cannot be table pressure with a 64 MB table, so either the test used a small table or there is a nondeterminism or stale-state issue; check this before trusting 'search instability' as a cause. (3) Several ablations judged at 10k nodes were later shown misleading at 100k (README ~line 165), so every diagnostic above should be read at 100k-300k nodes, not 10k. (4) Stockfish source must not be read; all comparisons rely only on UCI info output of the SF14.1 binary, which gives nodes, depth, seldepth and PV per iteration but no internal cutoff statistics.

proposals.title: Equal-depth factorization: split the 2-3x into 'bigger tree per depth' vs 'worse move per depth'
proposals.mechanism: Run ext/quality.py (copy under the scratchpad, edit the 'go nodes N' line to 'go depth D') for BOTH engines with the same network (ours with SF14.1 net vs SF14.1) at fixed depths D=10,12,14 on the same ~2000-position subset (the full 8,964 only if time). Record for every position nodes used (from the final 'info nodes') and the move-quality loss. Then: N_ours(D)/N_sf(D) = tree-size factor T; Loss_ours(D) vs Loss_sf(D) = per-depth quality factor Q. Interpretation: if quality at equal depth is equal and only nodes differ, the gap is purely pruning/reduction aggressiveness (our tree is wider; look at LMR/futility/RFP/NMP formulas, move counts, qsearch size: 28% of nodes are qsearch). If SF is better at equal depth, the gap is selectivity or ordering (extensions, TT use, history quality, singular, correction history), not tree width. Also report seldepth, which tells about extension/qsearch depth. This tells the lead which family of ideas is worth any hours and kills the other half.
proposals.evidence: Depth at equal nodes table, ext/README.md ~line 374 (ours 14.5 vs SF 16.1 at 300k; 20.8 vs 24.1 at 3M) with 12 positions only; yardstick fact 3 (2.0x/2.8x/3.1x nodes). The README says options meant to deepen the search change depth at 3M nodes by at most 0.7 ply, i.e. depth is not what knobs move. No equal-depth quality measurement exists in the repo (grep of README finds none). Weak evidence for what the result will be; this is a measurement, not a fix.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 directly; steers work worth perhaps +10 to +40 Elo if it identifies one mechanism (the gap is 120 Elo; realistic recovery of a quarter to a third)
proposals.cheap_test: Edit a copy of ext/quality.py in the scratchpad to take depth; 2 engines x 3 depths x 2000 positions at ~0.1-1 s per position on 20 parallel single-thread processes is roughly 30-60 min of machine time; SF 4M-node reference analysis is cached already.
proposals.where_in_our_code: ext/quality.py, ext/depth_at_nodes.py (same positions list in zero/bench.py); no change to calc/calc_s19.c needed because 'go depth' and 'info nodes' are standard UCI.

proposals.title: Per-iteration trace comparison: nodes-to-stable-best-move distribution and effective branching factor, ours(SF-net) vs SF14.1
proposals.mechanism: On 2000 positions run both engines with 'go nodes 3000000' (or movetime) and log every 'info depth/nodes/score/pv' line. Compute per position: (a) EBF = nodes(d)/nodes(d-1) averaged over d=8..16, giving a per-depth curve for both engines; (b) nodes at which the best move first becomes equal to the 4M-node reference move and stays so to the end (node-to-solution, a test-suite-like metric but on 9k realistic positions, avoiding saturated tactical suites); (c) distribution of ratio ours/SF of that number: if the median ratio is ~2.5 for everyone the gap is a uniform EBF problem (reduction/pruning shape); if the mean is dominated by a heavy tail (say 10% of positions needing 20x) the gap is instability or missed deep tactics (extensions, TT/graph interaction, aspiration re-searches). (d) number of best-move changes and score swings between iterations (our iteration noise vs SF). Then stratify by piece count, in-check at root, eval volatility (the Vol feature already exists in the engine) and tactical vs quiet (reference move is a capture/check). The stratum with the worst ratio names the mechanism to attack.
proposals.evidence: Hash-instability measurement (fact 9: 19% of our moves change with table size vs 1.1% for SF; 0.1% vs 0.4% under a 1% node change) suggests that a tail of unstable positions may dominate the mean; README search statistics at 300k nodes: 60% of main-search nodes end by reverse futility, 82% of move-loop cutoffs on first move, null move succeeds 41% (README ~line 172): these are single-engine numbers with nothing to compare to, so the comparison trace is the missing half. No per-iteration comparison exists in repo. Method (nodes-to-solution, EBF) is standard; no external measurement claimed.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 directly; if a tail or a depth-band is localized, targeted fix perhaps +10 to +30
proposals.cheap_test: Pure log parsing, one Python script under 100 lines, over 2 runs of 2000 positions at 3M nodes (about 2.5 s per position per engine, 20 parallel processes: roughly 10 min). Verify our engine prints per-iteration info lines (it prints 'info' lines already, see calc_s19.c uci output near line 2250) and, if not, take nodes only at end for the fixed-node ladder 30k/100k/300k/1M and compute the node-to-solution as the smallest budget at which the move matches and stays matched.
proposals.where_in_our_code: Parsing script in scratchpad; stratification uses the Vol/volatility term (par VolMix, VOL_*) and bench FENs in zero/bench.py; engine side only needs per-iteration info lines in the main iterative deepening loop around calc_s19.c:1917 (tt_age increments per search) if absent.

proposals.title: Bisect the search chaos: per-component perturbation sensitivity audit against SF's 0.4% baseline
proposals.mechanism: Define flip rate = fraction of positions where the chosen move changes when the node budget is changed by 1% (and separately when hash is 64MB vs 32MB, with a table large enough that no entry pressure exists, to separate real collisions from chaos). SF scores 0.4% / 1.1%; ours 0.1% / 19% (fact 9; note the 19% looks inconsistent with the 0.1% unless the hash-size test was with a tiny table, so first re-run with 64 vs 128 MB: if the 19% was table pressure at small size it is not chaos but replacement policy, if it persists it is a determinism-sensitive component). Then toggle one component at a time and re-measure flip rate and the quality score: (1) TT cutoffs only at non-PV and depth >= d+k (no exact-bound cuts), (2) correction histories and continuation histories reset per iteration vs carried, (3) IIR, (4) aspiration window width (Asp), (5) singular extension, (6) probcut, (7) always-replace TT vs the existing TtBucket two-entry option, (8) tt_age handling. The component whose removal brings flips to the SF level and does not cost quality names a graph-history-interaction / noise source. Additionally log how often a TT hit with depth below required is used for move ordering only vs cutoff.
proposals.evidence: Fact 9 in task text; TT in calc_s19.c:369 is single 16-byte entry, key, move, score, depth, flag, without stored static eval, always-replace in default (tt_find returns &tt[key & mask] when TtBucket=0, lines 1068-1075); the code comment itself (line 1063) says TtBucket is +19 Elo at 1 MB table but -9 to -10 at 64 MB, so table pressure is not the story at 64MB, which makes a 19% flip rate at 300k nodes genuinely strange: 300k nodes x 16 B is well under 64 MB. Possible causes: lazy/incremental accumulator not being bit-identical across paths (int16 wrap, README line ~474 notes wraparound is consistent), history tables or correction histories persisting between searches within one process, thread-local state not reset by 'ucinewgame' in the quality harness. Hypothesis only; no measured attribution yet.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +20; if a determinism bug or stale-state contamination is found it could be larger, but a priori unlikely
proposals.cheap_test: Flip-rate test on 1000 positions at 300k nodes: ~0.3 s each = 5 min per configuration on 20 processes; 10 configurations in about 1 hour. Include a sanity run: same position searched twice in the same process with identical settings must give an identical bestmove and node count (bit determinism check); any difference is a bug to fix immediately.
