proposals.where_in_our_code: calc_s19.c: tt_find/TTF at ~1068-1077, ucinewgame reset at 2153 (note it clears histories and corrhist but history is not cleared between searches in the same game, which quality.py handles with a fresh hash), aspiration and iteration loop near 1917, par[] toggles at 1015-1016 so most ablations need no recompilation.

summary: Our root/aspiration/draw code is basic but not broken, and I see no large Elo in this angle (likely 0 to +5 total). Three cheap items are worth a test: upcoming-repetition (cuckoo) detection, draw-score dithering plus a cheaper is_draw, and PV-node IIR plus a gentler aspiration schedule. None can explain the 19% hash-instability or the 2-3x search-efficiency gap, so this angle should be ranked low versus pruning/LMR/history work.
warnings: No injected instructions seen in fetched pages. Observed code issues: (1) is_draw() is evaluated before the mate check and treats a single earlier occurrence (even pre-root) as a draw; (2) fail-low re-search does not move beta and window growth is x3, unlike Stockfish's gentle growth; (3) IID/IIR is a flat depth-1 at depth>=4 for all nodes, with an extra reduction only for cut nodes at depth>=8, so PV nodes are not treated differently; (4) I did not find any cause for the 19% hash-table instability in this angle (draw-by-repetition path dependence in the TT could contribute slightly but Stockfish has the same property, so look at replacement policy/bucket aging instead). Elo numbers for cuckoo come from small hobby engines with wide error bars, so treat as unreliable. No Stockfish source was fetched; only commit pages for aspiration formulas were seen via search snippets.

proposals.title: Upcoming-repetition (cuckoo) detection in search()
proposals.mechanism: Add a Zobrist-delta cuckoo table (keys of all reversible-move piece/square pairs XOR zside) and has_game_cycle(ply) as in the public Marcel van Kervinck / CuckooChess scheme. In search(), for non-root nodes with P.half>=3 and alpha<0: if a legal reversible move would reach a position already on the path (or in game history), raise alpha to 0 (draw), and if alpha>=beta return alpha. Only needs the existing keys[]/hply stack. Reimplement from the algorithm description, not copied code (CuckooChess is GPL; algorithm itself is public).
proposals.evidence: Weak and engine-specific: a cuckoo patch in another engine gave +2.49 +-1.86 (https://github.com/HasanFakih21/JustBot/pull/199); another engine reports +11.2 (+3.7..+18.7) over 2,640 games (https://github.com/arhancanli/arhanpassant/releases/tag/v0.13.0); a Viridithas fix test was inconclusive (https://github.com/cosmobobak/viridithas/pull/470). Our code has none: is_draw() at /home/user/seek/calc/calc_s19.c:1109 only sees repetitions already played. Our games are 62% draws and we are the weaker side, so a cheaply found forced repetition matters a bit more than usual.
proposals.expected_elo: +1 to +4 (maybe +0 at fixed-node quality tests, since it only matters in repetitive positions)
proposals.cheap_test: Fixed-node quality run at 300k on the 9,000 positions (expect ~0 unit: positions are mostly not repetitive), then a 1,000-game 10+0.1 match vs the baseline binary; an SPRT-sized gain of 2 Elo is not detectable in 1,000 games, so judge mainly on no-regression plus a nps check and a perft/bench sanity check.

proposals.title: Draw-score dithering and cheaper is_draw (early exit when half<4)
proposals.mechanism: (a) Return a draw score of 1-(nodes&2) (i.e. +-1 cp, the standard anti-blindness trick) instead of exactly 0 for repetition/50-move draws in search() and qsearch(), so the tree does not mistake all drawn lines as equal and TT/ordering ties break differently. (b) In is_draw(), skip the repetition loop when P.half<4 and loop only over the distance min(P.half,hply) with a step of 2 (it already does) after checking the cheap insufficient-material test first; also test 50-move after checkmate/stalemate is known (currently is_draw() returns 0 at search():1543 before the mate check, so a mating move at half==100 is scored as a draw; rare). (c) Treat a single repetition inside the search tree as draw but require a second occurrence for positions before the root (standard 2-fold-in-tree rule); today any one earlier occurrence, even before the root, is scored 0, which makes the engine overly drawish at the root when the opponent could deviate.
proposals.evidence: Mechanism is standard practice in public engines (draw randomisation +-1 and in-tree 2-fold / pre-root 3-fold). No Elo number found for it specifically. Our code: is_draw() at /home/user/seek/calc/calc_s19.c:1109-1115 (loop over keys[] from hply-2 down to hply-half, single hit = draw regardless of whether it is before the root). Evidence for Elo is weak; speed part is a tiny nps gain (loop runs on every node including qsearch via line 1543 and qsearch is_draw).
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +3
proposals.cheap_test: nps bench (should be unchanged or +1%); quality run at 300k nodes; a 1,000-game match vs baseline. Also count how many root decisions differ in a repetition-heavy position set (e.g. the endgame subset of the 9,000 positions).

proposals.title: Gentler aspiration schedule, score-dependent delta, PV-node IIR
proposals.mechanism: (1) In search_root(): on fail-low also pull beta toward alpha ((alpha+beta)/2) and on fail-high reduce the re-search depth by 1 while the score is not a mate (up to 3 times), growing delta by delta/2 + a few cp instead of x3; make the starting delta depend on |last score| (delta = 33 + score^2/~10000) so lopsided positions get wider windows. Currently delta*=3 after every miss (calc_s19.c:~1946-1950), fixed ASP=33, and no depth reduction on fail-high. (2) In search(), after the existing IIR at line 1617, add: for PV nodes with no tt move and depth>=4 reduce depth by one more (Stockfish-15-style PV IIR); today only cut nodes at depth>=8 and a plain depth-- at depth>=4 apply. (3) Make the fail-high re-search of the root first move reuse partial-iteration result only when it came from a full-window search.
proposals.evidence: Stockfish aspiration formulas are score-dependent: e.g. 10+avg*avg/9828 (https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/commit/99f1bacfd6864afca86ae74f33232b9cdfb3828c) and 9+avg^2/13181 (https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/commit/a6fd17f27d7675332166e9e6ea8210237281fc77); window centre uses a running average of previous scores (https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/commit/a0259d8ab9661b7f625474d2cbe18481ef69bbf2). TalkChess discussion suggests aspiration benefit is small and window growth schedule matters little (https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=76115). Per-parameter Elo not found; treat as unmeasured. At 300k nodes (depth ~15-18) root re-search overhead is a few percent of nodes at most.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +3 (aspiration part probably ~0; PV-IIR part uncertain, could be negative given the dead ends listed for reduction changes)
proposals.cheap_test: Count nodes spent in re-searches per root iteration on the 9,000 positions (logging only), then quality run at 300k nodes for each of the two changes separately; keep only if <= -0.3 units (one std error). A 2-hour test, no match needed unless it passes.

summary: Fact 3/4 say the evaluator already ties Stockfish 14.1's net, so architecture work can only buy single-digit to low-teens Elo each, not the ~120 Elo search gap. Our own tests already show a layered read-out (+12) and product terms (+6) cost 15-18% speed and do not pay (ext/README.md ~l.350); the free 32 queen-aware heads (+11) are the only clear win and are not yet in a full-scale net. The best remaining architecture bets are threat inputs (SF18, about +14 LTC for that patch, a separate Stockfish figure) and cheap-to-test confirmations of the queen heads; expect at most +10 to +25 Elo combined.
warnings: I did not read any engine source and did not fetch Stockfish source. Web evidence on pairwise multiplication, dual activations and layer stacks was thin: one search returned only Viridithas blog claims (Swish vs SCReLU about +5.5 to +13.8, from https://hn.jakechampion.name/reader/https://cosmo.tardis.ac/files/2026-01-27-activation-2.html) and no Elo for pairwise multiplication or output buckets themselves, so I deliberately did not propose those. Our own README records that product terms (+6) and the layered read-out (+12) already failed to pay for their 15-18% speed cost at this scale. Dual activation and factorizer training were not researched in depth; our shared-table-plus-correction per king bucket already works as a factorizer. The honest conclusion for this angle is that evaluator architecture is a low-ceiling lever here.

proposals.title: Ship queen-aware read-out heads in full-scale BIGS-class net, then add finer material/phase buckets
proposals.mechanism: Retrain the 768-wide, 16 king-bucket net at full scale (8.2B positions) with --buckets 32 --obk 2 (piece count x my queen x opp queen). Optionally go further to 64 heads (add a coarse pawn-count or imbalance axis). Read-out heads are cost-free at runtime, since only the final 768x2 dot-product weights are duplicated per bucket; the extra cost is only cache footprint, so check that nodes/s is unchanged on the bench.
proposals.evidence: Own measurement: +11 (0 to +22) at 30k nodes, 2,000 games, -184 vs -195 reference against SF14.1 at 10k nodes (ext/README.md ~l.605-611, zero/results/vault_vault_probe.log). Output buckets by material are standard in permissively licensed engines; one TalkChess Leorik devlog post says +14 Elo for output buckets in another engine (weak, anecdotal): https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?p=987387. Held-out loss gain is tiny (0.54415 to 0.54397), so the Elo may be partly noise.
proposals.expected_elo: +5 to +12 at 10+0.1 (the 10+0.1 match is single-thread and noisy; CI will overlap 0)
proposals.cheap_test: Already measured at probe scale. Full-scale confirmation: ext/quality.py at 300k nodes on the 9,000 positions (se ~0.3 units, so detects 1 unit=40 Elo easily but 0.25 unit = 10 Elo only marginally; use two seeds), then 1,000-game match vs SF14.1 only if quality improves. Also cheap: try 64 heads in a one-pass 1.09B probe via ext/vault_probe.sh (~hours of GPU, no match machine time).
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/train_nnue.py (--buckets/--obk flags); engine read-out select in calc/calc_s19.c (bucket index computation from piece counts and queen bitboards)

proposals.title: Threat inputs (piece-attacks-piece features) as an added sparse input block, tested at full scale
proposals.mechanism: Add a second input block to the feature transformer: for each (attacker piece type+colour, attacked piece type+colour, attacker square or attacked square) pair active on the board, one input row, accumulated incrementally like piece-square features (on make/unmake, update the threats whose attack lines changed: sliding-piece x-ray changes are the costly part). Start with a restricted set (only attacks onto non-pawn pieces, own-king-bucket independent) to bound update cost. Reuse the existing int16 lazy accumulator and train via the existing --am attack-map flag path in calc/train_nnue.py as a baseline before writing the engine side.
proposals.evidence: Stockfish 18 added full-threat inputs (SFNNv10) and the patch's own test log shows an LTC estimate of about +13.9 +-1.9 Elo on ARM; release claims up to +46 over SF17 for the whole release (not just threats): https://stockfishchess.org/blog/2026/stockfish-18/ and the patch listing at https://nextchessmove.com/dev-builds/sf14/8e5392d79a36aba5b997cf6fb590937e3e624e80. Credited prior art in Monty, Yukari, PlentyChess (I did not read their licences; check before reading source). Counter-evidence in our own history: attack-map and threat inputs were in the shelved 40-variant study at 384 wide on only 59M positions (zero/results/architecture_probe.md) and never re-run on 8.2B; our README states more positions no longer help the plain 768/16-bucket design, i.e. new information in the inputs is exactly what is needed, and threats supply features the net otherwise has to compute in its hidden layer.
proposals.expected_elo: +5 to +20 evaluator-only; minus 10-25% nps from update cost, so net after speed plausibly 0 to +10 at 10+0.1
proposals.cheap_test: Step 1 (no engine work): train --am probe on 1.09B positions (about same cost as the vault probe) and compare held-out loss to r0 0.54415 and the 10,334 clear-case pairs (fact 4 metric; quiet-pair score 73.2% BIGS baseline). Proceed to engine only if held-out loss drops by >= 0.003 (the queen heads only moved 0.0002 and gave +11, so even 0.001 is a signal) or quiet-pair accuracy rises >= 1 point. Step 2: nodetime.py speed measurement, then quality.py.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/train_nnue.py --am (exists); calc/calc_s19.c accumulator update functions; ext/vault_probe.sh to run the probe

proposals.title: Spend the evaluator budget on search-side use of the net rather than architecture: eval-confidence / correction input for LMR and pruning, tested as net outputs
proposals.mechanism: Add a second scalar read-out head (same 768x2 hidden, 32 queen/material buckets) trained to predict |search-score minus static-eval| (or the sign-aware residual). Use it in the engine for (a) reducing LMR less at nodes with high predicted residual, (b) skipping futility/razoring when predicted residual is large, (c) scaling the static eval used in correction history. This targets fact 3 (search needs 2-3x nodes) and fact 9 (instability) using a free extra head, instead of improving a static evaluator that already matches SF's net.
proposals.evidence: Weak/indirect: our learned-LMR model (AUC 0.907 vs 0.822 hand rule) was level in play (README fact 8), which suggests a better predictor alone does not translate; this proposal differs only in that the signal comes from the net at near-zero cost. No external measured Elo found for a residual-prediction head in a permissive engine in my searches; correction history in general is established (SF) but is search-side and belongs to another angle. Treat this as speculative.
proposals.cheap_test: Train the extra head on existing self-play/search-labelled positions (need search-vs-static labels from a dump: a 300k-node search per position is costly; use 20k nodes on 2M positions, about 1 CPU-day split over 24 threads, which exceeds the minute-scale budget but is a sanity step), check head AUC predicting 'search changes best move', then wire only into LMR and run quality.py at 300k nodes.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/train_nnue.py (extra head), calc/calc_s19.c LMR reduction computation and futility conditions (par[] table near line 1015)

angle: training-data: targets, lambda/WDL blending, rescoring, filtering, volume vs quality for the fast evaluator
summary: The evidence in our own README says the data axis is nearly exhausted: more data and more passes add 0 to +8 Elo at 768 wide (ext/README.md:32, :328-331), the evaluator ties Stockfish 14.1's network on move choice, and the gap is mostly search efficiency, so no data change is likely to be worth more than about +5 to +15 Elo of the -111. The one measured evaluator gap that remains is absolute value error against the 4M-node reference: BIGS 22.7 against Stockfish's network 18.6 in thousandths of squared score error (ext/README.md ~line 582; the SF net is also scored on its own distribution), while our training loss is log-loss, not squared score error. What is left is cheap to test (a probe is about 20 minutes of GPU at ~900k positions/s, zero/results/vault_vault_probe.log), so the proposals are ranked by cost-to-information, not by size of expected gain.
warnings:
1) Honest ceiling: the data axis looks saturated at this capacity (more data +3 to +8 Elo at 768 wide; six probes of label/teacher variants all land within 1,000-game noise of each other, README:219), so I would not spend scarce hours here before the search-side results come back. 2) The web did not confirm Stockfish's exact loss exponent, lambda schedule effects or rescoring gains: Stockfish PR 4314 (https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/pull/4314) shows lambda 1.0 -> 0.75 schedule, skipping plies <= 28, depth-6 multipv-2 filtering of best-move captures, with +5.1 +-1.5 at 25k nodes but confounded with other changes; the same thread says skipping early plies LOST ~9 Elo on DFRC books at STC, so do not copy ply skipping (our filter starts at move 9, which is fine). Lambda below 1 vs our game-result mixing: our probes showed no separation at 1,000 games (README:207-219), so I do not propose a lambda search. 3) The Hugging Face dataset page linrock/test80-2024 has no dataset card. Fetched pages contained no instructions to AI models. 4) brain_err favours Stockfish's net because it is judged against Stockfish's own deep search and, per README, on its own distribution; part of the 18% gap is not recoverable by us. 5) Licence: nothing copied; no third-party source read."
}

proposals.title: Loss exponent probe (--pow 2.0 / 2.5) matched to the error our search feels
proposals.mechanism: Re-run the standing recipe probe (768 wide, 16 kings buckets, 32 queen-aware heads, half labels + half two teachers, 1.09B positions, one pass) with --pow 2.0 and --pow 2.5 in calc/train_nnue.py (line ~609: loss = |sigmoid(out)-target|^pow, already implemented, never run on this line, README:597). Rationale: log-loss over-weights decided positions, where the search never needs precision, while alpha-beta decisions live in the mid-range; our metric of record (brain_err, squared expected-score error) is exactly a power-2 loss and the SF net leads us there by 18% while tying us on pair choice. I recall Stockfish's own trainer using a power around 2.5 on win-chance error, but could not confirm this on the web, so treat it as memory, not evidence. Judge by brain_err (ext/brain_err.py) and the match, NOT by held-out log-loss, which will get worse by construction. Because the exponent changes the effective scale of the exported value, also play each probe at EvalScale 80/100/120 (a too-large scale costs far more than too-small, README:207-215).
proposals.evidence: Weak-to-moderate and indirect: README:597 lists --pow as never run; brain_err numbers (ext/README.md around line 582: BIGM 24.0, BIGS 22.7, BIGX 22.2, SF net 18.6) show a squared-error gap that our current objective does not directly minimise; steeper labels (--sharp 2) gave +5 (-6 to +16) vs reference and -209/-210 vs -218 at 10k nodes (README:320-323), showing the objective shape moves play a little. No external controlled Elo figure found (web search could not confirm nnue-pytorch's exponent).
proposals.expected_elo: -5 to +10 at 10+0.1; most likely +0 to +4
proposals.cheap_test: Two probes from scratch on the 1.09B mix (~20 min each on the 4080, per vault_vault_probe.log), then ext/brain_err.py on the 15,553 positions (minutes), then 2,000 games at 30,000 nodes vs the r0 reference (the existing probe harness). Only if brain_err drops by >=0.5 thousandths or the match is >= +10, play 1,000 games at 10+0.1.

proposals.title: Distribution-matched fine-tune mix: Stockfish 14.1 deep labels on positions from OUR search trees
proposals.mechanism: Collect ~20-30M leaf and interior positions visited by our engine at 100k-300k nodes on its own matches/analysis (the quiet-after-qsearch ones plus the awkward post-pruning ones human games never contain), label them with Stockfish 14.1 at ~20k-50k nodes (binary is already used for matches; this is use as an oracle, not source reading) or with the 4M-node-style reference at small scale, and mix 10-20% into a from-scratch recipe or a low-LR fine-tune together with the existing data. This differs from the failed self-play generations (README:498-515, G1b -18) because the label comes from a stronger searcher than the player, not from our own 5,000-node search. FIRST run a diagnostic: bucket brain_err by source (held-out human-game positions vs search-tree positions). If error on tree positions is much higher, the shift is real.
proposals.evidence: Indirect. README (~line 186) states the quality-test positions were chosen by our own search and that 'this biases this test against our networks by an unknown amount' - i.e. our nets are already known to do worse on search-chosen positions; Stockfish's own nets are trained on its self-play data (S1/S2 files) which we found worth about +65 Elo at probe scale over Lichess-only data (README:207-220), so the engine-game distribution does matter. Counter-evidence: generations with shallow self labels hurt (README:498-515), and 85% engine-game share was -9 (README:341), so the benefit saturates around half-and-half.
proposals.expected_elo: -5 to +15; unknown sign until the diagnostic is read
proposals.cheap_test: Diagnostic (1h, no new labelling needed beyond ~20k positions at 200k nodes, which README:183 shows was done once before): MSE of BIGS on search-tree positions vs held-out Lichess positions, against SF 4M-node truth. If the ratio is >1.3, label 20M positions (24 threads, ~1,500-2,000 positions/s at 20k nodes, roughly 3-4 h wall, competing with matches for CPU), fine-tune BIGS with a 20% mix at LR 3e-4 for one pass on 1B positions (~20 min), compare against the matched-control without the new data (as ext/gen_round.sh does), 2,000 games at 30,000 nodes.

proposals.title: Transformer value as a third teacher on a cached subset of quiet positions
proposals.mechanism: Add the L2 transformer's value (batch inference on the 4080, offline) as a third term in the teacher mean (--distill ...+sf:...+<ouro cache>) for a probe on a cached 100-200M positions subset of the mix, restricted to quiet positions where the transformer leads (75.6-76.0% vs 73.2% pair accuracy, README ~line 679). Stay at dw 0.5. Cache the transformer's logits once to disk (a teacher function over a cache replaces TEACH in train_nnue.py line ~447-453) so the probe runs at normal speed.
proposals.evidence: Weak. Teachers helped consistently (half labels + half SF net +38 vs labels only, README:262-267; BIGS two teachers +16 vs BIGM, README:477-480) and the transformer is the best judge of quiet positions we have. But README:706-710 and fact 7 (sibling-pair training learns the pairs, 71.3->73.1% held out, with zero transfer to deep play) say the fast network lacks the means to represent what the transformer sees, and a teacher added to a finished network gave only +7 (-4 to +18, README:275-277). Throughput of the L2 server for bulk labelling is unmeasured by me; at the 7 ms Python path it is useless, it needs a direct batched GPU path.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +8 at equal nodes; probably 0 at the clock
proposals.cheap_test: Check first with an existing instrument: take the 15,553-position brain_err set and score the transformer's value MSE against the 4M reference; if it is not clearly below BIGS's 22.7 there is nothing to distil. If it is, cache 150M positions (estimate 1-3 h at plausible 20-50k positions/s batched; unmeasured), train a probe with the 3-teacher mean on that subset against a 2-teacher control on the same subset, 2,000 games at 30,000 nodes.

summary: Our 16 mirrored buckets with a shared table plus a per-bucket correction is already at the saturation point: your own probes give 7 buckets ~= 16 ~= 32 (held-out loss 0.54263 / 0.54250 / 0.54253), and 32 buckets gave -3 Elo-equivalent at 768 wide. Open engines report the same pattern (gains from bucket count shrink with data, mirroring and a factoriser are the real wins, and you already have both). The input-bucket layout is therefore not where the gap is; the remaining cheap bucket-adjacent wins are the already-planned 32 queen-aware output heads and, for speed, refresh avoidance. The one structurally new input idea with large measured upside in open engines is threat inputs, but it is costly and x86 results are mixed.
warnings: The web results about other engines' bucket Elo (pawnstar, etc.) are self-reported fixed-depth numbers on different data, not comparable; the Stockfish 18 threat-input figures come from a release tweet and forum posts, no SPRT logs read. No injected instructions found in the fetched pages. I did not read Stockfish source. Conclusion that the layout is saturated rests on loss differences of ~0.0001 and a -3 (-14 to +9) match at 30k nodes, which is within noise, so a different layout could still matter by a few Elo but is not worth testing.

proposals.title: Ship 32 queen-aware read-out heads in the standing net (do not spend more on input buckets)
proposals.mechanism: Retrain the standing recipe (768 wide, 16 mirrored shared+correction buckets, half labels / half teachers) with --buckets 32 --obk 2 (piece count x my queen x opponent queen) and export; keep the king-bucket layout exactly as is. Optionally sanity-check that dropping to 7 buckets does not lose play, which would free training capacity, but do not pursue more input buckets.
proposals.evidence: ext/README.md:607-611: 32 queen-aware heads +11 (0 to +22) vs r0 at 30k nodes, zero runtime cost; ext/README.md:237 and :281: 32 input buckets -3 and no better than 1024 wide alone; ext/README.md:363-364: held-out loss plain 0.54447, 16 buckets 0.54250, 32 buckets 0.54253, 7 buckets 0.54263 (layout saturated); ext/README.md:58-61 bucketing itself gave +33 at 30k nodes but BIGK2 with more data -2. Weak point: +11 was measured vs a probe, one pass, 1.09B positions; transfer to BIGS-scale and to the clock is untested, and fact 4 shows evaluator quality is not the bottleneck.
proposals.expected_elo: +0 to +8 at 10+0.1 vs SF14.1 (evaluator already matches SF net; the rest is search efficiency)
proposals.cheap_test: Already designed: 2,000-game 30k-node match vs the current BIGS-recipe probe plus the quality-instrument run at 300k nodes (target below -0.1 unit, SE 0.3, so likely undetectable) and a 1,000-game 10+0.1 vs SF14.1.

proposals.title: Finny-table (per-bucket cached accumulator) refresh to cut king-move refresh cost
proposals.mechanism: Keep, per perspective and per (mirrored) king bucket, a cached accumulator plus the piece bitboards it was built from. On a king move that crosses bucket or the mirror flag, instead of rebuilding from all ~30 pieces, diff the current position against the cached bitboards of the target bucket and apply only the add/sub differences, then store back. Compare whole perspective state (bucket and mirror flag), not just the bucket index, to avoid wrong evals. With 16 buckets and a 768-wide int16 accumulator the cache is 16*2*768*2 B = 48 KB per thread; fits L1/L2. Cost per refresh falls from ~30 row adds to typically 4-10.
proposals.evidence: Common practice in open engines using king buckets (pattern described in several repos, e.g. https://github.com/reckless-technology/pawnstar/pull/38 notes refresh-state pitfalls); no clean Elo figure found, so evidence is weak. Our own facts: 1.1-1.3 Mnps (fact 10) and every node-speed gain converts to quality because Stockfish needs 1/2-1/3 of our nodes; need to profile how large the refresh share is in calc_s19.c (lazy accumulators already avoid some).
proposals.expected_elo: +0 to +6 (depends on the refresh share of node time; if under 5% of time it is worth nothing)
proposals.cheap_test: First a 10-minute perf profile / counter: fraction of evaluations that trigger a full king-bucket refresh and their cycles share. Only if share >5%, implement and compare nodes/s on the bench (ext/nodetime.py) and run a 1,000-game 10+0.1 match against the old build (identical network, results should be bit-identical in nodes searched, so a 2,000-position bench-signature check validates correctness).

proposals.title: Threat inputs as a small extra feature block (only if the budget allows a full retrain)
proposals.mechanism: Add a sparse second input block to the first layer: for each (attacker piece type, attacked piece type, relation square) a small set of features, e.g. 'piece X on square s attacks/defends piece Y' reduced to (attacker type x victim type x victim square, mirrored with the king bucket), updated incrementally on moves. The repo already has an attack-map trainer path (calc/train_nnue.py --am, 'not yet in the engine') which is the cheapest route to measure the information value before engine work: train 768-wide with --am for one pass on 1.09B positions and compare the held-out loss and the 30k-node match.
proposals.evidence: Stockfish 18 release: up to +46 Elo over SF17, driven by SFNNv10 threat inputs (https://x.com/stockfishchess/status/2017624780430614998). TalkChess thread https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?t=85656: 20-25% speed loss vs same-size non-threat net, a STC regression at first, gain grows with time control, ~+15 on ARM but roughly neutral on x86 at the time of that post (informal, unverified). Our README line 596-600: --am 'not yet in the engine', and attack maps never run at this scale. Caution: our evaluator already ties SF's net on static judgment (fact 4), and a 20-25% slowdown costs ~ the same as it gains at our time control.
proposals.expected_elo: -10 to +10; speculative, likely neutral at 10+0.1
proposals.cheap_test: Held-out loss and quiet-pair accuracy of a one-pass --am probe vs the r0 probe (0.54415) using the existing ext/vault_probe.sh; proceed to engine work only if loss drops by more than ~0.002 (the size of the 16-bucket gain), which would signal a real information gain.

summary: The transformer's training targets cover only the few moves the Lichess eval database labels (soft policy over labelled moves, tau=0.015, BCE per-move value on labelled moves only, lm/train_lm.py:51-63), on game-position distribution, whereas the search needs a ranking of ALL moves, especially the late quiet tail, at search-node positions. The DeepMind evidence says per-move Q over all ~29 legal moves is the right target, but its advantage largely vanishes at equal data (+252 vs +264 Elo state vs action at 40M points), and HL-Gauss vs log-loss is a wash, so changing the loss shape is a weak lever; changing label coverage and position distribution is the strong one. Honest ceiling: measured transformer-prior gain is already ~0 at 300k nodes (fact 5), so any objective change mainly helps ordering/reductions at depth, and the cheap offline tests should be run before any retraining.
warnings: No injected instructions seen in fetched pages. I did not run any measurements myself; all Elo ranges are guesses informed by facts 5 and 8 and should be treated as optimistic. The ChessBench table shows that most of the action-value advantage disappears at equal data points, so do not expect the objective form (HL-Gauss, two-hot) to matter. One flaw in our setup: policy and q heads are trained only on database-labelled top moves, so late-move behaviour (what ordering/LMR needs) is extrapolation, and the lm trainer's tau=0.015 makes the policy very sharp. The pending PolW/PolLmr result will tell whether any further LM investment is worth it: if the policy-based version shows zero gain at 300k nodes, deprioritise proposals 2 and 3 and keep only the free q-gap test.

proposals.title: Zero-training test first: use the existing per-move Q head (serve.py already returns q) for reductions as a sibling gap, not the policy softmax
proposals.mechanism: serve.py:30-34 already returns per-move values 'q' next to 'p'. In calc, for nodes with LmDepth or more plies left, compute gap_i = q_best - q_i (in win-prob or cp) for each quiet move and use it for the LMR adjustment (PolLmr) and for ordering, instead of or blended with log p_i. Reason: the policy was trained as a softmax over labelled moves with a sharp tau, which is calibrated for 'which is best' and says little about 'how much worse is the late move', which is what an LMR/LMP decision needs; the q head is trained per move with BCE on win prob so gaps are directly the quantity. Add options PolQ (weight of q gap in ordering) and QLmr (reduction per gap bucket, e.g. -1 ply if gap<0.01, +1 if gap>0.08).
proposals.evidence: Training targets: /home/user/seek/lm/train_lm.py:56-60 (policy softmax over labelled moves only; q BCE only on labelled moves). DeepMind searchless chess Table 2 (99M): action-value 83.3% puzzles, Kendall tau 0.259 vs state-value 77.5/0.215 vs behavioural cloning 65.7/0.116 (https://arxiv.org/html/2402.04494v2), i.e. per-move values rank moves better than policy-style targets. Caveat: our q head is only trained on the 1-5 labelled moves per position, so its tail gaps are untrained extrapolation; this is exactly what the test reveals. Evidence for the gain in our search is weak/none.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +8 at 10+0.1 (most likely ~0; fact 5 shows prior gain vanishing by 300k nodes)
proposals.cheap_test: Quality test at 30k and 300k nodes, 8964 positions, 22 workers (the lm/lmtree_test.sh pattern, ~minutes per cell): compare PolW/PolLmr (policy) vs q-gap variants vs both; first offline check on ~2000 deep nodes: Spearman between q-gap and the engine's actual re-search fail-low depth of late moves.

proposals.title: Fine-tune on all-legal-move Q labels at SEARCH-NODE positions (fix label coverage and distribution shift), with a cutoff-move target
proposals.mechanism: (a) Position source: dump FENs from calc itself at nodes with depth >= 8 plies left (all node types, including positions reached after weak moves that never occur in Lichess games) during quality-set-like runs; sample ~1-3M. (b) Labels, per legal move (ChessBench style, ~29 moves/position): score of the child from a fixed-depth/fixed-node search by our own engine or Stockfish 14.1 binary (MultiPV=all at ~20k nodes is ~1 s/position, so ~1M positions in ~12 h on 24 threads is too much for the budget; take 300-500k positions, ~4-6 h of machine time, at $0.28/h negligible money but real wall time). Also record the first cutoff move and the set of moves that fail low at reduced depth. (c) Objective: init from L2 weights (train_lm.py --init), keep old losses on Lichess shards at lower weight as regulariser, add per-move value as HL-Gauss/two-hot over 64-128 bins of win-prob (Gaussian sigma ~0.75 bin width) over ALL legal moves, plus a BCE head 'is cutoff/best at depth' per move. HL-Gauss is optional: it matched log-loss in DeepMind's ablation, but gives calibrated distributions for the gap computation in proposal 1 and is cheap to add. Fine-tune ~1-2 epochs of a few hundred thousand positions plus replay; ~30-60 min of GPU on the 4080S.
proposals.evidence: ChessBench labels every legal move (~29/board, 15.3B action values over ~530M boards) vs ours 1-5 labelled moves (https://arxiv.org/html/2402.04494v2). Table 2: HL-Gauss 82.0 puzzles/tau 0.257 vs log-loss 80.6/0.257 vs L2 80.8/0.240 (small effect; bins 16-256 within 83.0-84.4). Important counter-evidence in the same paper: with data points matched (40M), action-value +252 vs state-value +264 Elo: the target form matters much less than data volume. So the expected benefit comes from tail coverage and distribution match, which is my inference, not measured by anyone for alpha-beta guidance. Our own related result: a learned LMR model reached AUC 0.907 vs 0.822 but was level in play (README fact 8), a warning that better offline ranking may not convert.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +10 (ordering/reduction guidance only; pessimistic end likely given fact 5 and the learned-LMR precedent)
proposals.cheap_test: Offline first (~1 h after data exists): on held-out search-node positions measure (i) top-1 and top-3 cutoff-move rate of transformer ordering vs calc's own history/killer ordering, (ii) AUC of 'move fails low at reduced depth' for q-gap vs engine's current LMR features. Only if transformer adds clear information beyond history (e.g. AUC gain >0.03 when combined) run quality test at 100k/300k nodes with PolW/PolLmr on the new checkpoint.

proposals.title: Policy target from search-derived cutoff statistics instead of eval-database multipv, to give the net a job distinct from the evaluator
proposals.mechanism: Replace the soft-policy target exp((wps-wps0)/tau) over database moves by an empirical distribution from our alpha-beta search: at each logged deep node, target = indicator/soft mass on the move that produced the beta cutoff (or the best move at node end), with PV/cut/all node-type as an extra input token or conditioning bit. This trains P(move causes cutoff) directly, which is what ordering and LMR consume, and can be used with the 2-3-token approach already in model.py (policy head, 4288 moves). Combine with the per-move heads of proposal 2 in one fine-tune rather than a separate run.
proposals.evidence: Leela moved from RL policy to training the policy to replicate MCTS visit statistics (unverified forum quote: https://hn.nuxtjs.org/item/25759430), but visit counts do not map to alpha-beta, so cutoff statistics are the alpha-beta analogue. No published number for this in alpha-beta engines was found; mainstream Stockfish uses handcrafted ordering with no learned policy (low-authority source: chessbio.com policy-network glossary). So evidence is weak/inferential.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +5; mostly redundant with proposal 2, which is why it should be merged into it
proposals.cheap_test: Same offline top-1/top-3 cutoff-move rate as proposal 2 using only the cutoff head; no match needed unless it beats calc's history ordering by a clear margin (e.g. +5 points top-1 at cut nodes).

summary: Data is not the binding constraint: the pilot (5.8M params, 15M positions, 18 min) already beats SF14 net on quiet pairs, and the deep results (facts 5/6) did not move when the transformer improved, so more/better transformer data alone is unlikely to buy Elo at 10+0.1. The cheapest real data upside is that the Lichess eval DB has grown to ~418M positions (we used 257M; HF mirror ~1B rows, 44 GB parquet, CC0, updated monthly), and ChessBench gives dense all-legal-move action values (free, CC0/CC-BY) that fill a verified labelling gap in our q-head (only top-5 moves labelled). The only proposal with real Elo potential is using the transformer as a data labeller (teacher) for the fast net on quiet positions, which is a different experiment from the failed sibling-pair one, but confidence is low.
warnings: Measurement/approach flags: (1) Fact 5/6 imply that no data improvement for the transformer will move the 10+0.1 result unless the transformer is used inside the tree, which the Python server (7 ms/reply, single Python thread) cannot support at 1M nps; data work therefore has low expected Elo and I would put the GPU hours elsewhere (search efficiency, fact 3). (2) Leela training data: storage.lczero.org training_data exists, licence stated in a 2021 Leela blog as Open Database License / Database Contents License (https://draft.lczero.org/blog/2021/06/the-importance-of-open-data), but I could not verify current layout, sizes or terms (older notes say tar.gz of 10k-game chunks; V6 chunk format is large and needs lc0 tooling); labels are self-play visit counts and Q for lc0 nets, not Stockfish evals, so it does not match our target pipeline and I recommend skipping it. (3) The ChessBench HF/GitHub page lists action-value train as 1.1 TB (a '1.2 GB' number in my fetch looked like the test column swapped; sizes: action-value test 141 MB, BC train 34 GB, state-value train 36 GB), treat sizes as approximate. ChessBench dataset licence is mixed (CC0 for Lichess-derived parts, CC-BY-4.0 for the rest): attribution needed if weights are redistributed. (4) No injected instructions seen in the pages fetched (arxiv, lichess database page, github searchless_chess, HF dataset card, web search results). (5) The ChessBench paper figures I report are from the arxiv HTML summary via a small model; the 2299 Elo / 95.4% puzzle numbers are as I know them and consistent. (6) Our quality instrument cannot detect effects below ~0.6 units (~25 Elo) at 300k nodes with one run, so +3 Elo proposals are untestable by it; gate on the brain_quiet/brain_metric pair metrics instead."]

proposals.title: Distil the transformer's quiet-position judgment into BIGS via relabelling (teacher labels, not database sibling pairs)
proposals.mechanism: Take ~100-200M quiet positions (already in the BIGS training set, filtered where captures/checks do not change BIGS score by >X cp, as in ext/brain_quiet.py). Run L2 (or L1p) in fp16 batch inference on the 4080 to get its value (and optionally per-move values for the quiet best two moves). Fine-tune BIGS with a target mix: current half-labels + w*L2 value (w~0.25-0.5), same recipe/epoch count as the c0 control in the sib probe so the control is matched. Gate on ext/brain_quiet.py quiet-pair accuracy (BIGS 73.2% -> hope >=74.5%, transformer 75.6-76.0%) BEFORE spending quality-test time. Difference from the failed sib probe (fact 7): that used database pair labels the net could learn but not transfer; here the target is the transformer's own smooth function, which carries what the database labels did not (the transformer transferred from the same labels).
proposals.evidence: Transformer quiet-pair 76.0/75.6% vs BIGS 73.2% vs SF net 72.0% (ext/README.md lines 675-688). Sibling fine-tune learned 71.3->73.1% held-out pairs but 70.68->71.25% on deep pairs, no deep transfer (README 690-704). README line 701-703 itself says what is missing is the means to see relations, not the signal, so distillation to a 768-wide MLP net may hit the same wall (BIGX width did not help). Throughput: training ran 14,200 pos/s for the pilot; inference should be several times faster (my estimate, not measured), so 150M positions is roughly 1-2 GPU hours. No external evidence found of transformer-to-NNUE distillation at this scale; weak.
proposals.expected_elo: -5 to +15 Elo at 10+0.1 (most likely ~0); the gate metric will show quickly if it is dead
proposals.cheap_test: Step 1 (30 min): label 5M held-out quiet positions with L1p/L2, check teacher-student agreement and that L2 value correlates with SF-4M value better than BIGS does (ext/brain_metric.py). Step 2 (~2 h): fine-tune BIGS on 20M relabelled positions vs matched control, read quiet-pair accuracy via ext/brain_quiet.py. Only if >=+1.0 pt, run the 300k-node quality test (SE 0.3 units) and then a 1,000-game match.
proposals.where_in_our_code: lm/serve.py or a new batch-label script reading lm shards (lm/prep_lm.py format); calc/train_nnue.py target mix (it already supports teacher labels, 'two teachers'); eval via ext/brain_quiet.py and ext/quality.py

proposals.title: Add ChessBench action-value shards to train the per-move value head on ALL legal moves (fills the q-head's selection-bias gap)
proposals.mechanism: train_lm.py (lines 51-63) trains the per-move head ql only on the <=5 labelled candidate moves per position (l_q masked by valid), so q for the other ~30 legal moves, the ones LMR/LMP ordering must reject, is never supervised and is pure extrapolation; the policy gets pushed down on them only through softmax normalisation. ChessBench action-value data labels every legal move with a Stockfish-16 win probability (15.3B records over ~530M states; train split 2,148 shards; format .bag read by bagz.py; whole set ~1.1 TB but shards are independent, download 10-30 shards = ~5-15 GB). Convert win prob to our wps, mix 20-30% of each batch from ChessBench with the full-legal-move loss for ql (keep policy loss restricted to top moves, e.g. drop moves with wp < best - 0.1 from the target so the policy does not learn from 50 ms labels), keep Lichess deep labels for the value/policy heads. Then re-test PolW/PolLmr (fact 11) with the q-head or policy from this model.
proposals.evidence: ChessBench: https://github.com/google-deepmind/searchless_chess (sizes above; code Apache-2.0, dataset CC0 for Lichess parts and CC-BY-4.0 otherwise); paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04494: action-value targets beat state-value (puzzle 83.3 vs 77.5 vs 65.7% BC) in the ablation, but at equal data size (40M points) state-value matches action-value, so the advantage is mostly data volume. Models there are far bigger/longer trained (9M model = 2025 tournament Elo, 88.9% puzzles, 10M steps x 4096 on 128 TPUs; our budget is ~4 orders smaller). Caveat: labels are 50 ms Stockfish 16, much shallower than Lichess depth 30+ evals, so use them for 'is this move bad' not for fine ranking. Our L1p already gets 55.3% best-move on the ChessBench test, so there is no evidence the held-out metric limits us. No measured Elo effect; mechanism is my inference from the code.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +8 Elo, and only if the in-progress PolW/PolLmr run (fact 11) shows the policy has any use inside the tree; otherwise 0
proposals.cheap_test: Download 5 shards (~2-3 GB), fine-tune L1p 20 min with the mixed loss, compare on (a) ChessBench test blunder rate / value error (currently 4.0% / 0.044) and (b) the rank of the true-best move among all legal moves for the q-head vs current; if blunder rate falls below ~3.5% rerun the PolLmr quality test at 300k nodes. Skip entirely if fact 11 comes back null.
proposals.where_in_our_code: lm/train_lm.py:51-63 loss_fn (l_q masking), lm/prep_lm.py (add a ChessBench converter; needs bagz.py reader from the DeepMind repo, Apache-2.0)

proposals.title: Refresh the transformer corpus with the grown Lichess eval database (418M positions vs the 257M we used) and train L2 on deduplicated data
proposals.mechanism: The Lichess evaluation database page now states 417,862,375 evaluated positions (CC0, jsonl.zst; depth typically 31-36, use highest-depth eval first PV); the HF mirror Lichess/chess-position-evaluations has 1,003,347,246 rows, 44.1 GB parquet, CC0-1.0, one PV per row (multiple rows per FEN = the multi-candidate lines), updated monthly (last Oct 7 2026). Our shards cover 171M positions from the 257M snapshot. Rebuild with the HF parquet (pull with the hf CLI, no jsonl parsing), keep positions of the new ~160M not seen before, dedupe by FEN-hash, and only continue L2 training on the new positions rather than a restart. Prefer this over more epochs because the pilot/L2 comparison at 6% suggests the run is data-limited only mildly (held-out 50.4% after 6% vs pilot 51.6% full).
proposals.evidence: https://database.lichess.org/#evals (417,862,375 positions, CC0); https://huggingface.co/datasets/Lichess/chess-position-evaluations (1.003B rows, 44.1 GB, CC0-1.0, updated Oct 2026). ChessBench scaling (https://arxiv.org/html/2402.04494 section 3.3): accuracy rises with dataset size for every model size, overfitting only at 10K games for >=7M params; at 171M positions a 14M model is not near overfitting, so new unique positions matter less than steps. Our own result (README 641-655): a better transformer did not change deep results. Expect a small held-out gain (<=0.5 pt best-move) and no clock effect.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +3 Elo at the clock (transformer is only used at the root or low-weight ordering)
proposals.cheap_test: No GPU cost to check: compare FEN overlap of the new HF snapshot against our nine shards (script under 1 minute on a sample) to see how many unique positions are really new; if <100M new, drop the proposal. Otherwise append 2 shards to the L2 run and read held-out best move / ChessBench test.
proposals.where_in_our_code: lm/prep_lm.sh, lm/prep_lm.py, ext/lichess_hf.sh (already fetches from HF), ext/lconv.c

summary: Architecture is not where the missing Elo is: a better root-prior transformer has already measured ~0 at the clock (fact 5), and the leaf-judging test (fact 6) shows that even a strong static judge does not help through search. The one architectural fact with a measured effect is that exact rule relations are worth a lot for the transformer (repo ablation: no-relations blunder rate 22% vs 15% at similar steps, and ChessBench-style literature shows GAB/relative bias +40 to +83 Elo over absolute encoding), and the fast net lacks exactly that, so the strongest proposal is to move the relations into the fast net as threat inputs, gated by a no-engine quiet-pair test. Transformer-side changes (smolgen, unshared blocks instead of loops, size at fixed latency) are cheap to test but should be expected to give about 0 at the clock unless the pending PolW/PolLmr run shows policy quality at inner nodes matters.
warnings: 1) Repo ablations (logs/ab2_*, logs/abl_*) are tiny (about 2M parameters, under 1k steps) and compared at unequal steps, so they only show that rules help a lot and that loops matter little, not by how much at 14M. 2) I did not find a number in ext/README.md for any smolgen run, and I could not find final L2 results (the logs dir has no L2/L1 jsonl), so L2's final quality is unknown to me. 3) I could not verify an Elo figure for Stockfish threat inputs; one source claims they never shipped in 17.1 and others date them to SFNNv10 / Stockfish 18; fishtest data not retrieved. 4) The Stockfish documentation/commit pages were read via search summaries only, I did not fetch Stockfish source code. 5) Third-party reimplementation (slackfish) numbers are 256-game matches with wide CIs and a different codebase. 6) No injected instructions seen in fetched pages. 7) Licence: only design ideas from Lc0 (GPL-3) and the Chessformer paper were read in descriptions, no code copied. 8) One structural point for the lead: fact 6 plus fact 5 say a stronger static judge or prior has so far not reached play, so I would rank any pure transformer-architecture change below changes that cut search nodes (my angle's expected return is small)."}

proposals.title: Give the fast net the transformer's missing ingredient: attack/threat relation inputs (gate it on quiet-pair accuracy before touching the engine)
proposals.mechanism: ext/README.md (sib-probe section) concludes the fast net lacks 'the means to see' relations between pieces, not the teaching signal; the transformer's edge is concentrated in quiet pairs (+2.4 to +2.8 points over BIGS). Add sparse 'threat' features to the NNUE input set on top of the 768x16 piece-square features: for each (attacker piece type+square, attacked piece type+square) pair, in the style of Stockfish's newest threat inputs (own/opp, mirrored by king bucket, redundant reverse pairs removed). Step 1, no engine: add the feature extractor to calc/train_nnue.py as an extra sparse block feeding the same first layer (an additional embedding table summed into the accumulator, zero-initialised), train a control and a threat net with the identical recipe on the same ~0.5-1B positions, and score both with ext/brain_quiet.py / brain_metric.py (quiet-pair choice, 10,334 clear cases). Step 2 only if quiet-pair accuracy rises by >= 1.5 points: implement incremental threat updates in calc_s19.c (a move changes the attack sets of only the moved piece and the sliders whose rays it opens or closes; cap with a per-move changed-feature list), measure nps loss, then run the quality test at 300k nodes and a 1,000-game match. Teacher-side alternative to test in the same run: add L2's value on quiet positions as an extra label term (cheaper, no engine change, but the sibling-pair result in fact 7 warns that learning the labels alone did not transfer).
proposals.evidence: Repo: logs/abl_full.jsonl vs logs/abl_norule.jsonl (same tiny model, rules off: blunder rate 22.4% at step 750 vs 15.4% at step 450 with rules, policy loss 2.78 vs 2.46, i.e. relations dominate what the transformer learns early). Repo: ext/README.md lines ~680-705 (quiet pairs: BIGS 73.2, SF net 72.0, transformer 75.6-76.0; sibling fine-tune learned in-distribution 71.3->73.1 without transfer; width BIGX 1536 no better). External: Stockfish added 'Full Threats' inputs on top of HalfKAv2_hm in SFNNv10 (https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/commit/8e5392d79a36aba5b997cf6fb590937e3e624e80 ; docs https://official-stockfish.github.io/docs/nnue-pytorch-wiki/docs/nnue.html); I could not retrieve a fishtest Elo for it and I recall a gain of several tens of Elo only from memory, so treat the external size of effect as unverified. Chessformer table 5 (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.19091v1): relative/geometric bias +40 / +83 Elo over absolute at equal size, which supports 'relations are worth a lot' but is for a transformer, not for NNUE.
proposals.expected_elo: -5 to +25 Elo at 10+0.1 single thread (wide: threat features cost nps, perhaps 10-25% at 1.2M nps, which is ~-10 to -20 Elo by itself, so the eval gain must beat that; the search-efficiency gap (120 Elo) is not touched by this). Most likely outcome is about 0.
proposals.cheap_test: Step 1 only: two equal-recipe trainings of ~0.5B positions on the GPU (control vs threats), then ext/brain_quiet.py and ext/brain_metric.py quiet-pair accuracy; no engine build, no match. Kill if quiet-pair gain < 1.5 points. Roughly 2 x 3 h GPU, small CPU time.

proposals.title: Transformer at equal latency: untested smolgen, unshared blocks instead of loops, and size (the GPU is latency-bound, not the model)
proposals.mechanism: Three pilot-sized 18-minute trainings in the L1p recipe (d=?, same data shards, lm/train_lm.py already has --smolgen), each compared to the L1p numbers (held-out best move 51.6%, ChessBench 55.3% / 4.0% blunders / value err 0.044): (a) --smolgen 128 (model.py already implements the shared 8-number token squeeze -> bottleneck -> per-head 64x64 bias, zero-initialised, one generator for recurrent and one for output block); (b) loops=1 with n_rec raised so compute is equal (e.g. n_rec 4 loops 2 -> n_rec 8 unshared loops 1; at inference same FLOPs and about the same kernel count, double the parameters, no state-resumption machinery), because Lc0 and Chessformer use 8-15 unshared layers and no one has shown looped sharing winning at equal compute; (c) heads 8 -> 16 with head dim 16 (Lc0 reports head depth down to 8 helps once smolgen is on). Separately measure the latency of the existing 5.8M and 14.3M models on the 4080 at batch 1..64 in lm/serve.py: with python-chess parsing and move generation being the bottleneck (lm/serve.py lines 27-30, engine.py Net.evaluate legal()), the 14.3M model and even a 30-60M one probably cost nothing extra in latency, so the size scale-up should be chosen by training budget, not by latency.
proposals.evidence: Repo: logs/ab2_full.jsonl vs logs/ab2_noloop.jsonl at step 800/900: loop count barely matters at tiny scale (top-1 37.3/37.9/37.9% for loops k=1/2/4 with loops vs 37.9/37.5/37.0% for no-loop training; differences ~0.5 point, within noise, only a ~2 M-parameter model and 800 steps, so weak). model.py:212-275 (smolgen implemented but ext/README.md never reports a smolgen run: it is untested). Lc0 blog (https://lczero.org/blog/2024/02/transformer-progress/): smolgen = 'play as if 50% larger with 10% throughput loss', head depth gains down to 8, FFN 1x->4x almost no gain. Slackfish reimplementation (https://github.com/leungt30/slackfish/pull/28): smolgen +67 Elo (CI +31..+106) at equal time and +96 at depth 2, but 36% slower in search at batch 20-64, and a separate 8-head ablation ties. Chessformer (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.19091v1): GAB-4M +83 Elo vs absolute; no depth-vs-width ablation exists there either. Caveat: our exact rule biases already supply most of what smolgen supplies, so the marginal gain is likely smaller than the published ones.
proposals.expected_elo: About 0 (-3 to +5) at the clock for the root prior, because fact 5 says a better transformer did not change the deep result. Worth ~+0.3 to +0.8 units (12-30 Elo) at 30k nodes at most. It matters only if the pending PolW/PolLmr run is positive, in which case policy accuracy at inner nodes is the lever.
proposals.cheap_test: Three 18-minute pilot trainings plus lm/train_lm.py evals (CB best move / blunders / value error) against L1p; then only for the winner run ext/brain_lm.py quiet pairs. No engine run until the PolW result is known. Do not start these until the PolW/PolLmr result is in.

proposals.title: Cut transformer call latency 7 ms -> ~1 ms so it can be asked at many more nodes (fixed-shape GPU graph, board encoding from the C engine)
proposals.mechanism: The model's GPU compute is not the cost; the reply path is python-chess FEN parse + legal-move generation + JSON/text in a single Python thread. Let the C engine send the 64-square byte encoding (board, castle, ep) and its own legal-move list indices (from*64+to with promotion info) over the socket, so the server only does tensor copy + forward; capture the forward as a fixed-batch CUDA graph (batch sizes 1,4,16,64; the model.py graph relations are already tensor-only: RuleGraph and Block are pure torch ops, torch.compile mode reduce-overhead or manual torch.cuda.CUDAGraph), return policy logits for the sent legal moves only. Do requests asynchronously from the search (search issues the call at the node, continues with other moves, uses the prior if it arrives, as many engines do for lazy policy) so the clock cost is never a blocking ~7 ms. With the PolW/PolLmr ordering and reduction use currently limited to >= 8 plies (~250 calls per 300k nodes), a 5-10x cheaper call is the precondition for testing >= 4-5 plies (several thousand calls per search), which is where a quiet-move ordering and reduction signal could give search-efficiency gains, the 120 Elo gap.
proposals.evidence: Repo: lm/serve.py lines 20-37 and engine.py:50-64 (python-chess boards and legal-move generation per request on the critical path; ext/README.md states ~7 ms per reply and that the single Python thread is the bottleneck). Fact 8 (learned LMR with AUC 0.907 vs 0.822 stayed level in play) is a warning that better move-quality prediction alone does not turn into Elo; fact 5 says the transformer root prior is worth ~0 at 300k nodes. No external evidence for the Elo of inner-node transformer policies in alpha-beta; weak. External for cheap GPU batching feasibility only: Lc0 reports throughput measured in thousands of positions/s per GPU for much larger nets (https://lczero.org/blog/2024/02/transformer-progress/ gives no latency numbers, so none quoted).
proposals.expected_elo: -5 to +10 (it only enables the experiment above; value comes from the PolW result and a deeper LmDepth). I would not start it unless the PolW run at >= 8 plies is positive in the quality test, since otherwise the extra calls can only cost clock time.
proposals.cheap_test: Step 0 (30 minutes, no engineering): run the pending PolW/PolLmr quality test at LmDepth 8 vs 6 vs 5 at 300k nodes with the existing slow server (calls cost no node budget in the quality test); if the unit does not improve as LmDepth decreases, drop this proposal. Only if it does improve: implement the C-side encoding + CUDA-graph server and re-measure the clock match.

summary: Self-play generations for the transformer are very unlikely to pay here: our own generation test on the fast net (ext/README.md:493-515) lost to its control, the transformer's teacher (Stockfish deep labels) is stronger than any search of ours, and its root-prior value is already ~0 at 300k nodes, so even a perfect generation gain lands where it is worth nothing. The literature I could verify gives no per-generation Elo for an external-teacher-plus-self-play setting; the one hard number I found is a ~260 Elo loss from fine-tuning on a fixed off-distribution set. The one version worth a cheap test is not self-play but on-distribution relabelling (DAgger style): positions from our own search and games, labelled by Stockfish 14.1 (a stronger teacher), and only after the pending PolW/PolLmr result shows the transformer can help inside the tree at all.
warnings: 1) The fast-net generation test (README:493-515) already shows the failure mode: when labels come from deeper analysis than your own search, self-play data lowers strength; the transformer is in the same situation (Stockfish 4M-node labels), so I advise against building a full AlphaZero-style generation loop. 2) The transformer's root-prior gain vanishes at 300k nodes and at the clock was -122 vs -111, so generation-driven accuracy gains have no known channel to Elo; the only untested channel is interior use (PolW/PolLmr, pending). 3) Self-play-vs-self-play match Elo overstates gains against other engines (Lc0 wiki); evaluate only on quality units / matches vs Stockfish. 4) Web results used: arxiv 2608.27757 was read through a summarising fetch, so numbers (260 Elo, 93.9->94.9%) are second-hand; the targeted-search-control paper PDF (arxiv 2302.12359) could not be read. No injected instructions seen in fetched pages. Licences: no code read or copied. Labelling via a Stockfish 14.1 binary over UCI is an oracle use and does not need its source, but check this fits the user's pending decision about Stockfish before running it.

proposals.title: On-distribution relabelling (DAgger round) of the transformer with a stronger teacher, gated on the PolW/PolLmr result
proposals.mechanism: Do NOT use our own search as the policy-improvement operator (it is weaker than the Stockfish-4M-node labels the transformer already learns from). Instead: (1) harvest ~1-2M positions that OUR search actually visits or reaches: positions from the 1,000-game 10+0.1 match logs vs Stockfish plus interior nodes (depth>=8, the nodes where PolW/PolLmr query it), prioritising 'unstable' positions where our 30k-node and 300k-node best moves disagree (fact 9: hash changes alone flip 19% of choices, so these are plentiful). (2) Label them with Stockfish 14.1 as an oracle process through UCI only (multipv 5, ~100k-500k nodes, win-chance per move, same label format as lm/prep_lm.py), no source needed; 24 threads give roughly 100-300k positions per hour at 100k nodes. (3) Fine-tune L1p/L2 on a mix: 30% new relabelled data, 70% old evaldb shards, low LR (as in the failed fast-net rounds, a high LR/high dose of new data hurt: G1b -18). (4) Control: same fine-tune on old shards only. Repeat for a second round only if round 1 beats its control in quality units.
proposals.evidence: Weak-to-moderate, mostly indirect. Directly relevant negative: ext/README.md:493-515, fast-net self-play generations, no child beat its parent, stronger dose clearly worse (G1b -18, 2,000 games) because labels already came from deeper analysis. Distribution-shift warning: a fixed-set/puzzle-only fine-tune loses ~260 Elo versus the base (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27757, abstract-level read, treat as unverified secondary detail; same paper reports its self-play RL stage moved puzzle accuracy only 93.9 -> 94.9% with strength level). Teacher-quality principle: Lc0 policy targets come from MCTS visits only because no stronger teacher exists (https://draft.lczero.org/blog/2018/10/lc0-training/); Grandmaster-level-without-search used Stockfish action-values as the target, not self-search (https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04494). No source gives an Elo per generation for an external-teacher setting; Stockfish NNUE docs describe iterating data generation with the previous net but publish no per-iteration Elo (https://github-wiki-see.page/m/official-stockfish/nnue-pytorch/wiki/Training-datasets). Our own transformer facts: prior worth -2.5 units at 30k, ~0 at 300k (README 'The transformer again'), so any gain must come via interior use (PolW/PolLmr), which is still pending.
proposals.expected_elo: Most likely 0 (-3 to +5) at 10+0.1 single thread. A better transformer did not change the 300k figure before (README: 'a better transformer did not change the deep figure'). Upside only if interior ordering/reduction use proves valuable and is limited by transformer accuracy on search-visited positions.
proposals.cheap_test: Gate first: read the PolW/PolLmr quality result; if no gain with the current pilot at 300k, STOP (accuracy is not the bottleneck). If it shows gain, run round 1: label 500k positions (~2-3 h of 24 threads while the GPU trains), fine-tune pilot for ~15 min vs control, then (a) held-out best-move accuracy on a split of the NEW distribution and on ChessBench, (b) ext/quality.py at 100k and 300k nodes with PolW+PolLmr on. Accept only if new beats control by >1 unit (SE ~0.3).
proposals.where_in_our_code: Position harvest: add a dump in calc/calc_s19.c at the points where lm calls are made (LmDepth path) or parse match PGNs; labelling: adapt lm/prep_lm.py (same shard format) to read a FEN list and query a Stockfish 14.1 binary over UCI; fine-tune: lm/train_lm.py with a new shard mix; eval: ext/quality.py, lm/lm_test.sh.

proposals.title: One-hour gate experiment: does search-derived policy target beat Stockfish-label target at all (kills or justifies any generation loop)
proposals.mechanism: Before building a loop, test its core premise on the pilot only. Take 2-3M positions already in the evaldb shards. Make two versions of the policy target: A = existing Stockfish-deep multi-candidate win-chance distribution (control); B = softmax of our own two-brain search root scores at 100k nodes (the AlphaZero improvement operator, ~0.1 s/position over 24 threads = ~2.5 h for 3M... so use 1M positions, ~50 min). Train the 5.8M pilot on equal numbers of positions with A vs B (same schedule, ~10 min each, 14k pos/s) plus A+B averaged. Compare held-out best-move accuracy vs Stockfish 4M labels (ext/brain_lm.py, 10,334 clear pairs, quiet pairs 76.0% pilot) and the 30k-node prior quality number (-2.53 for the pilot at prior 16/cap 80).
proposals.evidence: Predictive, not measured: our fast net got worse from its own 5,000-node search targets (README:503-515), while the transformer learned from Stockfish deep labels already beats BIGS/SF net on quiet pairs (76.0% vs 73.2%). The expected outcome is B < A; the value of running it is a cheap, definitive answer to the user's belief that generations are key, and to see whether the mixture A+B (label smoothing by search, a KL-regularised policy improvement as in https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27757 forward-KL-to-own-prior idea) helps at all. Search-vs-self-play Elo inflation warning: Lc0 wiki notes self-play gains overstate gains against other engines (https://lczero.org/dev/wiki/), which is why the metric must be vs Stockfish-labelled quality, not self-play matches.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 Elo directly (diagnostic). Probability >85% that B is worse than A and A+B is level; a win for A+B at the 1-unit level at 30k would justify only a modest follow-up.
proposals.cheap_test: As described: three 10-minute pilot trainings plus brain_lm.py and quality.py at 30k and 100k nodes. Needs ~1M positions searched at 100k nodes (CPU, 50 min on 24 threads) which also yields the 'unstable position' list used in proposal 1.
proposals.where_in_our_code: lm/train_lm.py (target construction), lm/prep_lm.py (shard writer), ext/brain_lm.py, ext/quality.py; search-score dump from calc/calc_s19.c root (multi-PV / TwoLines path in duo_uci.py).

summary: Evidence from our own logs says the transformer prior is worth about 100 Elo at 30k nodes and nothing at 300k, so a smaller or faster transformer student cannot beat the teacher; its only value is making calls cheap enough to be applied inside the tree. The one use not yet ruled out is a ~1 ms transformer called at about 5-10k-node intervals for ordering and reductions (PolW/PolLmr, currently pending with ~250 calls at 7 ms), and the fact-5 result (no clock gain) argues the benefit must come from the interior of the tree rather than the root. I found no published measurement of a distilled transformer policy used inside an alpha-beta search at this scale, so every Elo figure below is extrapolated from our own tables, not from literature.
warnings: I read only the transformer section of ext/README.md and grepped lm/serve.py; I did not read the model.py forward cost, so the FLOP and latency figures are my own arithmetic and not benchmarked. The web search turned up no direct evidence on distilling a transformer policy into an alpha-beta engine at this scale (Chessformer, arXiv 2605.19091, was not read in detail). Fact 8 (learned LMR with better AUC giving no Elo) and fact 7 imply all three proposals are likely to land near zero, and I consider proposal 1 the only one cheap enough to be worth doing first. The fetched search results contained no instructions aimed at the model.

proposals.title: Gate the PolW/PolLmr result before building anything: measure the call-budget curve, then only distil if interior calls help
proposals.mechanism: Do not train a student yet. When the pending PolW/PolLmr run finishes, run the same quality test with LmDepth swept (calls per search ~50/250/1000) and with a fake zero-latency oracle (answers precomputed offline for those positions, so latency is excluded). If the zero-latency version at 1000 calls gives less than -1.0 unit at 300k nodes, a student is worthless and the angle is closed; if it gives more than -1.5, build the student (proposal 2). Budget rule from facts 10 and 11: at 1.2M nps, 10,000 nodes is ~8 ms of search, so a 20% slowdown allows ~1.7 ms per call if the call is synchronous, or any latency if async with a batched cache (calls overlap with search and the cost is only the CPU side, which is the Python python-chess parse at ~1 ms).
proposals.evidence: ext/README.md lines ~620-660 (L1p prior -2.05 at 30k, -0.87 at 100k, -0.30 at 300k; no clock gain, -122 vs -111). Our own measured ~7 ms/reply with Python board parsing as the bottleneck. No external evidence; an inference from our tables.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +15 at 10+0.1 (most likely ~0); the real output is a go/no-go on the whole angle
proposals.cheap_test: Quality test at 300k nodes with LmDepth swept and a precomputed-oracle mode; roughly 1 CPU-hour of quality.py per setting.

proposals.title: Latency-first student: distil L2 (14.3M) into a ~1-2M-param, 1-loop student, served by in-process C inference (no Python, no python-chess)
proposals.mechanism: Train the student on L2 outputs (soft policy over 4288 moves via KL, value and per-move value via MSE on the 171M positions already prepared), with 1 loop of the shared block and d_model about 128, fp16 weights in training and int8 weight/activation post-training quantisation afterwards. Because attention is over 64 tokens with a fixed bias, a 1-2M model costs about 2 x params x 64 tokens = 0.15-0.25 GFLOP per position, which is ~20-40 microseconds on one core with AVX2 int8 and ~0.3 ms batched on the GPU. The measured 7 ms reply is dominated by Python board parsing and the socket, not the network; so the larger win is moving feature extraction (the 64 token inputs and the rule relation indices) into the engine's own board representation and sending a binary struct over shared memory, which removes the python-chess cost and makes ~1 ms round trips realistic. Run it asynchronously: search requests priors at a node, continues with default ordering and consumes the answer at the next visit via a TT-like cache keyed by hash. Choose the student by a latency table: for each of {0.5M, 1M, 2M, 5.8M(L1p)} report held-out best-move accuracy and quality-test delta at 30k nodes; the L1p already reaches 55.3% ChessBench best move, so the question is how much of that a 1M student keeps.
proposals.evidence: Param/latency estimate is arithmetic, not measured. Distillation with a stronger teacher works for Lc0 nets, dkappe's distilled 112x9 CPU nets and the CCRL 256x40 to 128x10 experiment (https://github.com/dkappe/leela-chess-weights/wiki/Distilled-Networks, https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?p=787865). Evidence for the main claim, that a distilled policy helps inside alpha-beta, is absent; weak. Our own results: 5.8M pilot 55.3% vs 2.0M old 48.9% best-move, and old 2M prior was within 0.6 units of the pilot at 30k (-1.44 vs -2.05), so a smaller student keeps much of the root benefit.
proposals.expected_elo: +0 to +10 at the clock if proposal 1 passes its gate; negative if the gate fails
proposals.cheap_test: Train the 1M student on the existing L2 shards for ~20 minutes (the pilot took 18 minutes at 14,200 pos/s), then run lm_test.sh at 30k and 100k nodes comparing to L1p; then a 300-game match at 10+0.1 only if it matches L1p within 0.3 units.

proposals.title: Put the prior inside the NNUE: distil the transformer policy into a cheap move-ordering head on the accumulators already computed
proposals.mechanism: Skip the separate network at all. Add a small policy head (from-square x to-square, 64x64 logits, or a 4288-wide output over the existing 2x768 accumulator after the clipped squared activation) to BIGS's output layer, trained on the transformer's soft move probabilities (L2 teacher) plus the Stockfish best-move label, with the trunk frozen so evaluation strength is untouched. Cost is one extra 768x(a few hundred) dot-product set at nodes where it is read (~5% nps if computed only at depth >= 6 non-PV nodes), with no Python or GPU. It is used as history-like ordering and as an LMR signal, replacing the PolW path. This reaches every node, not every ~1200th, which is where the transformer's knowledge cannot reach otherwise. Fact 7 is a caution: fast-net sibling-move training learned the pairs but did not transfer to the deep test, which suggests the information is already in the search; the head only has to beat history ordering, a much lower bar than beating the evaluator.
proposals.evidence: Fact 7 (sibling pairs 71.3 to 73.1%, no deep transfer) is evidence against transfer for the value side; fact 8 (a learned late-move-reduction model with AUC 0.907 vs 0.822 level in play) is strong evidence that better ordering/reduction predictors do not convert to Elo in our search. Both lower confidence here. Supportive only by analogy: Leela's policy head is what makes low node counts viable (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.19091 for a modern chess-model survey, not verified against our setting).
proposals.cheap_test: Train only the head on the existing BIGS accumulators for a few hundred million positions (hours of the 4080); check first-move cutoff rate and the ordering metric offline, then quality test at 300k nodes.

summary: The root-level time scaling is already an SF-style dynamic scheme (node fraction, stability, score drop, eval-volatility), so any LM hardness signal can only add the marginal gain over those three. The evidence that the transformer predicts hardness better is indirect: it is better at quiet-pair judgment (75.6-76.0% vs 73.2%) and fact 9 shows our choices are chaotic in 19% of positions. Search-internal use (singular prediction, extension) looks weak: singular tests are about 4% of nodes, the README's single-rule-off study shows no rule throws away the missed moves, and fact 6 shows LM value mixing hurts. The only proposals worth testing are a cheap oracle upper bound for time allocation, then an LM-feature hardness model for the clock, expected at most a few Elo.
warnings: I did not find internal evidence of any LM criticality predictor being trained; both proposals reuse existing heads and are unverified. The README's single-rule-off study (ext/README.md lines 564-572) says missed moves are near coin tosses, which caps what any hardness predictor can achieve. Web sources are individual engine GitHub PRs with self-reported SPRT numbers and small samples; treat as anecdotal. No injected instructions seen in fetched results. Search results gave no usable Stockfish 'complexity' evidence (I could not confirm what the 2019 'Scale down complexity' entry did), so I make no claim there. Honest expectation: the best Elo lever here is small compared with the 111 Elo gap, which is mainly search efficiency.

proposals.title: Gate then build: LM-feature hardness predictor for time allocation (oracle upper bound first)
proposals.mechanism: Step 1 (offline, no engine change): on the ~9,000 quality-instrument positions, take best move and move-quality at 100k/300k/1M nodes. Define hardness = quality(1M) - quality(300k) or 'chosen move changes between 300k and 1M'. Compute the oracle gain: reallocate the same total node budget across positions proportional to true hardness and read the quality change in units (x40 Elo). If the oracle gain is under ~1 unit, abandon. Step 2: one transformer call at the root (about 7 ms, ~2-5% of a 10+0.1 move) giving features: policy entropy, top-1 and top-2 probability, per-move-value gap between top two moves, LM value minus BIGS static value (disagreement), plus existing signals (root_vol, node fraction, stability). Fit a logistic regression on hardness and compare AUC with the existing signals alone. Step 3: if the added AUC is meaningful, multiply the existing `scale` in search_root (calc_s19.c:1982-1985, same place as the VOL_TM term) by a clipped factor (0.6-1.6) from the LM score; stop early when LM top-1 is above 0.9, and it agrees with search after depth 8.
proposals.evidence: Weak and indirect. Existing TM already has node-fraction, stability and drop terms plus a volatility term (calc_s19.c:1976-1985); this is the standard recipe, and other engines report +15 +/-7 Elo at 10+0.1 for adding stability scaling (https://github.com/LupeHiguera/ChessSI/pull/26), +27 +/-17 for smarter time use (https://github.com/conorosully27-cloud/Chess_Engine/pull/25), but those start from naive TM so our marginal gain is smaller. A separate analysis found extra time helps most right after the best move changes and vanishes beyond about +/-400 cp (https://github.com/changcheng967/Luminex/pull/45), which suggests the useful signal is mostly search-internal (score and move change), not LM. Fact 4 (LM 75.6-76% on quiet pairs) and fact 9 (19% move changes from hash size alone) show many positions are near coin tosses where more time cannot be predicted to help. No measurement exists of whether LM features add information beyond root_vol; that is exactly what step 2 tests.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +6 at 10+0.1 single thread (central guess +2). Clock-match noise at 1,000 games is about +/-12 Elo, so a gain this size cannot be confirmed by a match; decide by the offline oracle and AUC, not by match.
proposals.cheap_test: Steps 1-2 are purely offline on existing quality-instrument data plus one batched LM pass over the same 9,000 positions (a few minutes on the GPU via lm/serve.py). Only if the oracle gain is at least 1 unit and AUC rises by at least 0.03 over root_vol+node-fraction+stability, run one 1,000-game 10+0.1 match with the factor on vs off.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c search_root around lines 1976-1985 (tm_dynamic scale); root LM call plumbing like the existing LmDepth/OURO_SOCK code near line 1239; labels from ext/quality.py and zero/results logs; feature extraction via lm/serve.py.

proposals.title: LM-gated easy-move stop plus reinvestment into hard moves (two-sided time shift)
proposals.mechanism: Use the root policy and per-move values from one LM call to define an 'easy' class: LM top-1 prob above a threshold and top-1 per-move value above the second by a margin, and the engine's own root best equals the LM top-1 at depth >= 8 with no score drop. In that class cut the soft limit to about 35-45% of the base share (currently tm_soft=55 times scale, scale floor about 0.2 when frac is high). In the 'LM and search disagree on the top move' class (both confident but different), raise the limit up to the hard limit, since a disagreement indicates a position where extra search is most likely to change the move. Time saved in easy positions feeds the clock for later moves automatically via t/20 allocation.
proposals.evidence: Easy-move stopping is the classic scheme; its gain in other engines comes from the same stability signals already in our code. The LM-specific part (disagreement class) is unmeasured.
