Supporting indirect facts: LM root prior gives about +100 Elo-equivalent at 30k nodes but ~0 at 300k, which means the LM mostly agrees with a 300k search (easy class would be large), and at the clock BIGS+LM was -122 vs -111, so the LM call overhead must stay below noise. Fact 9 warns that about 19% of choices are unstable, so the disagreement class is likely a substantial fraction and need not be rare.
proposals.expected_elo: -3 to +5 (central +1). Risk: early stopping on a wrongly confident LM costs more than saved time gains.
proposals.cheap_test: Offline on the quality-instrument set: for positions classed easy, measure how often the 300k-node move equals the 3M-node move (want above 97%); for the disagreement class measure the fraction where 1M differs from 100k, versus baseline. If easy-class stability is no better than the existing node-fraction rule, stop. Otherwise a 1,000-game 10+0.1 match with a 6-hour budget limit.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c search_root time check (lines 1976-1987) with the root LM result passed in like root_vol; policy/value heads in lm/serve.py and model.py.

summary: I found no uncertainty-aware search method with a fishtest-verified or otherwise solid measured gain for alpha-beta. The only positive numbers are self-reported Lc0 fork results (about +10 Elo at short time control, +5 at long, labelled "not recommended"), and a 2026 Lund thesis found variance-aware PUCT worse than plain PUCT. Our own volatility options were already tested (zero/best_options.md:57-65): about +30 Elo at 50k nodes, +8 at 5+0.05, +1 at 60+0.6 (-22 to +24). So this angle is largely exhausted for our setup, and I would not spend more than a few hours on it.
warnings: The search tool returned only titles and snippets, so I did not fetch or read the sources in full. I did not verify the Stockfish complexity/time-management claims against fishtest, and I did not fetch Stockfish source. No injected instructions were seen in the results. The Ergodice lc0 fork is on GitHub, but I did not check its licence, which is probably GPL since Lc0 is GPL-3. Do not copy code from it. The Vol option results at 60+0.6 (300 games) have wide error bars (-22 to +24), so "no gain at long time control" is not firmly established either. Measurements are in zero/best_options.md and zero/results/lab_tests_evening.log.

proposals.title: Search-derived instability signal (eval-vs-search delta, best-move changes) in LMR and time use, without a network head
proposals.mechanism: Replace the learned volatility value with signals the search already has. (a) A complexity term |staticEval - bestValue| (or the TT/search score minus static eval, optionally corrected by a correction-history entry), used to reduce LMR slightly less when large and slightly more when small. (b) A time-management multiplier from root best-move changes and score fall between iterations, replacing or complementing VolTm. Write each as one par[] option, defaulting to off, so it fits the existing option table.
proposals.evidence: WEAK. From memory (not re-verified here): later Stockfish versions use a complexity term in reductions and a falling-eval/best-move-instability factor in time management. I could not verify the Elo numbers from fishtest in this session. Our own VolTm gave +10.3 (-6.6 to +27.2) at 5+0.05 over 778 games (zero/results/lab_tests_evening.log:2). VolLmr gave +5.8 (-6.3 to +17.9) at 60k nodes (same log, line 3). VolNmp gave +0.7 (line 4). These are the prior on what this family is worth.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +8 at 10+0.1; most likely about +2. Time management is the most plausible part.
proposals.cheap_test: Quality test at 300k nodes (SE about 0.3 units), then a 1,000-game 10+0.1 run against BIGS with the option off. For the time-management part use 10+0.1 matches only, since fixed nodes cannot show it. Stop early if the quality test is worse than +0.3 units.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c: the LMR reduction computation and the time-allocation code; the existing VolLmr/VolTm branches are the template (par_name list near line 1015).

proposals.title: Fix hash-dependent move instability before any uncertainty work (diagnostic, not a feature)
proposals.mechanism: Fact 9 says changing only the hash size changes our chosen move in 19% of positions at 300k nodes, against 1.1% for Stockfish. That much noise points to search-path dependence on the table (replacement policy, stale entries, TT cutoffs at PV nodes, depth-preferred overwrite, or mate/score-bound handling), and it can drown out real effects. Run a controlled bisect: disable TT cutoffs in non-PV nodes, TT-dependent pruning and reductions (NmpTt, TtCapLmr, CutLmr, CutIir, IIR) one at a time, and measure the move-change rate at hash 16 vs 64 MB on about 1,000 positions. The option that collapses the rate is the suspect. Also check generation aging and that bound types are stored correctly.
proposals.evidence: MEDIUM that this is a real defect, from our own measurement (fact 9). Whether fixing it gains Elo is unproven. A move-change rate 17 times Stockfish's is not explained by chaos alone.
proposals.expected_elo: -3 to +15 at 10+0.1. The gap to Stockfish is about 120 Elo, and some of it could be a latent search bug.
proposals.cheap_test: A script with two hash sizes over 1,000 positions at 300k nodes, reading off the fraction of changed moves per disabled feature. About 30 min of CPU per configuration. Then the quality test on any fix.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c: TT probe/store, replacement and aging code, and the TT-dependent flags in par[] (NmpTt, TtCapLmr, CutIir).

proposals.title: Do not pursue: transformer variance or value-distribution heads, B*, conspiracy numbers, Bayesian search for alpha-beta
proposals.mechanism: This is a negative recommendation. Our transformer is already worse as a leaf judge (fact 6, +6.3 units) and gives no gain at the clock (fact 5). A variance head would inherit the same weakness, and the call latency of about 7 ms is too high to steer reductions at scale. Conspiracy numbers and B* have no modern evidence against alpha-beta+NNUE. The one empirical hit I found is the 2026 Lund thesis, which reports variance-aware PUCT underperforming standard PUCT.
proposals.evidence: WEAK to MEDIUM. https://lup.lub.lu.se/student-papers/record/9249101 (variance-aware tree policy, negative). https://github.com/Ergodice/lc0 (self-reported +10 STC / +5 LTC on a fork, author does not recommend it). I did not read either in full, and the search snippets are my only source. No fishtest evidence found for any uncertainty-driven search in Stockfish.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 (do not spend time here)
proposals.cheap_test: None needed. If you want a sanity check, the existing VolMix/VolRef options with a 60+0.6 match already showed +1.
proposals.where_in_our_code: n/a

summary: Our engine has no tablebase code (no Syzygy, no probe, no SyzygyPath option) and BIGS evaluation applies no rule-50 damping or endgame scaling, although our own sf_eval copy of Stockfish's formula does. The best-measured outside number is about +7 Elo (Stockfish wiki, SF14, 6-man), and our 1,000-game matches (±~12 Elo) cannot resolve that, so tablebases are not a way to close the 111-Elo gap, which is mostly search efficiency. Fair-test rules matter more than the gain: probing on one side only would be an unfair gain, so any probing must be on in both or in neither, with 64 MB hash and one thread.
warnings: I did not verify the tablebase files exist on the machine or the fair-test conventions of the test harness; the cutechess-style harness scripts (zero/*.sh, ext/vs_sf.sh) were not read for adjudication settings. If the harness adjudicates by tablebase or by score, results may already be shaped by that. The wiki figure of 7.3 +/- 1.4 Elo for SF14 came from a search summary, not a page I read in full, so its time control is unknown. No injected instructions were seen in the search results. No source code of other engines was read, so no licence issue arises yet; Fathom is MIT-licensed according to my memory and should be checked before use.

proposals.title: Rule-50 and shuffling damping of the BIGS static evaluation (cheap, ~0 cost at runtime)
proposals.mechanism: In evaluate() (calc/calc_s19.c ~line 960, the final `int v = (int)(out*271.58f)` return) apply v = v*(100 - min(P.half,100))/100, exactly what sf_eval already does at line 883 for the Stockfish-network path. Stockfish applies this damping in its evaluation, and our search sees half-move counts up to the draw at 100 with no pull toward the draw. Optionally also a small material-based endgame scale (e.g. opposite-coloured-bishop and few-pawn positions shrink toward 0), but start with the plain rule-50 factor only. Needs P.half be correct inside the search (it is maintained in make/unmake, lines 386-411). Corrhist/TT: the TT stores static eval and scores that depend on P.half, so keep damping on the raw eval only, before the correction history is added, and test with it on the standing TT scheme.
proposals.evidence: No damping in the BIGS path: grep shows P.half used only at lines 883, 1110 (is_draw) and 1272 (FEN output). sf_eval's version shows the project already copied Stockfish's formula for its own-network yardstick. Stockfish 14.1 documents shuffling damp in its eval (not fetched from source; known from the public description of its evaluation). No measured Elo for this in our code; the expected size is small because blocked/shuffling positions are rare at 10+0.1 with 64 MB hash. Weak evidence of gain, strong evidence that it is missing.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +5 (not resolvable in 1,000 games)
proposals.cheap_test: Option EvalR50=1. Quality instrument at 300k nodes on the ~9,000 positions (does not exercise high half-move counts much, so it mainly checks no regression, SE 0.3 units) plus a targeted set: ~500 positions from engine games with halfmove >= 30 and compare chosen move against Stockfish 4M-node analysis. Then one 1,000-game match at 10+0.1 only if the targeted set moves.

proposals.title: Syzygy 5-man (or 6-man) probing in the engine, only as a fair both-sides-on condition
proposals.mechanism: Add a probe module (own implementation or a permissively licensed one; Fathom is MIT-licensed, check before reading, do not copy GPL code) and call it in two places: (1) WDL probe at interior nodes when piece count <= N and half == 0 (after captures/pawn moves), returning a TB score bounded to mate-ish values (+-(TB_WIN - ply)), with TT storage; (2) DTZ probe at the root to filter moves that keep the win and avoid the 50-move trap. Add options SyzygyPath and SyzygyProbeDepth. Run the opponent Stockfish 14.1 with the same SyzygyPath and the same cap (SyzygyProbeLimit) so the condition is symmetric; equally allowed is both off (the current setting, the cleanest comparison). Lack of tablebases currently makes our engine misplay won/drawn 5-man endings and rely on is_draw (line 1109) which only knows K v K and K+minor v K (misses K+N+N v K being unforced, fine, but also nothing for known theoretical draws like KRB v KR, or 50-move accounting).
proposals.evidence: Stockfish wiki Useful-data page lists the syzygy gain for SF14 as 7.3 +/- 1.4 Elo (https://official-stockfish.github.io/docs/stockfish-wiki/Useful-data.html; time control and tablebase size not stated in the snippet I saw). Wiki Advanced topics says tablebases give only a limited strength increase for general play. A fishtest-era 6-man test at 60+0.6 reported +10.55 +/- 2.25; a forum estimate claimed STC ~20 and LTC ~10 Elo for 6-man (TalkChess t=72820, weak, anecdotal). Gain shrank after NNUE: only 2.7 Elo for SF15 and -1.26 +/- 1.46 at 10+0.1 for SF17.1 (blog https://chessengines.blogspot.com/2023/04/stockfish-depth-vs-tc.html). Our net is weaker in endgames than a tablebase so the gain could be somewhat above Stockfish's, but nothing was measured on our engine. Tablebases are not on the machine to my knowledge; 5-man is ~1 GB, 6-man ~150 GB, so only 5-man (or 3-4-5) is practical on a rented box, and the RAM/disk of the rented machine is unverified.
proposals.expected_elo: +2 to +8 if both sides probe (our share of that is no help to the gap: the opponent gains the same); +5 to +10 if only we probe, which is NOT a fair test and must not be reported as a match against Stockfish 14.1 under fair conditions
proposals.cheap_test: First measure the upper bound without any code: count in the existing game logs (zero/results/*.log, PGNs if kept) how many of the 342 losses and 624 draws reached <= 5 pieces with a winning or drawn result that differs from the TB value; if fewer than ~3% of games, stop. Then build the probe, run a 1,000-game match both-on versus Stockfish 14.1 with the same 5-man tables, compare with the both-off -111 baseline (noise +-12).

proposals.title: Recognise more theoretical draws and decided endgames in is_draw and in the evaluation (no tables needed)
proposals.mechanism: Extend is_draw (line 1109) from K v K / K+minor v K to: K+B v K+B same-coloured bishops without pawns, K+N+N v K (draw unless the weaker side blunders; at least return a heavy damp rather than a win), and scale the evaluation toward 0 for rook-less pawnless positions with a material edge below a rook, KBN-insufficient configurations, and opposite-coloured-bishop endings (multiply by ~0.5 to 0.7 as in the standard eval-scaling idea). Implement as an endgame scale factor applied after the network output and before correction history, switchable with an option.
proposals.evidence: Current code returns draws only for K v K and K+minor v K (lines 1109-1115); the network has 8 piece-count buckets and a tapered shortcut but no explicit scale. The README says Stockfish 'compresses its endgame scores' in balanced endgames (ext/README.md line ~182), which indicates endgame scaling affects evaluation comparison, but no match or quality measurement of an endgame scale exists in our logs. Stockfish 14.1 NNUE itself uses only the material-based scale and rule-50 damp, so the upside is limited to cases the network mis-scores; 8.2 billion training positions with Stockfish labels already include these scores implicitly.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +3
proposals.cheap_test: Build a position set from the 9,000 quality positions with <= 8 non-pawn-king pieces and low material difference, run the quality test with the option on and off at 300k nodes; accept only if the units on that subset improve by more than 2 standard errors.

angle: draw-conversion / where do we lose (game-record autopsy)
summary: The repo keeps NO game records: gauntlet.py one_game() builds the move list and per-side clocks in local variables and returns only (score, plies, flag); Engine.wait() throws away every 'info' line; zero/results/*.log and standing_g27.jsonl hold only W/D/L, Elo, avg_plies (152.3 for BIGS vs SF 14.1) and time-loss counts (0 for both sides). So today we cannot say whether the 342 losses are tactical blunders, slow bleed, endgames or time trouble; every previous diagnosis (quality.py on ~9,000 database positions, q_classes/q_fail) is on positions that are not the ones we actually reach and lose in. The cheapest high-value step is to re-run the standing 1,000-game match (25 min, ~$0.12) with a ~25-line logging patch and analyse every position with the local /usr/games/stockfish as oracle; the result also yields a loss-position test set that is better aimed than the database set. No Elo is claimed from the diagnosis itself.
warnings: Repo facts: no PGNs or per-game move records exist anywhere (searched for *.pgn across the filesystem; gauntlet.py discards moves). The 'Stockfish 14.1' opponent binary is /usr/games/stockfish; its version was not verified by me and the oracle should differ from or be stronger than the opponent to avoid bias toward its own mistakes (note opponent 'Stockfish 19' appears in standing_g27.jsonl, 200 games, 1-12-187). Match draws are decided by the harness (3-fold/50-move/500 plies), games are not deterministic (clock-driven), so a rerun will not reproduce the same 1,000 games; analyse the rerun, do not try to match old games. Openings (data/openings.txt, 3,500 balanced FENs from move 5-7) are not opening-theory tests, so 'lost in the opening' will mostly mean 'in the first 20 plies of play', not book errors. Oracle-vs-oracle noise: use the same 1/(1+exp(-cp/200)) mapping and the null table for SF's own moves. WebSearch results mentioned only Stockfish GitHub/TalkChess pages; none contained instructions aimed at AI models. The task statement said to read ext/README.md sections relevant to this angle; I grepped rather than read it fully, so some earlier game-level analysis could exist there that I did not see.

proposals.title: Game autopsy: log moves + our info lines, grade every ply with local Stockfish, classify losses by phase, clock, depth, blunder vs bleed
proposals.mechanism: (1) In a COPY of gauntlet.py (not the repo): make Engine.wait keep the last 'info depth .. score cp|mate .. nodes .. time ..' line before bestmove for our engine; in one_game record per ply: uci move, side, our depth/score/nodes/ms, clock[both] before the move; return the dict and append one JSON line per game (fen, us_white, moves, per-ply fields, result, how it ended: mate/stalemate/3-fold/50-move/insufficient/500 plies/flag). Note one_game ends draws by board.is_repetition(3) or halfmove>=100 (gauntlet.py lines ~62-64), so ending types are recoverable. (2) Rerun the exact standing config (BIGS, 10+0.1, Hash 64, 22 boards, 1,000 games, same openings/seed). (3) Offline: for every position of every game run /usr/games/stockfish (exists locally; version should be checked with 'uci' - a stronger oracle than the opponent is preferable, e.g. 'Stockfish 19' appears as an opponent in zero/results/standing_g27.jsonl) at fixed 200k-300k nodes with MultiPV 1, ~150k positions, ~10 CPU-min on 22 threads. Convert to win-probability with the repo's E(cp)=1/(1+exp(-cp/200)) (ext/q_classes.py) so losses are in the same unit as quality.py. (4) Tables, each normalised by the same table for Stockfish's own moves in the same games (null model: SF also loses win-prob per move vs deeper analysis): (a) mean win-prob loss per our move by phase (non-pawn material bands; <=6 pieces; first 20 plies after the opening FEN) and by our remaining clock (<0.5s,0.5-1.5s,1.5-4s,>4s) and by our reached depth bucket; (b) for each lost game the 'point of no return' ply (last ply where oracle eval >= -0.5 pawn for us) and the drop at that ply: single drop >=0.12 win-prob = blunder, else slow bleed (sum of many 0.01-0.04 losses); (c) share of blunders whose oracle-best move is each q_classes.klass class (quiet check, quiet piece offered, pawn to 6th/7th, capture risky, ...) - reuse ext/q_classes.klass directly; (d) calibration: our own reported score vs oracle eval at the ply before each blunder (overconfident by how much?); (e) draws: share of drawn games where oracle said >= +0.5 for us for 10+ plies (missed conversions; we only win 34 of 1,000, so probably few) and share where oracle said <= -1.0 for 10+ plies for us (escapes), plus how each draw ended.
proposals.evidence: Absence of records verified by reading /home/user/seek/gauntlet.py (one_game returns only (score, plies, flag); Engine.wait discards non-bestmove lines), match.py, and the result logs (zero/results/vault_clock.log:BIGS 34-624-342 avg_plies 152.3, our_time_losses 0). Decision value: what each pattern points to is mapped as - mostly single blunders at low reached depth in tactical classes -> search selectivity/ordering (consistent with fact 3, 2-3x node gap; points to ext/q_fail.py style rule-off tests on THESE positions); bleed in quiet middlegames with normal depth -> evaluator judgment/scaling (SF net swap on these positions); loss concentrated at clock <1s or depth <=8 -> time management (calc_s19.c:2197-2204, t/20+3/4*inc, TmSoft SPSA-tuned to 61 only once, lab_spsa_test.log:1; not re-checked at the clock); concentrated in <=6-piece endings -> endgame knowledge (no tablebases, no draw scaling in the engine, is_draw handles only K v K/K+minor, calc_s19.c:1109-1115); calibration gap -> eval scale/contempt. Analogous practice: fishtest/Stockfish developers analyse failed games, but I have no measured Elo for this specific method; it is diagnostic only.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 directly (diagnosis). Indirect: aims the remaining hours; if one class explains >=40% of the lost win-probability, a fix targeted there could plausibly recover +10 to +30, but that is a guess.
proposals.cheap_test: This IS the cheap test: ~1 h to patch+run (match 25 min at 22 boards, no extra hardware), ~30 min oracle analysis, ~30 min tables. Sanity check first: 50-game dry run, verify moves replay legally with python-chess and that sum of results reproduces the W/D/L. Keep the games file (data/games_bigs_10p01.jsonl) permanently so later claims are re-analysable.
proposals.where_in_our_code: gauntlet.py: Engine.wait/go and one_game (lines ~21-75), play_pair; analysis script new, under ext/ (reuse ext/q_classes.klass, ext/quality.E, match.openings)

proposals.title: Blunder-position test set mined from our real losses, with an eval-vs-search-vs-instability attribution matrix
proposals.mechanism: From the autopsy (proposal 1) take the positions just before each blunder (oracle win-prob drop >= 0.10 on our move, our side to move; expect ~500-1,500 positions after dedup across 1,000 games), store as a new quality-style set (fen, oracle best move, oracle 2nd, cp). Run these configurations at fixed nodes and report the share of positions where we play a move within 0.03 win-prob of oracle best: (A) BIGS, 300k nodes, cold hash; (B) BIGS, 3M nodes (does 10x search fix it, i.e. efficiency problem, or not, i.e. judgment problem); (C) our search + Stockfish 14.1's network at 300k (README already has this config for the yardstick, ext/sfnet_*.sh); (D) BIGS with Hash 16/64/256 MB (fact 9: 19% of moves change with hash size; do blunders sit in the unstable subset?); (E) the in-game state: replay the same game prefix through the engine (position fen .. moves ..) at the same node count instead of a cold 'position fen' so persistent TT/history effects (tt_age, history tables not cleared between moves, calc_s19.c:1068-1077) are included, and compare with cold (A). Also run Stockfish itself at 300k as reference. Interpretation grid: B fixes, C does not -> pure search depth; C fixes, B does not -> evaluator; D flips many -> instability dominates (supports pursuing hash/TT determinism work); E differs from A -> the quality instrument understates (or overstates) in-game weakness.
proposals.evidence: Method follows the project's own instruments (ext/quality.py, q_fail.py, sfnet_ref/quality with 'sf net in our search' described in README Measured facts 3-4,9). Motivation: facts 3 and 4 say the gap is search efficiency (SF needs 1/2-1/3 of our nodes) while the evaluator is level on database positions; but database positions are not game-loss positions, and lost games are decided by few critical moves, so averaged quality units (~40 Elo/unit, SE 0.3) may hide that concentrated set. No external measured result; internal reasoning only. The in-game-state comparison (E) is a standard confound check, since all quality numbers are from cold single positions while matches use persistent state.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 directly. As a new instrument, a smaller faster-moving test (about 1,000 critical positions instead of 9,000 average ones) may cut screening cost, and an E-vs-A gap would flag a real in-game bug worth tens of Elo; unknown, could be zero.
proposals.cheap_test: After proposal 1 data exist: ~1 h to build the set, then each configuration is minutes (1,000 positions x 300k nodes / 22 threads = ~4 min; 3M nodes ~40 min). Decision rule: if (B) solves < 50% at 3M nodes the problem is not node count.
proposals.where_in_our_code: new script under ext/ modelled on ext/quality.py and ext/q_fail.py; options Hash, Off, network path via UCI as in q_fail.py header

proposals.title: Draw-handling audit plus Stockfish-style draw-score jitter (2-fold-in-path, +-1 on repetition scores)
proposals.mechanism: From the game files: classify how our drawn and lost games end (3-fold, 50-move, 500-ply cutoff, insufficient material) and find positions where we were shown to be worse by the oracle but a repetition/perpetual was available and missed, or where SF repeated while we were +0.5 or better. Code facts: is_draw() (calc_s19.c:1109-1115) scores every in-history or in-tree repetition and 50-move as exactly 0, with no jitter, and treats a single prior occurrence as a draw even from before the root; there is no contempt anywhere, and K+minor v K is the only insufficient-material rule (KNN v K and similar missing, minor). Change to test: return 0 +/- (nodes&1 ? 1 : -1) style jitter (Stockfish returns 2 - (nodes & 3) -> centipawn-scale +-1 on VALUE_DRAW, 'at depth > 3') for repetition draws only, and optionally require 3-fold for repetitions that lie wholly before the root. Test with the existing instruments only if the audit shows repetition-related losses/draws are a visible share (say >5% of games).
proposals.evidence: Stockfish added randomised draw value in PR 1770 (https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/pull/1770): passed STC, reported passing VLTC, motivated by '3-fold blindness' that matters more at longer time controls; a later commit removed part of it (https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/commit/1054a483ca0c560d30fb61617c0192cb4cd31528) because most effect came from 3-fold randomisation; repetition scoring debated in https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/pull/925 and https://www.talkchess.com/forum3/viewtopic.php?t=71707. Effect size in Elo is not given in what I could read; I did not fetch source (rule). Weak evidence; at 10+0.1 it is probably small. Stockfish is GPL; this is a description of a technique, not code.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +3 (likely unmeasurable at 1,000 games, SE ~12 Elo); the audit itself may reveal a larger repetition/50-move problem, unknown.
proposals.cheap_test: Audit is a by-product of proposal 1 (~20 min). If repetition-related, a 300k-node quality run is useless for this (no repetitions in single positions); only a 1,000-game match at 10+0.1 (25 min) with an SPRT pair test; expect inconclusive unless the audit finds a large effect. Do not run before the audit says it is worth it.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c is_draw() lines 1109-1115 and its uses at 1543 and 2081

angle: statistics: testing methodology, SPRT/pentanomial, quality-instrument validity
summary: Games cannot resolve +5 Elo on this machine: with 62-66% draws one game has SE ~0.0097 score (~6.5 Elo per 1000 games), so 80% power at +5 Elo needs ~14,000 games, +10 needs ~3,600 and +15 needs ~1,600 (my arithmetic: N = (2.8*695)^2*(1-d)/4/delta^2). The quality instrument is a sound screen (all 6+ paired rows in zero/results/vault_calib.log have the right sign, ~40 Elo per unit, e.g. HistV2=7 +0.49 (0.31) vs -18 Elo at the clock), but its SE (0.28 units = ~11 Elo at 300k) is dominated by chaotic move flips (26% of positions differ at 30k even for HistV2), not by signal, so the cheapest gain is to measure and then average that chaos away, and to stop the funnel from mis-ranking speed-changing candidates. Nothing here is a direct Elo gain; it makes +5 to +10 Elo search changes detectable, which the 12 dead-end variants and the -7 SPSA result show we currently cannot do.
warnings: No injected instructions were seen; I fetched no web pages (only read local files). Measurement flaws found: (1) match.elo_from uses a trinomial SE although both colours of every opening are played, so reported CIs are slightly too wide and pair statistics are never logged; the SPRT code in gauntlet.py does use pairs. (2) Quality test is equal-node, so speed changes are invisible to it (Sel was 5% slower, ~7 Elo). (3) Truth is Stockfish 14.1 at 4M nodes, which README:419 itself notes flatters Stockfish and biases the judge toward Stockfish-like choices, and positions come from BIGM-vs-SF games at 30k nodes, so they under-represent the clock-time distribution; paired comparisons between our own configs are less affected. (4) Calibration of ~40 Elo/unit rests on ~6 rows, all of them node-count or network changes, not search-heuristic changes; HistV2 and EvalScale are the only heuristic points. (5) The 19% move flip rate from hash size (versus Stockfish 1.1%) is itself suspicious as an engine issue (replacement or TT-cutoff/graph-history interaction) and is outside my angle, but it inflates all quality-test noise.

proposals.title: Empirical-null calibration and hash-size replicate averaging for the quality test
proposals.mechanism: Step 1 (null): run the standing config at 300k nodes with Hash=60,62,66,68,72,80 (meaningless changes; each flips ~19% of moves per fact 9) and compare every one to Hash=64 with ext/quality.py cmp. The spread of those 'differences' is the true noise floor; check that their sd matches the reported SE (0.27-0.31) and that the mean is 0. Step 2 (replicates): for any config under test, run K=6 hash sizes and average each position's loss over the K runs before pairing (moves already scored are cached, so Stockfish cost is small; engine time is ~2 min x K per config on 24 threads). This removes the per-position chaos component by a factor K, leaving only the real per-position effect heterogeneity. Use hash size, not node jitter, as the replicate source: README line 588-590 shows a 1% node change flips only 0.1% of our moves, so it gives no independent draws. Step 3 (more positions where it is cheap): judge lazily, i.e. only positions where the two configs chose different moves need a Stockfish search (two single-move or two-line searches at 1-2M nodes), so positions can be collected without the 4M-node truth for all; 3-4x more positions at the same cost.
proposals.evidence: ext/README.md:409-434 (SE 0.27-0.31 at 300k, 'one unit ~40 Elo', 2306 of 8964 positions differ at 30k for HistV2=7, zero/results/vault_calib.log line 5); ext/README.md:588-590 (hash size flips 19% of moves, 1% node change 0.1%; 2-entry buckets +0.72 (0.28)). Per-position diff sd implied by SE: 0.3*sqrt(8964) ~ 28 thousandths, versus a real +5 Elo effect of 0.125 units; so a +5 Elo effect needs ~200k position-equivalents unless the chaos part is averaged out. How large the chaos share is has NOT been measured; this is exactly what step 1-2 measure. Weak evidence on how much SE shrinks (could be 1.2x or 3x).
proposals.expected_elo: 0 directly; tool improvement. If chaos share is >=70% of variance, SE at 300k drops from ~11 to ~5-6 Elo per config pair (K=6), making +10 Elo changes detectable in ~15 minutes. If the share is small, we learn that quickly and the instrument's limit is position count.
proposals.cheap_test: 6 extra 300k runs of the standing config at different Hash values (~12 min engine time) plus cmp; then one real pair (HistV2=7 vs standing, known +0.49) averaged over 6 hash sizes each (~25 min) and compare SE and sign. Success: null sd matches reported SE and replicated SE <= 0.6x of single-run SE.

proposals.title: Funnel with time-adjusted nodes, a prediction-interval calibration table, and pentanomial logging in gauntlet.py
proposals.mechanism: (a) Quality runs are equal-node, so a candidate that is 5% slower (like Sel, which was 5% slower, README:530) looks 5% better than it plays. Convert measured nps ratio r to node budget 300k*r for the candidate and its reference (the 100k->300k row gives ~157 Elo per tripling, ~100 Elo per doubling, so 5% nps ~ 7 Elo ~ 0.18 units; apply as correction or run at scaled nodes). (b) Fit the existing (quality delta, game Elo) pairs (about 12 rows in README:409-422 plus HistV2, EvalScale, Sel, BIGX) with an errors-in-variables line, report slope and residual sd, and pre-commit the funnel: a candidate goes to a game match only if time-adjusted quality delta <= -0.1 units with replicated SE; game stage is gauntlet.py --stop 0,8 (pair-based SPSRT already exists, line 115-150), not a fixed 1000 games. (c) gauntlet.py/match.elo_from compute a trinomial CI (match.py:34-40) which ignores that both colours of one opening are paired; log pentanomial pair counts (LL, LD/DL, DD+WL, DW/WD, WW) in every result line so the real pair correlation can be measured and the reported CI tightened (fishtest practice; gain is typically a 5-20% variance reduction, unmeasured for us). (d) Add resign/draw adjudication only if both engines agree (|score|>6 pawns for 4 plies, or draw-score for 8 plies at ply>80): average game is 145-152 plies with no adjudication (vault_calib.log), typical saving 20-30%, which is 20-30% more games per hour; verify on 200 games that outcomes are unchanged.
proposals.evidence: Game-budget arithmetic from draw rates 62% (BIGS vs SF, 34-624-342) and 66% (HistV2 vs standing, 144-661-195, README:165): SE ~6.5 Elo per 1000 games, +5 Elo needs ~14k games at 80% power. Elo-per-unit consistency: README:427-428 (206 Elo for 5.80 units, 4 Stockfish rows ~40/unit). Sign agreement list at README:409-422. match.py:34-40 and gauntlet.py:115-150 read directly. Adjudication saving figure and pentanomial variance reduction are from general engine-testing practice, not measured on our data (weak).
proposals.expected_elo: 0 directly. Avoids accepting speed-costly changes that win at equal nodes but lose at the clock, and avoids spending ~1000-game matches on changes the screen already says are neutral; roughly doubles the number of candidates testable per hour of match time.
proposals.cheap_test: No engine run needed for (b): a 30-minute script over the table above. For (a), run Sel (5% slower) at 300k*0.95 nodes vs standing at 300k and see whether its +0.11..-0.33 spread collapses to the clock result. For (c), add one line that writes pair counts, replay the next match.

proposals.title: Re-run SPSA on the replicated quality objective (300k nodes) instead of game SPSA at short nodes
proposals.mechanism: ext/q_tune.py already does SPSA on the quality test with mirrored perturbations on the same positions (common random numbers). The earlier game SPSA of 15,000 iterations at short nodes (zero/results/lab_spsa_bigk_end.log) gave tuned values that tested -7 (-20 to +6) at 10+0.1 (README:341), and the SF-style group tests (README:555-565) have SE 0.33-0.40 against effects of 0.1-0.6, i.e. nothing established. Make each SPSA probe less noisy: evaluate each of the two mirrored settings with 3 hash sizes (replicates from proposal 1), batch 3000 positions, 300k nodes, and use an SF-sized parameter list but only 6-8 parameters at a time (LmrBase/LmrDiv, Rfp, NmpDiv/NmpEv, HistPrune, SeMul/SeDouble, FutMul). Accept the tuned set only if a held-out slice (--first/--limit) and then one 10+0.1 SPSRT match at --stop 0,8 agree.
proposals.evidence: ext/README.md:341 (tuned set -7), README:549-565 (group results within noise), README:383 (all settings tuned at 2.5k-30k nodes, search effects shift with depth), README:462 (CutLmr and similar all within +0.3 of standing: parameters look near a flat optimum at 300k). Evidence that SPSA at 300k would find anything is weak: the pruning/reduction variants were all slightly worse, suggesting the optimum is already near. Public fishtest practice gives only 1-3 Elo per tuned group.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +8 Elo at 10+0.1 (expected ~+3); low upside, mainly worthwhile because the infrastructure already exists and it runs unattended.
proposals.cheap_test: Run q_tune.py for 40 rounds on 6 parameters (batch 3000, ~3 min per round with replicates = 2 h unattended), then compare tuned vs standing on the held-out positions with SE <= 0.3; only if it is <= -0.3 units, run one SPSRT match.

summary: I found no per-step Elo logs for Obsidian, Berserk, Stormphrax, Viridithas, Alexandria, PlentyChess or Reckless on the open web. Release notes only give whole-version gains (+25 to +40 Elo per version on Chess324 pages), so any per-patch Elo below is community folklore, not evidence. Our search already has essentially the full small-engine feature list, and a clock-based SPSA over 24 parameters (15,000 iterations) gained nothing (-6.9, -19.5 to +5.6 at 1,000 games), so more tuning and more reduction variants are saturated. The three levers I can still defend are free speed (store the static evaluation in the hash table, which my reading of the code suggests is not done), a bundle of tiny post-Stockfish-14 refinements, and a more sensitive instrument so that 2-5 Elo patches become visible.
warnings: 1) Web evidence for per-step Elo of the named small engines was not found; claims in forums are self-reports and rarely measured in isolation. Treat all external numbers as folklore. 2) Node-count semantics: our search() increments `nodes` on every call, including null-move children and each singular-exclusion re-search at the same position (about 4% of nodes per README), whereas as I recall Stockfish counts moves made; the 2-3x node yardstick (fact 3) may therefore be overstated by roughly 5-15%. This is a recollection, I did not fetch Stockfish source (pending decision). Worth checking with a counter that counts only make() calls. 3) Hash instability (fact 9): at 300k nodes and a 64 MB table (about 4M slots) occupancy is low, so a 19% change from a table-size change means tiny collision differences are amplified chaotically. Our engine always overwrites the single slot, including a same-key deep entry by a shallower store in search() (the guard `SearchV3&64` exists but is off by default), while the 2-way bucket reduced instability to 1.3% yet scored +0.72 worse (SE 0.28, roughly 2.5 sigma, unexplained). A diagnostic worth running: a 512 MB table plays the same as 64 MB per the README, so this is variance, not strength. 4) Licences: the pages I read were Stockfish blog posts, a third-party rentry (no code), a lichess blog (403, unread) and TalkChess/forum summaries; no code was copied or fetched. The Reckless mirror pages disagree on licence (MIT vs AGPL v3), so do not read its source for copying. 5) No prompt-injection text was seen in the pages I fetched."

proposals.title: Store the raw static evaluation in the hash table and skip evaluate() on hits (search and qsearch)
proposals.mechanism: From my reading of calc_s19.c, evaluate() is called at every search and qsearch node and the table entry has no evaluation field (TTE at line 369 is key 8, move 4, score 2, depth 1, flag 1 = 16 bytes). Change TTE to `U64 key; unsigned move:17; int eval:15; short score; uchar depth, flag;` and store the raw net output, before eval_corr's correction, which is added afterwards as now (eval_corr line 1135 computes `evaluate()*scale/100 + c/256`). Alternatively keep Move as int and shrink the stored key (the low index bits are implied) to free 16 bits. In search() (line 1558 probe) and qsearch() (line 1494 probe), if `e->key==P.key` and eval != NONE, use the stored value instead of calling evaluate(). Write eval at every store site (lines 1536, 1638, 1882). Never store it for in-check nodes. Use a sentinel for eval above +/-16000. Qsearch stores currently pass through `e->depth==0` guards; keep those. In search nodes the stored eval is the one already computed at entry. The search tree should be bit-identical (same node count on bench, since only a redundant computation is skipped), so correctness is checkable exactly. Also try `-mprefer-vector-width=512` on Zen 4 for the accumulator update loops, which is a one-line build test.
proposals.evidence: ext/README.md ~lines 302-311 (evalcost, TSTAT build, bench depth 14): the evaluator is 45% of cycles per position searched (1,811 cycles: 511 bringing sums up to date = 26%, read-out 367 = 19%). Skipping evaluation on hits saves part of the read-out and any accumulator work no later node needs. Node mix from README ~line 541: quiescence 32%, depth-1 main nodes 33%, and iterative-deepening re-visits make hit rates at interior nodes high, but I have NOT measured the hit rate here. The 70 Elo per node doubling is derived from fact 3 (about 3x nodes worth about 120 Elo). Small engines treat TT-stored static eval as standard (general knowledge, not a fetched measurement). Weak point: qsearch hit rate may be low and the table has no spare bytes today, so the hit rate must be measured first.
proposals.expected_elo: +4 to +12 at 10+0.1 single thread (nps +6% to +17%; 10% nps is about 0.14 doublings, about 10 Elo). Zero effect on move quality at fixed nodes.
proposals.cheap_test: 1) 30 minutes: add a counter of evaluate() calls where tt_find(P.key) has a matching key (any depth) and run the bench; if under 25% of evaluate() calls could be skipped, stop. 2) Otherwise implement, check bench node counts are identical to before, and compare nps over 3 runs on a quiet machine (ext/nodetime.py, same binary flags). 3) Only if nps rises 5% or more, run one 1,000-game 10+0.1 match against the old binary as a sanity check; no quality-instrument run is needed.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c: TTE line 369; tt_alloc line 1010; qsearch probe ~1494 and store ~1532-1536; search probe 1558-1585 (ev = eval_corr()); probcut store 1638; final store 1876-1882; eval_corr 1135.

proposals.title: Bundle of cheap post-SF14 refinements that small engines adopted, tested as ONE bundle: qsearch TT stand-pat, fail-high blending, pawn-structure history, eval-delta history bonus
proposals.mechanism: (a) qsearch(): after `stand = best = eval_corr()`, if the TT entry is usable (bound compatible, as search() already does at line 1585-1586), replace the stand-pat by tt_score (search() does this for `ev`, qsearch does not). (b) On fail high in qsearch (and optionally main search at non-mate scores) return a blend, e.g. `best = (best*depth + beta)/(depth+1)` for search and `(3*best+beta)/4` in qsearch, but store the unblended score in the TT; small engines use this, SF's variant is as I recall it from general knowledge and I did not read SF source. (c) Pawn history: a new table `phist[pawn_key & 1023][piece][to]` added to hist_score() (line 1146) and updated with the same bonus as butterfly history, also used in the LMR history term (line 1766). (d) Eval-delta bonus: after a quiet move leads to a non-check node, update the butterfly history of the PREVIOUS move by a clamped function of `-(evals_stack[ply-1] + evals_stack[ply])` (how much the move changed the evaluation), as Stockfish 17-era and Obsidian-style engines do; implement as a new bit in HistV2. Each is behind an option bit so the instrument can ablate it.
proposals.evidence: WEAK. Community and engine-forum figures only: the rentry page https://rentry.co/sf_wisdom (third-party notes on Stockfish search; read as data) gives measured history numbers 'main history ~11 Elo, continuation histories ~63 Elo', fail-soft ~30 Elo, and quotes fail-high blending `(ttValue*3+beta)/4` without an Elo. A Stockfish commit comment cites history-based pruning as '~2 Elo' (https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/commit/4f24ee086828e28df7d0b2dce5c13732139e7c19). Individual items are typically +1 to +5 Elo at short time controls in SPRT, so each is below our instrument's noise (SE 0.3 units = about 12 Elo). Our code already has fail-soft, continuation histories 1/2/4/6, capture history, four correction tables, singular, probcut and IIR, so I expect the remaining headroom to be small.
proposals.expected_elo: +3 to +12 for the bundle; individual items unmeasurable. Could be 0 or slightly negative, as our 12 earlier variants were.
proposals.cheap_test: Implement (a)-(d) as option bits. Run ext/quality.py at 300k nodes on the 9,000 positions for baseline vs bundle with 3 repeats each (different hash size or a 1% node change as the perturbation, since fact 9 shows our moves change in 19% of positions under such noise, which is itself a variance source), and require the bundle at or below -0.3 units before any match. Ablate bits only if the bundle passes.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c: qsearch 1486-1538 (stand-pat at ~1504); hist_score 1146 and hist_update; LMR block ~1757-1780; fail-high return at line 1876-1890; options array lines 1015-1030 (new HistV2/SearchV3 bits).

proposals.title: Raise the instrument's power 3-4x before testing more search changes (more positions, paired repeats, and a fixed-node self-play check)
proposals.mechanism: The lesson from OpenBench-style small teams is that they ship only patches resolved by thousands of games or equivalent power, and typical modern patches are worth +1 to +5 Elo. Our quality test resolves about 12 Elo (SE 0.3 units, about 40 Elo/unit), and our matches vs SF resolve about 12 Elo at 1,000 games. So the 12 'slightly worse' variants and the 'maybe noise' two-entry result (+0.72, SE 0.28) cannot separate -3 from -10. Build a larger set: (1) extend the quality positions from about 9,000 to about 30,000 using Stockfish 4M-node references (about 2.5 s each at roughly 1.6 Mnps, about 20 CPU-hours, about 1 hour on 22 threads); (2) report each result as a paired difference per position with a bootstrap interval (same positions, same node budget), which reduces variance versus comparing two means; (3) add a fixed-100k-node self-play SPRT (new vs old binary, 1 thread each, 2-move random openings from zero/spsa.py's opening generator, about 7 s a game, about 10,000 games per hour on 22 threads, pentanomial LLR with bounds [0,3]) as a second gate for search-structure changes (it does not see speed or evaluator effects, but it does see tree-shape effects). Re-run the three most promising 'slightly worse' reduction variants (cutnode LMR CutLmr, CutIir, SeDouble from zero/best_options.md; they are off in the default par[] at line 1021) through the new gate, because Stockfish-lineage engines get real gains from exactly these and our verdict there rests on a 12-Elo-noise instrument.
proposals.evidence: Instrument noise: ext/quality.py SE 0.3 units at 300k nodes (task facts 2 and 8). zero/best_options.md reports CutIir, SeDouble, PvPrune as +43 at 60+0.6 over 122 games in November while the standing par[] (line 1021) now has CutLmr, CutIir, NegExt, SeDouble all 0, so some options were later judged 'dead ends' with errors of about 12 Elo each. zero/results/lab_spsa_bigk_end.log: tuned vs standing values at 10+0.1, 1,000 games, -6.9 (-19.5 to +5.6), so tuning is flat. Web evidence for how small teams test: community reports (one hobby-engine PR measured +4.4 +/- 7.3 and was 'undecided' at LLR -0.48, https://github.com/conorosully27-cloud/Chess_Engine/pull/16) and the Fishtest FAQ on SPRT (https://github.com/official-stockfish/fishtest/wiki/Fishtest-faq: Elo estimates of passing patches are biased, and failed-but-close patches are bundled and re-tested). This proposal adds measurement power, not Elo directly.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 directly; it makes +2 to +5 Elo patches (and the re-tested reduction options) detectable, worth maybe +10 to +25 Elo cumulatively over several patches, with the possibility that it confirms the current options are right.
proposals.cheap_test: Step 1 (1 hour): compute from existing per-position quality results the standard error of a paired difference between two runs of the SAME binary with different hash sizes (hash instability fact 9 makes this noise floor). If the paired SE is above 0.2 units, extend the set; if it is already small, skip to the self-play SPRT. Step 2 (1 hour): run the self-play gate on a known +10 Elo change (for example the VolTm or TmSoft difference, or a 1.1x node budget) and check it passes within 4,000 games.
proposals.where_in_our_code: ext/quality.py (paired difference, more positions); zero/spsa.py game() and openings() (reuse as self-play match runner with node budget); par[] at calc/calc_s19.c line 1021.

summary: The search parameters were already tuned by 20,000 self-play SPSA iterations at 2,500 to 5,000 nodes (+50 Elo at 2.5k, +37 at 10k), and a later 15,000-iteration run on BIGK ended within a few percent of the start; so more game-based SPSA of the same 17 parameters is not worth buying. What was never done is tuning at the budget where the gap lives (300k nodes) on the fixed-node quality instrument, and that is cheap on paper because the engine is deterministic and the test is paired. Even so, expect small gains (outside evidence says tuning usually gives 0 to 3 Elo per patch), so I rate it a bounded, cheap lottery ticket, not a breakthrough on a 120 Elo search-efficiency gap.
warnings: 1) Quality-instrument tuning optimizes loss at 300k nodes against Stockfish 14.1's 4M-node two-line analysis on ~9,000 positions drawn from BIGM vs SF games; the tuned values risk overfitting to those positions (hence the held-out slice) and to a node regime (300k) that is 3 to 10x deeper than a 10+0.1 clock move gets, where the +/-0.3 unit SE is about 12 Elo while a typical SPSA gain is 0 to 3 Elo. 2) q_tune.py's gain constant (0.5, decaying with (1+k/25)^0.6) and perturbation steps are untested: it has never been run, so budget a debugging pass. 3) Bit-flag options (SearchV3, HistV2, PruneV2, Off) must not be put in SPSA. 4) The web search I ran returned only old Talkchess threads and no authoritative fishtest SPSA statistics; the numbers cited are forum opinion. No injected instructions seen in the pages. I did not read or fetch Stockfish source.

proposals.title: Run ext/q_tune.py at 300k nodes on the 17 search parameters plus the never-tuned flag-group parameters, with a held-out confirmation slice
proposals.mechanism: Run SPSA on the quality instrument: python3 ext/q_tune.py with --nodes 300000 --batch 3000 --rounds ~150 --first 0 --limit ~6500, keeping the last ~2,400 usable positions for confirmation. Start with the parameters that were only ever tuned at 2.5k to 5k nodes (zero/spsa.py PARAMS list: Razor, Rfp, NmpEv, LmpBase, FutBase, FutMul, HistPrune, SeeQ, SeeC, SeMul, Asp, DeltaQ, LmrBase, LmrDiv, HbQuad, HbLin, HbMax) plus the depth-sensitive ones that fixed-node experiments flagged as inert at default: NmpBase/NmpDiv, SeDepth, LmpDepth, NmpMargin, ThrRfp/ThrLmr. Use pair-level ordering: each round compares two mirrored settings on the same 3,000 positions; the per-pair loss difference is a paired statistic with far lower variance than game results. The engine is deterministic at a node budget, so no per-game noise except where moves differ. Accept the final theta only if it beats the baseline on the held-out slice by more than 2 standard errors (SE ~0.3 units at full set, ~0.5 at 2,400 positions), then confirm by a 1,000-game 10+0.1 match against the standing config. Caveat: the 300k test and the 10+0.1 clock (about 1.1M nodes/s times ~0.5 s per move, so tens of thousands to ~100k nodes per move) are different regimes; consider running a second pass at 100k nodes, which is closer to what the clock actually gives.
proposals.where_in_our_code: ext/q_tune.py (exists, unrun); parameters in calc/calc_s19.c par[] table near line 1015 (par_name list, NPAR 61); previous tuner zero/spsa.py, results zero/spsa_result.json.
proposals.evidence: Direct measurements in our own repo: zero/spsa.py comment at calc_s19.c:~1018 says self-play SPSA gave +50 Elo at 2,500 nodes and +37 at 10,000 over the hand-set values, so tuning at a given node budget does pay at that budget. ext/README.md:341 says a later 15,000-iteration run at 20+0.2 on BIGK ended within a few percent of the start (-7, -20 to +6): near the optimum for that regime. ext/README.md:~383 states every setting was tuned at 2.5k to 30k nodes, none at 300k+. Outside evidence is weak and dated: a Talkchess forum opinion that fishtest SPSA gains are 'usually 0 - 3 elo' (https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?p=599487 area; forum, not measured), and a Stockfish dev build page citing 2 million SPSA games for king and pawn values (https://nextchessmove.com/dev-builds/d2d4e85f25061aacd65a8b458b79cad15b74a5bb). I found no authoritative fishtest statement of typical SPSA gain per run.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +8 at 10+0.1 (most likely +0 to +3); the 12 earlier variants of reduction/pruning at 300k were all slightly worse, which suggests the optimum is flat
proposals.cheap_test: Smoke test: 20 rounds with --workers 22 on a 3-4 parameter subset (LmrBase, LmrDiv, Rfp, FutMul) to measure round time; at 300k nodes and 1.2M nps one search is ~0.25 s, so 2 x 3,000 positions / 22 workers is ~2.5 minutes per round (about 7 hours for 150 rounds; cut --batch to 1,500 for ~3.5 hours). Check the loss difference per round exceeds the SE; if the plus/minus loss gap is pure noise at round 20, stop. Judge only on the held-out slice.

proposals.title: SPSA the volatility and hash-instability-related options with the quality test's paired metric, not the main reduction/pruning ones
proposals.mechanism: Fact 9 says table size alone changes our move in 19% of positions at 300k nodes versus 1.1% for Stockfish. That is a search-stability signal, not a tuning-of-pruning signal. Use q_tune.py on the options that influence how much the search trusts or shares information: TtBucket (two-entry buckets; +0.72 worse at 300k, maybe noise), SearchV3 flag 64 (keep deeper entry unless new is exact), SearchV3 flag 2 and 16 (PV and table-move preservation), VolMix/VolRef/VolLmr/VolNmp, CutIir, NegExt, ChkExt, SeDouble. These are the integer-valued ones SPSA handles; flags (bit fields) should be run as separate on/off paired comparisons, not SPSA (SPSA over bit flags is meaningless). Also add a stability metric: the fraction of positions where the move changes under a 1% node change or hash 64 to 128 MB, and track it during tuning as a secondary objective, since fact 9 suggests the instability itself may be a symptom of something systematic (e.g. replacement policy, history aging).
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c par[] table (TtBucket, SearchV3, VolMix, VolRef, VolLmr, VolNmp, CutIir, NegExt, ChkExt, SeDouble); ext/q_tune.py --params and --base; a small extra script around ext/quality.py for the stability fraction.
proposals.evidence: Our fact 9 (19% vs 1.1% move changes on hash size alone) and ext/README.md TtBucket comment at calc_s19.c:~1060 ('+19 Elo at 1 MB table, -9 at 60+0.6'). Weak evidence: no measurement links these options to the instability; this is a hypothesis. Bit-flag options cannot be tuned by SPSA, only by paired on/off, which is cheap on the quality instrument.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +5; the main value is diagnostic (find what drives the 19% instability)
proposals.cheap_test: First, a paired on/off quality run per flag at 300k nodes (each ~15 minutes with 22 workers on 9,000 positions, ~2 hours for ~8 flags), reporting both loss and fraction of moves changed versus the stock config and versus hash 128 MB. Only if some flag lowers the instability fraction below ~10% or beats baseline by 2 SE, tune the integer neighbours with q_tune.py.

proposals.title: Do not run more game-based SPSA; if anything is run on games, run it at the real clock with a tiny parameter set and a gating match
proposals.mechanism: Recommendation to stop spending on this path rather than a build: the previous game-based SPSA at 20+0.2 already converged (README:341), so the standing values are at a local optimum for the clock regime. If SPSA is wanted at the clock (zero/spsa_clock.py exists), restrict to 4 to 6 parameters with the highest sensitivity measured by a one-factor sweep on the quality test (step +/-20% of each parameter, paired, at 100k and 300k nodes; rank by |loss change|/SE), and require a final 1,000-game match before adoption. Rule of thumb from the literature: tens of thousands of games for a handful of parameters at about +/-2 Elo noise; ours at 660 games/hour (README:~383, at 1M nodes) or ~2,000/hour at 10+0.1 on 1 thread x ~11 concurrent games is too slow to justify.
proposals.where_in_our_code: zero/spsa_clock.py, zero/spsa.py, ext/q_tune.py; sensitivity sweep can be a loop over ext/quality.py with single-parameter overrides.
proposals.evidence: ext/README.md:341 (15,000-iteration clock SPSA ended within a few percent of the start, -7 (-20 to +6) against the standing values) and calc_s19.c:~1018 (20,000 iterations gave +50/+37 at low nodes only). Talkchess comments (https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?p=599487) that distributed SPSA needs ~10x the games of a local run and SPSA does not measure sensitivity (forum opinion, weak).
proposals.expected_elo: 0 (this proposal saves hours instead of earning Elo); a sensitivity sweep may show which 3 to 5 parameters even matter
proposals.cheap_test: One-factor sensitivity sweep: for each of the ~25 integer options, run quality at 300k nodes with value +20% and -20%; paired SE ~0.3 so |delta| below 0.6 units is noise. About 25 x 2 x 15 min is roughly 12 machine-hours at full 22 workers, so do a 3,000-position subset (about 4 hours); the result decides whether proposal 1 is worth running at all.

summary: Our history stack is SF14-era (main + 1/2-ply continuation + capture history, gravity /16384, same bonus for bonus and malus); no pawn-structure or low-ply history and no surprise-scaled bonus, all of which postdate 14.1. Published/fishtest evidence for these is only a few Elo each (I could verify one pawn-history-related fishtest entry at about +10 Elo, a later variant), so this angle is unlikely to close a 120 Elo gap by itself; the cheap wins are bonus scale retune at 300k nodes and pawn history. Bonus magnitudes were SPSA-tuned at 2.5k-10k nodes, and the README itself shows shallow-tested history changes (HistV2) reversing at depth, so they are untested at the budgets that matter.
warnings: The Stockfish bonus formula quoted (about 17d^2+134d-134) is from memory of SF14 and unverified; I did not fetch Stockfish source per the rules. One search result mentioned a 'Stockfish 19 release with 44 Elo' blog claim that I could not verify; ignored. No injected instructions seen in fetched pages. Measurement concern: shallow-node (2.5k-10k) tuning of search parameters (zero/spsa.py) is already known by the README to mis-rank history options; HbQuad/HbLin/HbMax and LmrHist were tuned there and may be mis-set for 10+0.1 play (the spsa_clock.py variant exists, check whether it was actually run for these params). Realistic ceiling of this angle is a few Elo; the ~120 Elo search gap is unlikely to be history-math.

proposals.title: Retune history bonus/gravity scale at 300k nodes (and fix the LMR/prune thresholds that read the same sum)
proposals.mechanism: Bonus is min(5d^2+33d, 1322) against a /16384 gravity (calc_s19.c:1569,1821; par HbQuad/HbLin/HbMax). SF14 used roughly 17d^2+134d-134 (cap near depth 13), 3-4x larger at the same gravity; the 'SF values' group (6,229,4167) measured -0.37 +-0.35 on the SF-net yardstick, i.e. not established either way, and our values came from SPSA at 2.5k-10k nodes (calc_s19.c:1018-1020) where the README shows history changes flip sign at depth (README ~l.164). Run a 3-parameter sweep (scale x0.5,1,2,3 on all three together, plus separate malus scale for quiets[q] at l.1823 e.g. 0.5x/1x) with LmrHist (hs/8192 clamp +-3, l.1768) and HistPrune (4245*depth) rescaled proportionally so the effective thresholds stay constant, otherwise a bigger bonus silently changes pruning. Also log the distribution of hs at LMR time to confirm the +-3 clamp is not saturated.
proposals.evidence: Weak/indirect. Our own: ext/README.md:554 (-0.37, noise level), README ~l.160-170 (HistV2 +19 at 10k nodes, -10/-9/-18 deeper). SPSA ranges in zero/spsa.py:18 and zero/spsa_clock.py:27-28 show HbMax was only ever searched 300-4000 at shallow nodes. No external measured Elo for the scale itself.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +8 (most likely +2); not a breakthrough
proposals.cheap_test: ext/quality.py at 300k nodes, 6 settings x ~9,000 positions; SE ~0.3 units so detects ~1 unit (40 Elo) cleanly but a 5 Elo effect (0.12 units) needs the 100k-node SF-net yardstick with repeated runs (SE 0.33-0.40 there, so ~3 repetitions). Then confirm one winner by a 1,000-game 10+0.1 match.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c par[] defaults line ~1019; update sites 1569, 1814, 1821-1831, 1844, 1849; LMR use 1768; prune use 1692-1715

proposals.title: Pawn-structure history (and low-ply history) added to the quiet-move score
proposals.mechanism: Add static short pawnh[512][12][64] indexed by (P.pkey & 511), moving piece, target (pkey already maintained incrementally, calc_s19.c:205-206, and used for corrhist at 1137). Add it to hist_score() (l.1144) with weight 1 and update it in hist_update() (l.1163) with the same bonus/malus and gravity; clear it at ucinewgame (l.2072,2153) and halve it between root searches like history_t (l.1914). Optional second table lowply[4][4096 from-to] for ply<4 (SF16-style) added only in the move-ordering score, with bonus about 8*bonus/ (depth+1) capped. Because it is a different signal from the continuation tables it should reduce the 'which quiet first' failure at shallow nodes that our 82% first-move cutoff rate hides; the yardstick uses SF14's search, which lacks it, so any gain here is beyond what SF14.1 has.
proposals.evidence: Mechanism exists in current Stockfish: DeepWiki move-picker page (https://deepwiki.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/4.4-move-ordering-and-move-picker) lists pawn-history table indexed by pawn structure, piece, destination; regression log (https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/wiki/Regression-Tests) shows an entry dated 2023-11-03 'Update pawn history based on static eval difference' at about +10 Elo (that is a refinement, not the introduction; original introduction gain not found). GPL licence: do not copy code, the idea is trivial. No result on our engine. Weak.
proposals.expected_elo: +2 to +10 at the clock; 0 to +0.15 units at 300k nodes
proposals.cheap_test: Implement as option PawnHist=0/1/2 (1 = ordering only, 2 = also LMR/prune sum), run quality at 100k and 300k nodes plus the SF-net yardstick at 100k (compare with the +2.77 behind-SF figure in README). Note README warns 10k-node results mislead; judge only at >=100k.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c: hist_score 1144-1152, hist_update 1163-1167, memsets 2072/2153, halving at 1914

proposals.title: Surprise-scaled bonus plus symmetric 'early-cutoff-only' update filter
proposals.mechanism: At the cutoff update (l.1821) use bonus(depth + (v > beta + margin ? 1 : 0)) with margin about 150-200 cp in our units (a cutoff far above beta is stronger evidence the move is good), and apply the quiet malus (l.1823) only when the cutoff move was found within the first ~4 moves (otherwise the list of 'failed' quiets is long and mostly noise, which punishes moves that were merely late-ordered). Also stop rewarding on cutoffs in nodes where the TT move is capture and node is cutnode with r>=3 reductions (noisy). The aim is to cut update noise, consistent with measured fact 9 (our move choice is ~17x more sensitive to hash size than SF's), since history values that depend on search order inject path-dependence.
proposals.evidence: Not measured by us. Stockfish later versions use depth+1 bonus on large beta-excess (I recall this from fishtest summaries; cannot cite a verified URL, treat as unverified memory). Our own HistV2 test shows rewarding extra non-cutoff moves (HistV2=4) hurt at 100k nodes (-15, README ~l.169), which argues that update noise matters at depth, so reducing noisy updates is plausible but untested.
proposals.expected_elo: -2 to +4; mostly a noise-reduction probe
proposals.cheap_test: Two flags (BonusSurprise, MalusEarly); quality at 300k nodes with the hash-size stability test of fact 9 as a second metric (fraction of positions where the chosen move changes when only the table size changes; current 19%). If stability does not improve, drop it without a match.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c 1819-1831 (cutoff update block), nq/quiets[] collection in the move loop

summary: Evidence says threshold-shifting is exhausted: 12 variants plus the SF-parameter bundle are all worse-or-level at SE 0.27-0.40, consistent with a flat optimum already tuned on this very test set (winner's curse makes every perturbation look slightly worse), and with reduction mistakes being self-correcting through re-search (the learned LMR model with AUC 0.907 bought nothing). A gain has to come from new information (a better pruning discriminator, an uncertainty signal BIGS lacks) or from a less noisy instrument, not from retuning depth-linear margins. I found no fishtest-grade public evidence for uncertainty-conditioned futility margins (only small engine PRs), so expectations are low.
warnings: No injected instructions seen. Web search returned only small-engine PRs (no fishtest-grade evidence, none cited as strong). Caveat: I could not confirm that BIGS has no reliability read-out head (have_vol); check have_vol on the standing net before proposal 2. All three proposals are low expected-Elo; the honest read is that pruning margins are near a flat optimum and the factor of three is more likely in move ordering/hash-instability than in pruning math. I did not read Stockfish source.

proposals.title: Use the learned move-judgment model as a PRUNER with a depth-dependent risk budget, not as a reducer
proposals.mechanism: The Sel additive model (calc_s19.c SEL/SEL_A/SEL_B, ext/lsel_fit.py) ranks late moves far better than the standing rule (depth 8+: only 2.0% of moves that matter fall in the half it judges safest vs 10.4%), but used as a reduction it was level because a reduced look that beats the bound gets re-searched anyway. Pruning has no such safety net, and 67% of nodes are spent inside reduced looks, mostly on moves that fail low. So: in the move loop (around line 1676-1705), for quiet moves at depth>=3 beyond LMP depth, compute the model log-odds p = P(move beats alpha at full depth) and skip the move when p < eps(depth), with eps from an explicit cost model: prune iff p * V_loss < c(depth) where c(depth) is the measured mean subtree size of the reduced look at that depth (available from SSTAT counters: main nodes by plies left 33%/14%/7.5%/5%) and V_loss is calibrated so that eps is about 0.5% at depth 3 rising to about 3% at depth 8+. Calibrate eps per depth bucket on the held-out 1.2M LSEL records (compute the fraction of true beats-bound moves lost vs nodes saved), then sweep one global multiplier on the quality test. Apply only at non-PV, non-check nodes; never to killers/TT move/first 2 moves; keep a verification: if a node's best score is below alpha-margin after all pruning at a cut-node, nothing extra.
proposals.evidence: ext/README.md lines 517-538: AUC 0.907 vs 0.822, 2.0% vs 10.4% misrank at depth 8+, yet 6 settings level (+0.11,-0.33,+0.16,+0.42,+0.06,-0.02) because rejected-by-reduction moves are re-searched. Lines 540-543: where nodes go. Lines 461-469: more pruning by rule is worse, which argues the gain must come from better discrimination, not more aggressive thresholds. No external evidence; this is our own inference, treat as a hypothesis. Risk: the model was trained on 2,399 self-play positions at 300k nodes only, so it may not transfer to the 9,000-position test (same Lichess-type distribution?) and costs 5% speed.
proposals.expected_elo: -10 to +15 (most likely about 0; a bad calibration loses quickly, a good one gets the saved reduced-look nodes at near-zero loss)
proposals.cheap_test: Add option SelPrune (eps thresholds per depth bucket) next to the existing Sel path; run ext/quality.py at 300k nodes on the 9,000 positions, 3 settings of the multiplier (x0.5, x1, x2). Accept only if some setting beats standing by more than 2 SE (about -0.6 units) and then confirm at 100k and 1M and in a 1,000-game 10+0.1 match.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c move loop lines ~1676-1740 (the want/ls_ok block already builds the 34-feature record and evaluates the Sel model for SEL; reuse it), options SEL/SEL_A/SEL_B, ext/lsel_fit.py for the per-depth calibration table

proposals.title: Uncertainty-conditioned margins using a free proxy (size of eval correction, TT-vs-static gap) through the existing VolMix path
proposals.mechanism: The engine already has margin scaling vm = 256 + VolMix*(vol*256/VolRef-256)/100 (lines 1589-1594) applied to razoring, RFP, futility, but vol comes from eval_vol(), a reliability read-out head that BIGS does not have (have_vol is presumably 0 for BIGS; it was last evaluated on generation-101 nets, where the uncertainty half gave +1 (-22 to 24) at 60+0.6, i.e. nothing). Instead of training a new head, define vol from signals available now: (a) |eval_corr() - raw static| (the correction-history magnitude already computed at line 1580, large correction = the static eval has been wrong in this structure), (b) |tt_score - static ev| when a TT entry of depth>=3 exists, (c) |ev - evals_stack[ply-2]| (swing). vol = clamp(base + k1*a + k2*b + k3*c). Fit k by regressing |search score at depth d - static ev| on these using the LSEL records (they carry ev_alpha, tt_alpha, depth, nodes) so margins scale with the real conditional error spread, not guess. Then enable via VolMix with VolRef set to the median proxy. A principled version: margin(depth) = z * sigma_hat(depth, proxy) with sigma_hat the conditional std of (search score - static eval) fitted per depth, replacing linear FutBase+FutMul*pd.
proposals.evidence: Mechanism exists in code (calc_s19.c:1589-1594) and zero/best_options.md:59 shows null result with a trained read-out on old nets, so weak. Correction-history feeding pruning is reported at +18.5 +/- 7.9 Elo at 10+0.1 in one small engine PR (https://github.com/conorosully27-cloud/Chess_Engine/pull/16 was the engine-3.1 PR in the search results; the correction-feeds-pruning PR was not identified by URL, so unverified). Our engine already corrects eval, so that gain is probably already collected. Fact 4 of the brief (BIGS error 22.7 vs SF net 18.6 in squared error) says our evaluator's error is slightly larger, which modestly favours wider margins rather than tighter.
proposals.cheap_test: 1) offline: from LSEL records (ext/lsel_collect.py output) compute correlation and a per-depth conditional std of search-minus-static against the three proxies; if the proxy explains less than about 5% of the variance of |error|, stop (about 1 hour). 2) otherwise add the proxy as vol and run quality.py at 300k with VolMix 50/100/150.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc_s19.c lines 1580-1594 (eval_corr, evals_stack, vm); eval_vol at calc_s18.c:858 shows what the head did; ext/lsel_collect.py and lsel_fit.py for the regression

proposals.title: Make the pruning scans resolvable: replicate-averaged quality instrument (hash size and 1%-node jitter) before concluding anything about pruning
proposals.mechanism: Fact 9 shows our chosen move flips in 19% of positions when only the hash size changes (Stockfish 1.1%) and 0.1% for a 1% node change. So each position's quality outcome at 300k nodes is a noisy draw, and the instrument SE of 0.27-0.31 per variant includes this chaos. Every one of the 12 variants was compared against the standing options with a single draw, and the standing options were themselves selected on the same set (winner's curse), so a pure-noise perturbation looks worse on average. Fix: run each variant and the baseline with 3 hash sizes (e.g. 16/64/256 MB) and average the per-position quality, and compare paired per position. Re-run the 4 or 5 most promising/near-zero variants (SearchV3=64 -0.17, SearchV3=16 -0.10, Sel 175/75 -0.33, SF reductions group -0.50 on yardstick) and the pruning group. Also split positions into tune (half) and held-out (half) to remove selection bias. Secondary finding to chase: the 19% flip rate itself is a search defect (likely path-dependence from TT cutoffs/replacement or the tt_score override of ev at line 1587); a deterministic-replay test with cut-offs by TT disabled at depth<=2 could localise it.
proposals.evidence: ext/README.md lines 588-589 (stability) and 461-469, 553-560 (variant tables with SE 0.27-0.40). Statistical argument: if averaging 3 replicates removes the hash-chaos share of per-position variance, SE falls by up to 1/sqrt(3) (0.17-0.18); the real reduction is unmeasured. No external source.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 directly; it decides whether the -0.5 SF-reductions group and -0.33/-0.17 variants are real wins of 10-20 Elo that were hidden by noise
proposals.cheap_test: Run quality.py at 300k for baseline and baseline with HASH differing (3 sizes), measure the per-position disagreement and the SE of the paired difference between baseline@64MB and baseline@16MB (expected 0 by construction; if the SE of that null comparison is above 0.3 the instrument cannot resolve pruning changes). Then repeat 4 variants with replicates.
proposals.where_in_our_code: ext/quality.py, zero/results/vault_stab.log, vault_screen300k.log; tt_find/replacement and line 1587 in calc_s19.c for the flip-rate investigation

summary: The learned-LMR failure (ext/README.md:517-538) is explained by the README's own diagnosis: LMR is self-correcting because a reduced look that beats the bound is re-searched, so a better ranking of late moves only recovers moves the standing rule was not losing. A learned control only pays where a wrong decision is not re-checked (null-move tries, node pruning margins, cutnode/allnode guesses), or where its target is node cost and not "does the move matter". I found no published chess-engine result showing Elo from a learned cutoff or reduction model. The web search was thin, and the only supporting evidence I could verify is the Stockfish commit for correction history and engine PRs for history-in-LMR.
warnings: The web search returned few relevant results; I found no verified paper or engine test of a neural or learned cutoff/reduction predictor gaining Elo, so claims about what 'design works' beyond the self-correction argument are inference. Elo figures from the Stockfish commit and rusty-chess PR are from search snippets, not re-read. No injected instructions seen in fetched pages. Licences: cited engine pages (GitHub PRs) were used for ideas only; no code was read or copied, and none of it should be copied if GPL. The hash-instability fact (19% move changes from table size alone) probably limits how visible any of these small gains are on the quality instrument; fixing it would improve the signal for every proposal here.

proposals.title: Learned null-move gate (predict try success, skip low-probability tries, optionally set R)
proposals.mechanism: Null-move tries take 17-20% of all nodes and succeed only 45-49% of the time (README.md:542), so about half of that spend is a wasted subtree, and unlike LMR a wrongly skipped or wrongly run try is never re-checked. Reuse the -DLSEL collection path (calc_s19.c ~1733-1790: feature struct lr, ls_logit, sampling buffer) at the null-move site (~line 1605). Log features at each node where a try is allowed: eval-beta, depth, cutnode, improving, ttpv, tt flag/depth/score minus beta, ply, piece-count phase, in-check-last-ply, last move capture, the parent's move number, and the try's outcome plus its subtree node count. Fit the same additive bucket model. Then (a) skip the try when predicted success is below a threshold p0 (sweep 0.15-0.30) and (b) optionally increase R when predicted success is above 0.8. Select the threshold by counting nodes saved against false skips. A false skip costs a missed cutoff, so cost-weight the label by subtree node count and not by a plain 0/1 label.
proposals.evidence: Measured on our engine: 45-49% try success and 17-20% of nodes inside tries (ext/README.md:542). The learned-LMR model showed that bucketed features reach AUC 0.907 versus 0.822 for the standing rule (README.md:527-531), so the null decision likely has similar slack, because the standing rule is a hand formula (calc_s19.c:1605: base + depth/div + (ev-beta)/NMP_EV capped). Counter-evidence: NmpBase/NmpDiv sweeps were level or worse (README.md:463, 555), meaning the plateau is flat along the depth/eval axes, and the gain would have to come from the other features. No published number found; the evidence for a gain is weak.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +15 at 10+0.1; most likely about +3, since the LMR analogue gave 0
proposals.cheap_test: Step 1 (about 2 h): collect about 5M null-try records from the same 2,399 self-play positions at 300k nodes, fit offline, and report the share of nodes saved against the share of successful tries skipped at a few thresholds. Stop if no threshold skips 15%+ of tries while losing under 3% of successes. Step 2: add options NmpSel and NmpSelThr (the same shape as Sel/SelFile) and run the quality test at 300k nodes against the standing rule, with the 100k search-only yardstick as a second check.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c null-move block near line 1605 (NMP_BASE/NMP_DIV/NMP_EV); LSEL feature and collection scaffolding near 1733 and 1778-1792; ext/lsel_collect.py and ext/lsel_fit.py as templates.

proposals.title: Cost-aware reduction target: fit the reduction to expected subtree size and re-search probability, not to 'the move matters'
proposals.mechanism: The Sel model's label was whether the full-depth look beats the bound, but nearly every such move also beats it at reduced depth and is re-searched, so the label ranks moves the engine was already handling. Re-label with two quantities per late move: p_re (the reduced look fails high, which forces a re-search) and the node count of the reduced look at reduction r, taken from sampled r in {0,1,2,3} (LSEL already samples r=0; extend it to also run the reduced look at two or three r values with the node counter). Choose r per move to minimise E[nodes] = N(r) + p_re(r)*N(0), with a hard cap on p_re of about 0.10 to 0.15. The current 5.5% re-search rate (README.md:542) suggests the engine sits far on the safe side in aggregate, while uniform extra reduction was worse (LmrBase tests, README.md:462-466). So the gain must come from non-uniform reduction, large r where p_re is tiny and small r elsewhere. Add depth as an interaction feature; the current linear-in-logit mapping SelA - SelB*(z+5) (calc_s19.c:1780) is too crude, so use a per-depth lookup of z to r tuned to equalise the marginal re-search rate.
proposals.evidence: Own data: Sel at six (A,B) settings was level to +/-0.4 units (README.md:535, SE 0.26-0.30) despite log-loss removal of 31.6% versus 15.3%, and the README's own diagnosis is that re-search makes the ranking irrelevant. The Stockfish 14.1 reduction group was -0.50 (better but not significant) at 100k on the yardstick (README.md:553). Elsewhere: history-scaled reductions give +11 +/- 9 in a small engine PR (https://github.com/conorosully27-cloud/Chess_Engine/pull/19), which is weak evidence that the move-feature route yields only small gains.
proposals.expected_elo: -5 to +10; the central estimate is about +2, with a real chance of nothing, since the LMR family has been near-flat across 12+ variants
proposals.cheap_test: Offline first (1 h): from the existing 16.5M records plus a second pass logging reduced-look node counts, compute expected nodes per search under the standing rule versus the cost-aware policy at equal p_re. If predicted node saving is under 8%, stop (it would be under about 0.5 ply, below what the quality test can see). Otherwise run the quality test at 300k nodes with SE about 0.3 against Sel's best setting.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c 1756-1787 (reduction computation and SEL override), 1794-1801 (re-search path); ext/lsel_fit.py to refit with the cost label.
