proposals.title: Extend correction history beyond pawn structure (non-pawn, minor/major piece, continuation) as an online-learned control signal
proposals.mechanism: Correction history is the one form of 'learned search control' with consistent engine-test gains: it learns online how wrong the static eval is for a context and shifts the eval used for pruning and reduction decisions. The checkout has only pawn-structure correction (corrhist[2][16384], calc_s19.c:1131-1137). Add 2-3 more tables keyed by (a) non-pawn piece hashes per colour, (b) minor-piece key, (c) a continuation key from the previous two moves (piece, to-square), update by history-gravity on (search score - static eval) weighted by depth at nodes with a stored exact/bound score, and sum the weighted corrections into the eval used for RFP, futility, null-move and 'improving' decisions. Also use |correction| or the eval-vs-search disagreement as an input to the existing VOL_LMR class (par[VOL_LMR], line 1772) so reduction is lower where the eval is known to be unreliable.
proposals.evidence: Stockfish's introducing commit annotates the corrected-eval piece at about 13 Elo and the use of eval difference in quiet ordering at about 9 Elo (https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/commit/b4d995d0d910044cf4ea2ad3ee30fd1d21070cd8, from a search snippet; I did not re-read it); a separate Rust engine reports +7.4 +/- 4.7 timed and +9.8 +/- 5.7 at fixed nodes for pawn correction alone (https://github.com/jwallace145/rusty-chess-v2/pull/221); the chess programming wiki lists pawn, material, threat, minor and continuation variants (https://chessprogramming.org/Static_Evaluation_Correction_History). A claim that the gain grows with search time comes from a single engine issue and is unverified. Caveat: our net already matches Stockfish's evaluator (fact 4), so the correction signal may be smaller, and it adds noise to a hash-unstable search (fact 9).
proposals.expected_elo: +3 to +10 beyond the current pawn table; below the resolution of the 300k quality test, so judge by match
proposals.cheap_test: Quality test at 300k and 1M nodes (SE 0.3 means only about 12 Elo resolution, so run both, and also the 100k search-only yardstick); then a 1,000-game 10+0.1 match against the current build, as that is the only instrument that can see +5 Elo.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c corrhist array and its read/update sites near 1131-1140, the static-eval computation at the top of search(), and the update point after the move loop where the final score is known.

summary: Our root (search_root, calc/calc_s19.c:1901-1992) is already close to standard PVS iterative deepening with aspiration. No root change has a strong expected return, because the measured gap is search efficiency inside the tree. The one root-level inefficiency I measured is that 60-70% of nodes go to null-window searches of non-best root moves at full depth. The two existing flags that attack this (RootLmr, RootOrd) were only tested at 40k nodes per move, with confidence intervals of +-13 Elo. Reading the code and probing it with the tiny g6 net (the BIGS net is not in the checkout), I found that aspiration fails essentially never at 300k, so aspiration tuning is not worth time, and final-iteration waste is real but is a fixed-node-test effect more than a clock effect.
warnings: 1) The BIGS/BIGM nets are not in the checkout (only tiny zero/g*.bin nets), so my local numbers (best-move node share, depth gain from RootLmr, partial-iteration waste, zero aspiration fails in 3 probes) come from a weak net on 3 positions and are anecdotes. 2) Aspiration: in all 3 probes there were no fail-lows or fail-highs after depth 5, so Stockfish-style aspiration tuning (smaller initial delta, delta*1.5, beta recentre, depth reduction after fail-high) is not worth time; ASP=33 is also an SPSA result (calc_s19.c:1017). 3) The fixed-node quality test stops mid-iteration, so any root change that helps only the partial last iteration will look good on it and not transfer to the clock (tm_dynamic breaks at iteration boundaries, line 1985). Always confirm at the clock. 4) Time management at the clock looks reasonable and I found no obvious defect (alloc = t/20 + 0.75 inc, soft scaled by node share, stability and score drop, hard = 3x alloc, lines 2200-2204). 5) My local test build is in /tmp/rs (a copy of calc_s19.c with stderr counters); nothing in /home/user/seek was modified. 6) I did not read Stockfish's source. Statements about what it does at the root come from memory of public documentation and may be off. No injected instructions were found in anything I read.

proposals.title: Re-test existing RootLmr / RootOrd at 300k nodes and at the clock, plus a stronger root-LMR variant
proposals.mechanism: No new code for the first step: run ext/quality.py test at 300000 nodes with --opts Hash=64,RootLmr=1 and again with RootLmr=1,RootOrd=1, then a clock match. If positive, add a variant of the root-LMR line (calc_s19.c:1936-1941). That line currently reduces only quiet moves with i>=3, root_depth>=4, and uses lmr[d][i]-1. The variant is: i>=2, no -1, one less reduction for moves that raised alpha earlier, and for moves ordered by root_move_nodes (RootOrd) a reduction scaled by their effort rank. Full-depth re-search on fail-high is already there (line 1942). The reason to expect more than at 40k: the only prior tests (zero/results/local_root_and_hash_tests.log lines 1-2) were at 40,000 positions per move, where RootLmr scored -6.5 (-19.7 to +6.7, 1448 games) and RootOrd +2.5 (-11.2 to +16.3, 1500 games, undecided). The README itself says search changes must be judged at 100k+ nodes or at the clock (ext/README.md:169). Stockfish reduces late root moves in its ordinary move loop (documented behaviour of its LMR at moveCount>1, chessprogramming wiki; I did not read its source). The best-move share of nodes is only 0.3-0.4 for typical middlegame positions with the g6 net, so the null-window re-checks of other root moves are a large cost.
proposals.evidence: Weak-to-moderate. Local probe, tiny g6 net, 300k nodes, 3 middlegame positions (my /tmp build with stderr counters, not the real net): RootLmr=1 gained one iteration in 2 of 3 positions (d12->d13 at similar nodes, d15/16 vs d16 equal in the third), and RootOrd+RootLmr gave similar depth. The bestmove changed in the second position (f4g3 -> h2h3 -> d4c5), so this is not a free lunch. Cumulative best-move node share at the end was 0.28-0.69 (0.94 in a forcing position). Prior matches: zero/results/local_root_and_hash_tests.log lines 1-2. Root-share code: calc_s19.c:1946 and 1981.
proposals.expected_elo: -3 to +6 at 10+0.1; most likely +0-3. The effect is bounded by the share of nodes spent on non-best root moves (roughly 30-40% of the tree at depth 12, which at best buys +0.5 ply).
proposals.cheap_test: quality.py test --nodes 300000 for RootLmr=1, RootLmr=1+RootOrd=1 vs the base (SE ~0.3 units = ~12 Elo, so only a >=1 unit effect is visible), and run on 1000 games at 10+0.1 only if the quality unit moves by >=0.5 in the good direction. About 0.3 h per quality run on 22 boards.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c:1936-1944 (root LMR), 1963-1968 (ordering by effort), par defaults at line 1020 (RootLmr, RootOrd both 0)

proposals.title: Root candidate focusing: stop re-checking root moves that are clearly refuted, and spend the saved nodes on the top few
proposals.mechanism: After each completed iteration D>=8, take root_scores[] (fail-soft upper bounds for non-best moves, searched null-window at a-bon, lines 1941 and 1948). Mark a non-best move dead for the following iteration if its bound is < best - M, with M around 120-200 cp (decreasing with depth, e.g. 250 - 10*(D-8), floor 100), and skip it at the next iteration, except re-admit all moves whenever the best score drops by >=40 cp or the best move changes, or in the next iteration if that move was the TT move or gives check. This lets the final deeper iterations spend their nodes on the best move and the runner-up, which is exactly what the instrument rewards (choice between the two best moves). Variant B for the fixed-node test only: when remaining nodes < 1.2x the previous iteration's cost, run the next iteration with only the top-3 root moves instead of abandoning it halfway. Treat variant B as instrument-specific; it does not help at the clock because time management stops at iteration boundaries (line 1985).
proposals.evidence: Weak. Measured here: on the tiny net the best move gets 0.28-0.69 of all nodes and the final iteration is incomplete in all 3 probes (e.g. d12 finished at 135k, the remaining 165k nodes went to a partial d13; d11 finished at 171k, 130k to a partial d12), so 30-55% of the 300k budget lands in an iteration that only re-searches the first moves. That is the same in Stockfish at a fixed node limit, so it is not a defect, but it shows where concentration could help. No fishtest-scale evidence found for explicit root pruning in Stockfish-like engines (they use LMR rather than skipping), so this is a guess backed by node accounting, not by an Elo measurement.
proposals.expected_elo: -5 to +5; likely +0-3 at the clock, up to +1 unit (+40 Elo-equivalent) possible only on the fixed-node instrument for variant B, which would not transfer.
proposals.cheap_test: First a measurement, 0.5 h of coding: add counters under SSTAT for the share of nodes in root moves whose bound is < best-150 at depth>=8 (the real BIGS net, 300k nodes, 500 positions from the quality set); if that share is under 10% abandon the idea. Otherwise implement as a par flag (e.g. RootFocus=M), then quality.py at 300k and 100k, then a 1000-game clock match.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c:1925-1951 (root move loop, add a skip test against root_scores[i]), 1953-1962 (aspiration and best-move bookkeeping); stats via root_move_nodes[] at line 1094

proposals.title: Bisect the 19% table-size instability: switch off the correction histories and test whether root choices become stable
proposals.mechanism: Run the vault_stab test (zero/results/vault_stab.log) with one feature removed at a time: corrhist[] (calc_s19.c:1131-1137, updated at 1854), corr_mm, corr_np, corr_cont (NpCorr=1 and the pawn-keyed corrhist are on by default), HistV2 bits, TT replacement rule. Needs a tiny code change to gate eval_corr() and the update at line 1854 by a new flag. Rationale: a perturbation of roughly 3% of the table slots flips 19% of our final moves but 1.1% of Stockfish's; we have several search-state feedback loops (evaluation corrected by learned history, which changes pruning, which changes the next correction) that Stockfish 14.1 as documented does not have (pawn-keyed correction history entered Stockfish later; treat that date as unverified). Such a loop makes near-tied root decisions chaotic. If the instability drops sharply for one component and the quality score is not worse, remove or damp it (smaller update weight, 16-bit clamp, reset per search); if instability stays 19% with everything off, the cause is in the TT/PV handling and the next step is a PV-chain re-extension from the TT.
proposals.evidence: Indirect. The measured fact itself (ext/README.md:589-592, vault_stab.log) plus the fact that the quality harness sends ucinewgame before every position (ext/quality.py:53, 160-164), so history left over from other positions is not the cause. A 512 MB table plays the same as 64 MB, so the sensitivity is chaos, not loss of quality. I have not measured which component causes it.
proposals.expected_elo: -2 to +5; the instability itself costs nothing in expectation, so the gain only appears if a feedback loop is also hurting quality. Mostly this is a diagnostic that tells the lead whether to chase search noise at all.
proposals.cheap_test: vault_stab-style run at 300k nodes on ~2,000 positions, one config per feature (about 10 min each on 22 boards), reading both the changed-move rate and quality.py units for the same config.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c:1131-1140 (corrhist read), 1854 (update), corr_mm/corr_np/corr_cont arrays, tt_find at ~1066

summary: We already have the main "use the TT as a better eval" machinery in search (line 1587-1588 of calc_s19.c: ev replaced by tt_score when the bound is compatible, applied after the improving flag is computed, which is the same order Stockfish uses) and a rich correction history (pawn, non-pawn, continuation, minor/major). What we do NOT have is (a) the static eval stored in the TT, so every TT hit and every post-null-move node recomputes the network, (b) any use of the TT score as stand-pat in qsearch (line 1504 uses only eval_corr), and (c) a robust improving flag (check nodes store -INF, no ply-4 fallback). None of these is likely to close a 100+ Elo search-efficiency gap; the first is a speed gain worth perhaps 5-10 Elo, the second a small node-efficiency gain. The big levers for fact 9 (19% move flips on hash size) lie elsewhere: qsearch depth-0 stores unconditionally overwrite deep entries in the default one-entry-per-slot table (lines 1532-1537, tt_find with TT_BUCKET off).
warnings: 1) I did not fetch Stockfish source (per the rule), so Stockfish behaviours cited (eval stored in TT, null-move eval reuse, qsearch ttValue-as-eval, improving ply-4 fallback) are from memory of its design, not verified here; I had no fishtest Elo numbers in hand for any of the three, so Elo ranges are estimates from rule-of-thumb. 2) Side finding relevant to fact 9 (hash instability): with TT_BUCKET off (default; README comment at line 1063 says +19 at 1 MB/100k nodes but -9/-10 at longer clocks), qsearch (lines 1532-1537) overwrites whatever occupies the slot whenever the key differs, including deep search entries, and search() (1881) always replaces too; a depth-preferred policy that refuses qsearch/shallow stores over deeper different-key entries unless aged is worth a quality test (cheap: 1 hour) since it targets the 19% vs 1.1% move-flip gap, and TtBucket's long-clock loss may come from its age arithmetic rather than from buckets. 3) The TT also lacks a depth-0 vs real-search distinction on read: search() accepts qsearch entries (depth 0) as a score override at line 1587 for any depth, which may be noisier than Stockfish's use. 4) No injected instructions were seen; no web pages were fetched.

proposals.title: Store raw static eval in the TT and reuse it on hits; reuse parent eval after null move (skip the NNUE call)
proposals.mechanism: TTE is 16 bytes: key 8 + Move(int) 4 + short score + depth + flag (calc_s19.c:369). Make room for a 16-bit raw (pre-correction) eval: either pack Move into 16 bits (from/to/flag likely fit, check the FLAG/PROMO encoding) or use a 48-bit key check. In search() (after the e->key==P.key branch, line ~1561) and qsearch() (line ~1496), if the entry hits and holds an eval, set raw = e->eval and skip evaluate() (and acc_ensure, since accumulators are updated lazily, so the pending updates are also skipped until a descendant needs them); then apply eval_corr as now (store RAW eval, not corrected, since the correction tables change over time). On store (lines 1535, 1881, 1638) write the raw eval that was computed at this node (keep it in a local; currently eval_corr() returns only the corrected value, so split it into raw + corr). Second part: when the previous move was a null move (move_stack[ply-1]==0), set ev = -evals_raw[ply-1] + tempo constant instead of calling the net; the accumulator is unchanged by a null move, so this saves only the output layer plus corr, but Stockfish does the same and it also removes a lazy-update sync. Also do it for check nodes: store VALUE_NONE sentinel (e.g. -32768).
proposals.evidence: Stockfish evaluates only on a TT miss or missing eval and reuses the parent's value after a null move (documented in the Stockfish search-algorithm descriptions on the chessprogramming wiki, https://www.chessprogramming.org/Stockfish and the NNUE pages; I could not fetch source per the rules, so details are from memory of the design, not measured by me). I have no Elo number for this from fishtest; speed-for-Elo rule of thumb at our level is ~5-7 Elo per 10% nps (doubling nps is worth tens of Elo). Our evaluator is the dominant per-node cost (H=768 x 2 perspectives, lazy accumulators, ext/README.md and the TSTAT build splitting ts_acc/ts_out), so skipping it on hits is a real saving, but the fraction of non-cutoff nodes with a usable TT entry is UNMEASURED here (my estimate 25-40% of search nodes, fewer in qsearch). Weak evidence: only the mechanism is solid.
proposals.expected_elo: +3 to +10 Elo at 10+0.1 (nps +4% to +12%); negligible at fixed nodes (a pure speed change). Risk: slightly more TT memory traffic, and an eval stored at a different corrhist state is no worse than recomputing since raw is stored.
proposals.cheap_test: Build a variant, run bench for nps (1.1-1.3M now) and confirm the node count at fixed depth is IDENTICAL with eval-in-TT on/off when hash is large enough (determinism check; null-move reuse will legitimately change it, so test the two parts separately). Then a 1000-game 10+0.1 match vs the baseline binary, or SPRT-style 2000 games at the clock. The quality test at fixed nodes should read ~0 (sanity) and only the nps and clock match matter. Count with a counter how often evaluate() is skipped first (10 minutes).
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c: TTE typedef line 369; qsearch 1486-1539 (TT probe 1494-1501, eval 1504, store 1532-1537); search 1558-1588 (probe, eval_corr at 1580, TT-score override 1587); store 1876-1883; ProbCut store 1638; evaluate() 890; eval_corr 1136.

proposals.title: Qsearch: use TT score as the stand-pat / better evaluation when the bound is compatible, and probe TT eval
proposals.mechanism: In qsearch after computing stand = eval_corr() (line 1504), if the entry hit (e->key==P.key) and its score s (mate-adjusted, not a mate score) has bound compatible with moving best upward (fl==TT_EXACT, or fl==TT_LOWER and s > stand, or fl==TT_UPPER and s < stand), set best = stand = s for the purposes of the beta cutoff, delta pruning and alpha raising (keep a separate raw value for nothing else; qsearch has no correction update). Do not do it when in check. Optionally restrict to depth>=0 entries from real search (e->depth>=1) which are much more reliable than depth-0 qsearch entries; test both variants because our qsearch entries store depth 0 and are themselves stand-pat values (line 1535) so using them gives only a recycled eval. The existing search() already does the equivalent at 1587.
proposals.evidence: This is in Stockfish 14's qsearch (comment to the effect 'ttValue can be used as a better position evaluation') - from memory of the source; I did not fetch it. Search-side equivalent already present here, so the marginal effect is only qsearch leaves. Fishtest-style gains for such patches are typically +1 to +3 Elo; no measured number from a primary source is available to me. Our own measurements: 12 pruning/reduction variants were all slightly worse at 300k nodes, so prior for micro-changes in this regime is low.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +4 Elo; at fixed-node quality maybe -0.1 to -0.3 units (about 4 to 12 Elo equivalent) if it works, and could also be harmful because it increases dependence on the hash table, which fact 9 shows is already unstable (19% move changes on table size). If the quality test shows it increasing the table-size sensitivity, drop it.
proposals.cheap_test: Add par option QsTtEval; run ext/quality.py at 300k nodes (~9000 positions, SE 0.3 units) with option 0 and 1, plus the table-size flip rate (fact 9 measure) for both. One afternoon on one core group. Then the 1000-game match only if quality improves by >=0.5 units.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c qsearch lines 1494-1510 (add after 1504); new par[] entry beside the par_name table at ~1015.

proposals.title: Make the improving flag robust: ply-4 fallback when ply-2 was in check, and a graded improvement used in LMR/RFP
proposals.mechanism: Currently improving = !chk && ply>=2 && ev > evals_stack[ply-2] (line 1585), and evals_stack stores -INF when in check (line 1584 with ev=-INF), so after any check at ply-2 improving is always true. Change to: p = evals_stack[ply-2] if it is not -INF else evals_stack[ply-4] if not -INF else treat as improving=1 (matches what I recall of the reference engines). Second variant: keep delta = ev - p and use improving = delta > 0 for pruning but feed clamp(delta,-100,100)/25 additively into the LMR reduction (line 1758 currently r += !improving) and into the reverse-futility margin (line 1600, 'depth - improving'). Note that ev compared here is the corrected eval before TT adjustment, which is the right choice. Also make sure evals_stack is set before the early returns so stale values from previous iterations are never read (check that evals_stack[ply-2] is initialised at the root iteration for ply 0/1).
proposals.evidence: Weak. The Stockfish improving definition and the ply-4 fallback are from my memory of the design, no fishtest number checked. Our own evidence that LMR/pruning tuning is flat at 300k nodes (fact 8: 12 variants all slightly worse; learned LMR model with AUC 0.907 vs 0.822 level in play) argues that this will not move the needle; flagged as low value.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +3 Elo, most likely unmeasurable inside the +-12 Elo error of a 1000-game match.
proposals.cheap_test: Quality test at 300k and 30k nodes (SE ~0.3 units each); accept only if both improve. Do NOT spend match time on it unless quality gain >= 0.5 units. About 30-45 minutes of compute.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c lines 1580-1585 (evals_stack, improving), 1679-1688, 1758, 1600, 1620.

summary: I found no numerical problem worth Elo. BIGS runs per-unit int16 scales (about 128 steps per unit range, real sums reach 53 of a worst-case bound of 244), only 0.8% of units saturate, and finer scales were already measured as no effect, so quantization is not the lever. Two small and cheap things came out of reading the code: EvalScale was only ever tried at 140 on BIGS, and the native evaluate() has no shuffling damp although the Stockfish-net yardstick build does. Both are likely worth under 10 Elo.
warnings: No injected instructions seen; I fetched no web pages. Quantization closed: README:579-581 says the integer scale comes from a worst-case bound of 244 per unit (about 128 steps over the 0..1 working range) while real sums reach only 53. A data-driven bound (for example the 99.99th percentile with clipping) would give about 4x finer resolution, but the project already measured that finer scales gave no effect (fact 8), and the 3.1 cp mean engine-vs-trainer gap (18 cp max) is small next to the position-to-position spread. Hash-size sensitivity (fact 9) is search-side, not numerical. One caveat on the yardstick: the SFNET build also applies Stockfish's material scaling, and EvalScale=140 was chosen for it (README:441), so the 120 Elo search gap is slightly confounded by eval post-processing. I could not fully verify where EvalScale is applied in the native BIGS path (grep found only the comment at line 1041 and the par_name table), so confirm the option actually reaches evaluate() before sweeping it.

proposals.title: Bracket EvalScale below and above 100 on BIGS (margin recalibration)
proposals.mechanism: evaluate() returns v = out*271.58 with no EvalScale applied in the native path as far as I could see (the option is documented at calc_s19.c:1041 and in the par_name table at line 1016, but I did not find where the native path applies it). Check where the par is applied, then run EvalScale = 80, 90, 110, 120 on BIGS. Reason: every search margin (razor, rfp, futility, probcut, SEE, aspiration, singular) was tuned in the old centipawn scale. The BIGS logit*271.58 scale is a free choice that was never swept. Only 140 was tried on BIGS (worse). In effect this is a global joint rescale of all margins.
proposals.evidence: ext/README.md:424 shows EvalScale=140 vs 100 at 100k nodes gave +0.73 (0.40) units, worse in every match. No lower or finer values are reported for BIGS. README:199-209 shows EvalScale mattered by 20-40 Elo for networks trained on other label scales, so the search is scale-sensitive. Evidence for a gain on BIGS is weak: it is an untested neighbourhood, not a measured gradient.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +8 (most likely 0); a clear gain would show as -0.4 units or better at 300k
proposals.cheap_test: ext/quality.py at 300k nodes, 4 values of EvalScale, about 1.5 minutes of search plus under 1 minute of Stockfish checks each (README:429-430). Adopt only if two adjacent values improve by more than 0.5 units (about 2 standard errors), then confirm with a 10+0.1 match.

proposals.title: Add 50-move shuffling damp to the native evaluator
proposals.mechanism: At the end of evaluate() (calc_s19.c:954-958) do v = v * (100 - min(P.half,100)) / 100, the same form already used for the Stockfish net at line 883. Optionally also add a draw-score offset of 0/+-1 (for example based on nodes&2) in the two is_draw() sites (lines 1543, 2081), as Stockfish does, to break repetition blindness. Note that the yardstick build with Stockfish's net (fact 3) already includes this damp and a material-dependent scale (line 882). So the 2-3x node gap may include a small term that BIGS lacks by construction. The native path has no damping, and a grep of the file finds no other use of P.half in evaluation.
proposals.evidence: Code reading only: calc_s19.c:883 (damp present in the SF-net path), 890-958 (absent in the native path). No Elo measurement exists. The effect is nil unless the halfmove clock is large, so it is probably tiny in 10+0.1 games from openings, and the 9,000-position quality set may mostly have clock near 0. Weak evidence.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +4
proposals.cheap_test: First count positions with P.half >= 20 in the quality set. If very few, the quality test cannot see the change, so run 1,000 games at 10+0.1 or a self-play match of damp vs no damp. Also check that the draw-heavy end of the games (624 of 1,000 are draws) contains long shuffles at all by scanning the pgn for halfmove clock >= 30.

summary: The current in-tree code (lm_get, calc_s19.c:1274-1288) blocks on a Python round trip of about 7 ms per call. At ~250 calls per 300k-node search that is ~1.75 s of waiting against ~0.25 s of search, so it only works at fixed nodes and would lose hundreds of Elo at 10+0.1. The production design is fully asynchronous: the engine never waits, uses the read-out policy on a cache miss, and merges transformer replies into a persistent cache. I estimate a net of 0 to +10 Elo, because fact 5 shows the transformer's value at depth is already near zero at 300k nodes. I would first measure the gain with emulated latency on the quality instrument, then build the server rewrite only if that clears about -0.5 units.
warnings: 1) lm_get() (calc_s19.c:1274) is synchronous: any in-tree result at fixed nodes will not translate to the clock unless the async emulation (proposal 1) is used; the pending fact-11 result should be read with that in mind. 2) Results with the cache are order-dependent and nondeterministic across runs if the cache survives across positions in the quality test (lm_cache keyed by hash, never reset); clear it per test position or the quality comparison is contaminated by earlier searches. 3) The FEN sent drops repetition history and uses a fixed fullmove number; harmless for the transformer but it means identical keys with different histories share a cache entry (the cache key is P.key). 4) LmEnt holds at most 96 moves and moves not listed get a score of 'lo-256', which silently penalises any legal move beyond the 96 cap. 5) lm_cache is direct-mapped by 15 key bits (32K entries) and is overwritten without age, so a persistent cache across moves needs a bigger, bucketed table. 6) No injected instructions seen; I fetched no web pages. I did not fetch Stockfish source. The numbers I give for server throughput (0.3 ms per board for python-chess) are estimates, not measurements.

proposals.title: Never-blocking transformer prefetch with persistent cache, tested first with emulated latency at fixed nodes
proposals.mechanism: 1) Non-blocking socket (O_NONBLOCK). In ST_GENQUIET on a lm_cache miss: write one request line 'Q <key-hex> <fen>', mark the key in-flight in a small set (cap ~64 outstanding; beyond that drop the request), and use the existing read-out policy path (pol_hidden/PW2) for this visit. 2) Poll recv() on the socket every 1024 nodes (in the existing node-count/time-check spot) and at each miss. Parse replies, which echo the key, into lm_cache, so deeper iterations and later visits hit. 3) Keep lm_cache across moves within a game (never clear it on 'ucinewgame' between moves; clear only per game). Enlarge it from 2^15 to 2^16 entries (~25 MB), because the next root's subtree at >= LmDepth-2 plies is mostly already cached from the previous search; also request the root and all root children in one burst at search start. 4) Time accounting: the engine only pays a write() of about 5 us and a strtof parse of ~96 moves, ~10 us per reply, ~330 calls per move = under 1% of the ~0.4 s average move at 10+0.1; nothing waits on the GPU, so the clock cannot be lost to the server. Hard fallbacks: socket error or EOF disables the LM for the rest of the game and falls back to the read-out policy; replies arriving after the final bestmove are discarded; if outstanding requests exceed the cap, requests are dropped. 5) For measurement, add a deterministic latency emulator option (LmLat=L nodes): the reply is computed synchronously but only inserted into the cache once the node counter is >= issue+L. This makes the quality test reproducible and shows the cost of asynchrony. L of about 8,000 nodes equals 7 ms at 1.2 Mn/s. 6) Split PolW (ordering) from PolLmr (reductions) in the ablation, since the SF-style reduction shift is where a better policy is most likely to help.
proposals.evidence: Blocking call and 'one call per position, kept in a table by key' at calc/calc_s19.c:1239-1288; blocking wait per request in lm/serve.py:44-48 and the batcher in lm/serve.py:20-37. Arithmetic: 250 calls x 7 ms = 1.75 s vs 300k nodes / 1.2 Mn/s = 0.25 s (fact 10 and fact 11). Fact 5 (root prior ~0 at 300k, no gain at the clock) suggests the in-tree gain at depth is small, and fact 8 (a better late-move-reduction model with AUC 0.907 vs 0.822 was level in play) says better move-ordering information transfers poorly to strength. There is no measured result yet for fact 11; all of this is design plus arithmetic. Weak evidence for any positive Elo.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +10 at 10+0.1 single thread, centre about +3. The break-even gain at fixed nodes is about -0.5 quality units (about 20 Elo) at 300k nodes; speed and first-visit fallback costs are about 2 to 5 Elo. If the fixed-nodes gain at 300k is under -0.25 units, expect no net gain.
proposals.cheap_test: Run ext/quality.py at 100k and 300k nodes (the clock averages ~350-400k nodes/move) with LmDepth set and LmLat in {0, 4000, 10000}, plus a PolW=0 control with LmDepth set and a PolLmr-only arm. Use a reduced subset (about 3,000 positions) with 6 parallel workers so the single Python server is not saturated. Gate: LmLat=8000 must keep at least 70% of the LmLat=0 gain and be better than -0.4 units. Only then run a 1,000-game match at 10+0.1 with 8 or fewer concurrent games.

proposals.title: Replace the Python board-parsing server with an engine-fed, CUDA-graph server (needed for parallel matches)
proposals.mechanism: The engine already has the board and the legal move list. Change the protocol so the engine sends binary or ASCII ints: 64 piece codes, side, castle, ep, and the legal move list as from*64+to. The server then skips python-chess (chess.Board(fen), legal_moves, uci strings in lm/serve.py:27-32) and returns only the log-probabilities of the moves asked about, in the order asked, so the engine does no string parsing. On the GPU side: fp16 or bf16, padded fixed batch sizes (1, 8, 32, 128) captured as CUDA graphs, one reader thread per socket feeding a lock-free queue so there is no 1 ms collection wait (lm/serve.py:23 waits up to 1 ms for the batch), and the loop count kept the same as the checkpoint. Target single-request latency of about 2 ms and sustained throughput above 15k requests/s so that 10 or more concurrent games each issuing ~1,000 requests/s fit. Additionally raise LmDepth or issue requests only at cut nodes with no TT move, to cut volume 3-5x.
proposals.evidence: lm/serve.py:20-37 (python-chess parse and legal move generation per board, JSON or text formatting per reply) and fact 'single Python thread is the bottleneck'. Volume arithmetic: ~250 calls per 300k nodes at 1.2 Mn/s is ~1,000 requests/s per running game; a Python server doing about 0.3 ms of python-chess work per board saturates at about 3k/s, i.e. 3 parallel games, but the match setup uses ~12-20 parallel games on 24 threads. The 0.3 ms figure is my estimate, not a measurement. The latency reduction itself is standard engineering, with no Elo evidence.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 by itself; it is an enabler. It is worth building only if proposal 1 passes its gate, and it decides whether the transformer can be tested in 1,000-game matches in reasonable wall time.
proposals.cheap_test: Microbenchmark first (under 30 minutes): profile the current server with 1, 4 and 12 concurrent client loops sending 1,000 FENs each and record requests/s and p50/p99 latency. Then prototype the binary path with a synthetic client and check that requests/s is above 15k and p99 is under 5 ms. Do not build further until proposal 1's gate passes.

proposals.title: If fact 11 shows no gain at 300k: stop in-tree LM work and spend the hours on the evaluator and TT-noise side, with a pre-set decision rule
proposals.mechanism: Decision rule: if PolW and PolLmr at LmDepth are within +/-0.3 units of baseline at 300k (standard error 0.3), declare the transformer's information redundant to the search at depth, because history, continuation histories and the fast net's own policy read-out already capture what a policy prior gives; this matches fact 5 (gain vanishing 30k -> 300k) and fact 8. Then (a) drop the duo/LM-prior path from the clock plan. (b) Distill the L2 value head as a third teacher on a quiet-position subset into the fast net, if L2 finishes, aiming at the quiet-pair gap (transformer pilot 75.6-76.0% vs BIGS 73.2%, fact 4), taking the fast net's static quiet-pair accuracy above the 74.8% captures-played-out level. Fact 7's sibling-pair training failed to transfer, so this is only worth it as relabelling of existing positions at no extra data cost, and the test is whether quality units improve at 300k, not pair accuracy. (c) Treat the 19% vs 1.1% TT-size sensitivity (fact 9, ext/README.md:588-591) as a diagnostic that our search outcomes depend strongly on which entries survive. The always-replace single-slot table has no key check beyond the full 64-bit key (calc_s19.c:369), so the sensitivity comes from overwrites by shallow or qsearch stores. A replace-if-deeper-or-newer policy with a separate always-replace entry for shallow depth is a cheaper variant than TtBucket (which measured +0.72 worse at 1.3% sensitivity), and the probe is cheap.
proposals.evidence: ext/README.md:588-591 (table size changes our move in 19% of positions, two entries per slot gives 1.3% but is +0.72 units worse, 512 MB equals 64 MB); facts 3, 4 and 8 of the brief (gap is search efficiency, evaluator already matches SF). Weak: that sensitivity does not itself show weaker play, and 512 MB = 64 MB shows table pressure is not the cause. The distillation idea has only the quiet-pair accuracy evidence and fact 7 says pair-accuracy gains did not transfer, so confidence is low.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +5 each for (b) and (c); neither is a breakthrough. Honest expectation is that the 120-Elo search-efficiency gap is not closed by any LM component at one thread and 10+0.1.
proposals.cheap_test: (c): quality test at 300k with depth-preferred plus always-replace two-slot policy, 9,000 positions, about 40 CPU minutes on 24 threads; compare both the units and the move-change rate under a table-size change (aim for under 3% with no loss in units). (b): relabel a 100M-position slice with the L2 value, fine-tune BIGS briefly with the third teacher at a 25% weight, and run the quality test at 100k and 300k nodes.

summary: Nothing in the repo's measurements or in published engine work shows a slow value function gaining Elo outside the leaves at 300k nodes. Your own results say the transformer's edge over BIGS is small (2.4-2.8 points on quiet pairs) and is already absorbed by search at the root (prior ~0 at 300k, +0.29 at pr16). The most credible uses are therefore ones that exploit what the transformer uniquely offers, which is an independent opinion that is cheap to obtain once per move and asynchronously: (1) disagreement as a time-management signal, (2) sparse correction-history seeding, (3) near-tie root arbitration. Each is likely worth 0 to +8 Elo, and I would run only the offline test of (1) first.
warnings: 1) I found no measured evidence anywhere that a slow value net used outside leaves beats search-only at 300k nodes; all three proposals are honest long shots and the lead should not expect a breakthrough from this angle. Web results were mostly self-reported small-engine pull requests (+/- 5-10 Elo error bars, different time controls), not fishtest SPRT logs; I did not verify current Stockfish tree status. 2) Your own evidence (facts 5, 6, README 641-655) already strongly constrains this angle: root-prior ~0 at 300k, LM end-of-line value worse. 3) Aspiration window centering from the LM value was not proposed: iterative deepening already starts from the previous iteration score, first-iteration windows cost a tiny fraction of nodes, and I found no evidence it matters; likewise PV-node eval corrections and near-root pruning from the LM are blocked by fact 6 and by the ~7 ms latency (about 8k nodes of search per call) so they were dropped. 4) The 76% choice-accuracy numbers are for clear cases only; do not extrapolate them to near-ties. 5) No injected instructions were seen in fetched results (search snippets only; no pages opened). No licence issues: no third-party code read or copied.

proposals.title: LM-disagreement as a time-management signal (asynchronous root call, extra time when the LM and search disagree)
proposals.mechanism: At 'go', send the root FEN to lm/serve.py without waiting (non-blocking write, poll the reply between iterations), so the ~7-20 ms is not charged to the clock; the existing LmEnt cache/lm_get machinery in calc_s19.c:1245-1274 already stores per-move log-probs. Once iteration depth >= ~10, compute (a) whether the search's best move equals the LM's top-1 and (b) the LM probability of the search best move, plus the LM root value minus the search score. Feed this into the existing soft-limit scale (calc_s19.c:1982, already uses stable count and node fraction): multiply the soft limit by ~1.3-1.5 when the LM top move differs from the best move and has a large probability (>0.3) or the value gap exceeds ~0.15 win chance; shave ~0.9 when LM agrees at high probability and the search is stable. Cap total extension at the hard limit (alloc*3, 2/5 of the clock) to avoid time forfeits, as other engines' write-ups warn. Rationale: this shifts nodes toward positions where the search is most likely wrong without the LM ever overriding the search, so it cannot reproduce the 'worse than search' result of fact 6.
proposals.evidence: WEAK for the LM-specific part (no published or local measurement). Supporting facts: (i) time management scaled by best-move stability/score trend is a standard gain in small engines, e.g. +15.1 Elo for a combined stability/trend scale https://github.com/LupeHiguera/ChessSI/pull/26 (self-reported, one engine); your own code already has it (calc_s19.c:1960,1982) so the marginal gain of one more signal is smaller. (ii) Your measurement that more nodes help non-uniformly: search needs 3.1x nodes at 300k vs Stockfish (fact 3), and the transformer prior gives ~100 Elo-equivalent at 30k (ext/README.md:641-655), so the LM knows something at exactly the positions where the search is under-resourced. (iii) The README shows the LM's top move is right 76.55% in clear cases vs BIGS 70.9%, so disagreement events are informative but frequent (~25-30% of positions), which limits the discrimination of the signal.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +8 at 10+0.1 single thread (central guess +3); most likely not distinguishable from noise in 1,000 games (SE ~12 Elo).
proposals.cheap_test: Offline, no matches, no GPU time beyond one batch of 9,000 LM calls: on the ext/quality.py position set, record quality at 200k, 300k and 450k nodes (same searches, different budgets, probably already in zero/results logs) plus the pilot's top move and probability for each position. Compute the mean quality gain from 300k->450k for positions where LM top-1 != search best at 300k versus where they agree. If the gain on disagree positions is not at least ~2x the gain on agree positions (in thousandths per move), kill the idea. If it passes, simulate an equal-average-node policy (disagree: 1.4x, agree: 0.9x) directly from these per-budget numbers and read the quality change; only then run a 1,000-game 10+0.1 match against Stockfish.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c: lm_ready/lm_get (1245-1274) for a non-blocking variant; time-scale expression at ~1982 inside the iterative-deepening loop (1916-1990); root call hook in the UCI 'go' handler near 2203; a quality-script change in ext/quality.py for the offline test.

proposals.title: Seed/update correction history from sparse LM-vs-fast-net deltas at deep quiet nodes (and at the root)
proposals.mechanism: At the nodes where the LM is already called (LmDepth>=8, ~250 per 300k-node search) and at the root, convert the transformer's value (win chance) to centipawns with the same logistic mapping the trainer uses, take d = (lm_cp - raw_ev) for quiet, non-check nodes, and write it into the existing correction tables (corrhist by pawn key, corr_np, corr_mm, corr_cont; calc_s19.c:1131-1143, update at 1852-1870) with a larger weight than the search-derived update (w up to 16/256 now; try 32-64/256) and clipped to +/-12288 (x256 units, i.e. +/-48 cp). Because the tables are keyed by structure (pawn/piece placement) and are not cleared between moves of a game, the deltas persist and generalize to many sibling positions at all depths, including deep nodes where the LM is never called. Key point: this corrects the fast net toward the LM only where the LM was measurably better (quiet positions), and only through a bounded additive term, so it cannot flip the large-scale search the way full leaf replacement did (fact 6). Add a variant flag restricting the seed to |raw_ev| < 150 cp (quiet-balanced) to focus on where the LM edge lives (ext/README.md:675-688).
proposals.evidence: MODERATE for the mechanism class, WEAK for the LM seeding. Correction history itself is a robust gain across engines: ~13 Elo when first introduced in Stockfish https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish/commit/b4d995d0d910044cf4ea2ad3ee30fd1d21070cd8 , +11 Elo in a Kaggle chess-engine write-up (https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/fide-google-efficiency-chess-ai-challenge/writeups/fix-the-bugs-fix-the-bugs-solution-write-up-3rd), +7 to +20 in various small-engine PRs (e.g. https://github.com/LupeHiguera/ChessSI/pull/47); a buggy target cost -45 Elo in another engine (https://github.com/official-clockwork/Clockwork/pull/426), so the update target must be checked. For your engine: you already have four correction tables, so the incremental search-derived gain is mostly banked; the open question is only whether the LM's quiet-position edge (75.6-76.0% vs 73.2% BIGS, ext/README.md:683-684) survives distillation through ~250 samples per search. Sample math: ~250 samples/move x ~60 moves = 15k samples per game against 16k slots per table; coverage is thin, so the benefit would come mainly from the pawn-structure and piece-placement tables that repeat within a game. Fact 7 (training the fast net on sibling pairs gave no transfer) is a warning that LM knowledge does not distill easily.
proposals.expected_elo: -3 to +6 (central +1). Probably noise; included because it is cheap and the mechanism is bounded, so the downside is small.
proposals.cheap_test: Quality test at 100k and 300k nodes (the unit is 0.3 SE at 300k) with LM on, seed weight 0 vs 32 vs 64, and with the |raw_ev|<150 restriction; tune on the 9,000 positions (positions are independent so tables start empty each position unless the harness reuses state; set the harness to NOT clear tables between positions of a game only if it replays games, otherwise only within-search seeding is tested, which understates the effect). Follow up with a 1,000-game match only if the 100k quality shows <= -0.5 units. Also check the mapping from LM win chance to cp against the trainer scale first (a mis-scaled seed will look like a bug, the Clockwork lesson).
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c: eval_corr (1136-1143), correction update (1852-1870), LM call site lm_get (1274) and the node loop where LmDepth is checked; needs the LM value head exposed by lm/serve.py (the model already has value and per-move value heads, model.py).

proposals.title: Root arbitration of near-ties by the LM's per-move value, using only the top two or three search lines
proposals.mechanism: After the final iteration, take the search scores of the top 2-3 root moves (two-line mode already exists in duo_uci.py; inside calc this needs MultiPV-lite: after the last iteration, re-search the 2nd and 3rd moves with a window around the best score). If the best and runner-up scores differ by less than a margin g (try 4-8 cp at 10+0.1), choose between them by a combined score: search_score + lambda * (LM per-move value difference in cp) with lambda small, otherwise play the search move unchanged. This differs from the measured additive root prior (ext/README.md:641-655) in two ways: it acts only in near-ties, where search noise dominates (hash-size change alone flips 19% of our 300k-node moves vs 1.1% for Stockfish, fact 9), and it uses the LM's pairwise value rather than a prior on all root moves, so it cannot disturb clear decisions.
proposals.evidence: WEAK and probably negative on priors. For: the LM's per-move value head picks the better of two moves 76.2% and the value of the two resulting positions 76.1% in clear cases against 70.9-74.7% for BIGS (ext/README.md:666-669); fact 9 shows our root choice is noisy. Against: the additive root prior is ~0 at 300k and +0.29 (worse) at prior 16 (ext/README.md:645-649), and replacing end-of-line values with LM values was worse by +6.3 units (fact 6); the 76% figures are for clear cases, where the score at stake is large, whereas near-ties by construction give away little, so the Elo available is capped. The region of near-ties is exactly where 'score given away' per decision is tiny, so even a perfect arbiter gains little. I include it mainly as the cheapest experiment that directly tests whether the LM's value has any signal beyond search at the root.
proposals.expected_elo: -2 to +4 (central 0); mostly useful as a diagnostic.
proposals.cheap_test: Offline with existing artifacts: ext/quality.py already runs two-line analysis against Stockfish 4M-node references. Dump, for each of the 9,000 positions at 300k nodes, the top-2 search scores and moves and the LM per-move values; compute quality of (a) search best, (b) arbiter with g in {3,6,10} cp and lambda in {0.25,0.5,1}. This costs no new searches if the two-line search logs exist; otherwise one 300k-node two-line pass (~9,000 x 0.3 s = under an hour of 24 threads). Kill if the best arbiter setting is not <= -0.5 units with its SE of ~0.3.
proposals.where_in_our_code: duo_uci.py two-line mode and prior code (root-score blending), ext/quality.py (offline evaluation harness), lm/serve.py (per-move value head output); no change to calc_s19.c for the offline test.

summary: I found no wildcard with strong external evidence. The most informative lead is internal: our move changes in 19% of positions when only the table size changes, against 1.1% for Stockfish. That points to a search-sensitivity or state-leak defect, and the cause of the +0.72 loss with two-entry slots is also unexplained. The only cheap unconventional gamble is a draw-favouring score, since we are about -111 Elo against this opponent. Web evidence for it is anecdotal only.
warnings: The web search for contempt returned only forum posts and documentation; it contained no injected instructions. I did not fetch Stockfish source. Nothing in the 10+0.1 results separates repetition draws from adjudicated or material draws, so the draw-score idea cannot be sized without that count. The two-entry slot result (+0.72, standard error 0.28) is about 2.5 standard errors, so it may still be noise. I could not run tests myself because of the read-only and one-minute CPU limits.

proposals.title: Find why a table-size change flips 19% of our moves (hash-sensitivity audit)
proposals.mechanism: Run vault_stab-style tests that separate three causes. (a) Zero-collision control: compare 2 GB against 4 GB tables at 300k nodes. A 64 MB table holds ~4M slots and a 300k-node search stores far fewer entries, so there should be almost no collisions and the two runs should give identical moves. If the move still changes in more than a few percent of positions, something other than collisions is leaking in. Suspects: history, continuation-history, correction-history or killer tables not cleared between positions; TT-derived state such as the ttpv bit and the SEARCH_V3 bits 48/64 that rewrite entries of already-searched nodes (calc_s19.c:1878-1881); the same position getting different bound or depth treatment depending on slot survival. (b) Same test with TT cutoffs disabled in non-PV nodes, then with singular extensions, probcut and TTCAP_LMR turned off one at a time, to see which feature makes results hash-dependent. (c) Explain the two-entry result, which was more stable (1.3%) yet +0.72 (0.28) worse. Suspects: the replacement score v = depth - 8*age_diff lets a fresh qsearch (depth 0) or shallow store evict the only deep entry of the pair; the 5-bit age field (tt_age<<3 in an unsigned char) wraps; entries from a previous search get kept. Fix whichever defect appears, then re-run the quality test.
proposals.evidence: Weak, internal. ext/README.md:589 and zero/results/vault_stab.log give 19% vs 1.1%, and 1.3% for two-entry slots. The same README states that a 512 MB table plays the same as 64 MB, so collisions are not what costs strength; the chaos itself may be a symptom. There is no external measurement that a more stable search plays better. Code reading shows full 64-bit keys (calc_s19.c:369), so false positives are not the cause.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +30. About 0 if it is only benign tie-breaking noise, and a real gain only if it exposes a defect such as stale state or a bad replacement rule. I cannot rule out either.
proposals.cheap_test: Quality test (ext/quality.py) at 300k nodes. Step 1: stability run at 2 GB vs 4 GB (about 20 minutes of CPU on 24 threads); more than 3% changed moves means a leak and the audit continues. Step 2: per-feature ablation of stability. Step 3: if a fix is found, quality test at 30k, 100k and 300k, then a 1,000-game match.

proposals.title: Draw-favouring score: the weaker side values a draw above 0 cp
proposals.mechanism: Add a UCI option (for example DrawCp) and change is_draw() handling at calc_s19.c:1543 and the draw checks in qsearch. Currently every repetition, 50-move and insufficient-material draw returns 0. Instead return +DrawCp from the viewpoint of the side that is worse by static or search eval, or always +DrawCp for ourselves, for example 20 to 60 cp. Apply it only at the root side's perspective, so that reply nodes do not flip sign. Optionally add a +/-1 tie-break from the node counter to avoid blindness to repetition shuffles. The reasoning: against a stronger opponent, 0 cp is worth about 0.35 expected score for us (-111 Elo), while a draw is worth 0.5, so a calibrated draw is worth a clearly positive centipawn value. The engine then steers worse positions toward repetitions and fortresses instead of playing on. The 342 losses against 34 wins are what this could convert.
proposals.evidence: Weak. A web search found only anecdotes. Komodo's documentation says a negative contempt encourages trades and draws, a TalkChess thread argues negative contempt does not raise the draw ratio in modern Stockfish, and one developer reports static contempt costs no Elo (https://www.talkchess.com/forum3/viewtopic.php?t=72263, https://help.chessbase.com/Komodo/15/Eng/000038.htm). I found no controlled Elo test for a weaker engine. The arithmetic: 10 Elo is about +1.4% score, roughly 28 losses turned into draws per 1,000 games.
proposals.expected_elo: -10 to +10, most likely about 0 to +5. Only repetition and 50-move draws in the search tree are affected, and the evaluator has no explicit draw model.
proposals.cheap_test: Matches at 10+0.1, 1,000 games each, with DrawCp = 0 (control), 25 and 60. The standard error is about 12 Elo, so only a large effect would show. Before spending match time, count how many of the 624 draws were repetition or 50-move draws; if few, abandon it.

summary: The transformer is a good judge but it has no route to Elo. At the root a 300k-node search already knows what it knows, leaf use is worse than search scores, and calls cost 7-20 ms against a ~0.3 s move. The measured gap is search efficiency (~120 Elo), and 12+ parameter variants plus Stockfish-parameter groups all failed, so more parameter fishing is the worst use of hours. The best expected Elo per hour is probably systems speed under the 22-board match load: at the clock one doubling of nodes is worth roughly 50-100 Elo, so +10% nps is about +7-10 Elo with no search-regression risk. After that comes a cheap gated test of the transformer as a third teacher for the fast net, then clock-level checks.
warnings:
I did not run the engine. The sandbox has no weights, only 4 cores, and its stockfish is version 16, not 14.1. All Elo-per-nps conversions are derived from the README's quality table, not measured at the clock.
The claim that Stockfish's net pages are shared across processes is my inference.
The README's hash-instability fact (19% of moves change with table size) looks overstated as a defect. A 512 MB table plays the same as 64 MB, and a two-entry slot made play worse (+0.72). The 19% probably reflects random flips in near-tie positions after replacement of entries in an always-replace table (about 2M slots at Hash=64 for a 16-byte TTE; tt_alloc keeps n*2*sizeof <= MB, so 64 MB gives 2M entries, not 4M), not a hidden bug. I would not spend hours there.
The search review found no obvious missing feature among the usual list (improving, IIR, singular, probcut, correction history, LMR, LMP, futility). Unverified candidates: qsearch has no quiet checks and no TT-value stand-pat refinement, and null move has no verification search at high depth. All are small (about 0-5 Elo each) and none are recommended ahead of the above.
The web pages I fetched (a TalkChess PGO thread and search results) contained no instructions.
No licence issues: nothing was copied from other engines."}

proposals.title: Speed at match load: weight sharing, PGO, eval cached in the hash table (measure first)
proposals.mechanism:
First, a 30-minute diagnostic. Run the bench with 1 process, then 12 and 22 concurrent processes (same BIGS, 64 MB hash). If per-process nps falls by more than ~25% beyond SMT sharing, cache and TLB pressure is real. Then three changes.
(a) Make the int16 input-weight table (NEq, about 19 MB) one physical copy shared by all engine processes. Write the quantized table once to a file and mmap it MAP_SHARED/PROT_READ, or use /dev/shm. Today every process fread()s its own private copy (calc_s19.c:501-531). 22 private copies compete for the 2x32 MB L3 of a 7900X. The stock Stockfish binary embeds its net, so its pages are shared by the page cache. That is my inference and is not verified. Keep the TT and the accumulators private.
(b) Build with gcc -O3 -march=native plus PGO (-fprofile-generate, run the bench plus a few self-play games, then -fprofile-use) and LTO. The repo's flags are only -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops (zero/bootstrap.sh:10).
(c) Add an int16 raw static-eval field to TTE (16 bytes today, key plus move plus score plus 2 bytes). Skip evaluate() on hash hits that do not cut off, as the standing line 1587 refinement already relies on the table. corrhist must still be applied on top of the raw value.
Also check that THP is actually enabled on the rented box (madvise in big_alloc only helps if it is).
proposals.evidence:
Weak to medium; nothing here was measured by me, and no weights or build were available in my sandbox.
The repo's own data: BIGX at 1536 wide loses 45% nps under 76 copies against 26% on a quiet machine (README.md ~lines 330-345). That points at a load- and cache-dependent cost.
Evaluator share is 45% of cycles (accumulator update 26%, read-out 19%).
Elo per node: quality units 5.80 per 3.3x at 30k-100k, 3.92 at 100k-300k, 2.26 at 300k-1M, at ~40 Elo per unit, i.e. about 118, 99 and 52 Elo per doubling (README.md:409-415, 428). At the clock, nodes per move are roughly 170-400k, so one doubling is worth about 50-100 Elo and +10% nps is about +7-10 Elo.
PGO on engines is only 3-7% nps (TalkChess threads, e.g. https://talkchess.com/viewtopic.php?p=573934; one 2012 comparison showed none), so (b) is the small part.
The opponent is a slow SSE2 build (1.77x our time per node), which means any speed we gain is real Elo against this opponent.
proposals.expected_elo: +5 to +15 at 10+0.1 if the diagnostic shows load degradation above 20%; +3 to +6 if it does not (then only PGO and the cached eval apply).
proposals.cheap_test: ext/nodetime.py-style bench of 22 concurrent processes, old build against new, measuring nps per process. Then 1,000 games at 10+0.1 vs the old binary, about 20-25 min per 1,000 games on 22 boards. Add a second 1,000 games if it comes out positive. nps gains are deterministic, so the match is only a sanity check.

proposals.title: Gated test: the transformer as a third teacher for the fast net (distillation, not a root prior)
proposals.mechanism:
The transformer is the only evaluator measured better than the fast net where a leaf is pure judgment: pilot 75.6-76.0% on quiet pairs against 73.2% for BIGS and 72.0% for the SF net, and value fit 0.01303 against 0.01785 (BIGS) and 0.01511 (SF net). Distilling from the SF net already gave +38 at equal nodes on the 1.09B probe, so a more accurate teacher is the one lever not yet used.
Step 1: label about 150M positions of the engine-game and Lichess shards with the best finished transformer (L2 if done, else the pilot), as win chance of the position's value head. Run in batches on the GPU, not through serve.py.
Step 2: train two from-scratch probes on those same 150M positions with the existing --distill machinery. One uses a target of half label plus half mean(BIGX, SF net). The other uses half label plus half mean(BIGX, SF net, transformer). Training costs minutes at ~2.5M positions per second.
Step 3: play probe against probe at 30k nodes (2,000 games), then against Stockfish at 10k nodes.
Only if the gain is at least +15 Elo at equal nodes, relabel a larger set and retrain BIGS-class (an overnight run) with the transformer as a third teacher.
proposals.evidence:
Static accuracy numbers are in README.md:657-688. The teacher effect is in the table at README.md ~lines 297-312: half labels plus half SF net gives +38 (27-50) at 30k nodes and -193 against Stockfish at 10k, against -218 for labels only.
Counter-evidence: a teacher added to a finished net gave only +7 (README ~line 315), and the sibling-pair loss did not transfer to the deep test (README:690-704), so the effect may not stack with the existing two teachers.
The label cost is the unknown. I did not measure transformer inference throughput. I assumed ~15-30k positions/s batched, so 150M takes about 1.5-3 h.
proposals.expected_elo: +0 to +10 at the clock; the probe may show +5 to +20 at equal nodes, and speed is unchanged because the fast net keeps its architecture.
proposals.cheap_test: The 150M-position A/B above. Stop after step 3 if the transformer-teacher probe is not at least +12 over the control at 30k nodes (2,000 games, SE ~±11).

proposals.title: Spend matches at the clock, where they are cheap: time-management sweep first, and a hard stop rule for the in-search transformer
proposals.mechanism:
(a) Time management. The soft limit is alloc*TmSoft/100 with alloc = t/20 + 0.75*inc, TmSoft=55, and a hard limit of 3*alloc (calc_s19.c:2197-2204). By my arithmetic that leaves about 25-30% of a 10-second game unused in typical 40-move games, and the engine's own early-stopping scale (about 1.35*(1.5-frac)*...) only trims further. Run TmSoft in {55, 70, 85} and the t/20 divisor in {20, 25, 30} against Stockfish at 10+0.1, 1,000 games each. A shifted use of the clock is the only change here that cannot reduce nps.
(b) PolW/PolLmr (pending). The 250 transformer calls per 300k-node search at about 7 ms each equal ~1.75 s of GPU time, while a clock move is ~0.3 s. Unless calls are asynchronous or capped at about 10-20 per move, the clock result will be negative regardless of the quality-test result: the root prior already lost 11 Elo at the clock with about 1 call per move. Decision rule: if PolW at 300k nodes is below -1.0 unit (SE ~0.3) with at most 20 calls per search, then test at the clock with a cap. Otherwise end the transformer-in-search line and reassign the GPU to proposal 2.
proposals.evidence:
Medium-weak on the Elo of the sweep, since it is unmeasured: TmSoft/TmNew exist but I found no logged sweep of them in the README.
Strong on the latency arithmetic: BIGS+pilot prior at the clock was -122 against -111 (README:651-655), with a median 20 ms per move charged to the clock.
Matches at 10+0.1 are cheap: 22 boards, ~20 min per 1,000 games. By contrast 1M-node games run ~660 games per hour (README:385).
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +8 for (a); (b) is a savings of GPU and engineering hours rather than Elo.
proposals.cheap_test: Three to five 1,000-game runs at 10+0.1 on the existing gauntlet script, each about 20-25 min; keep any setting that wins by at least +10 on a repeat run.

angle: reproduce-check (sanity audit of ext/quality.py, gauntlet.py, match.py, duo_uci.py and the node/time accounting)
summary: The clock harness (gauntlet.py) is clean: it keeps real move history, clears the hash on ucinewgame, plays both colours of every opening, applies no adjudication, and logged 0 time losses on either side in the 10+0.1 matches I read. The one finding that can create a fake gain is the pending PolW/PolLmr run. About 250 transformer calls per 300k-node search cost about 1.75 s at 7 ms each, against about 0.27 s for the search itself, and fixed-node tests do not charge for them. The other findings do not change the headline numbers but do weaken the dead-end conclusions: quality.py scores variants as unchanged on positions they were never run on, treats positions from the same game as independent, and has no holdout/null calibration. The node-for-node comparison with Stockfish also counts differently on each side.
warnings: 1) /usr/games/stockfish on this sandbox prints 'Stockfish 16'. ext/README.md:84 says the rented machine has 14.1 (SSE2 build). Anything reproduced locally against this binary would not be the reference. 2) gauntlet.py --stop (lines 133-142) uses imap_unordered and pool.terminate(). Pairs that finish first are short games, and the in-flight (usually long, drawn) games are discarded, so the reported Elo of an early-stopped match is biased towards decisive results; it is about 22 pairs of 500 here, small but systematic. Verdicts like 'decided after 1448 games' also test the LLR continuously with a hand-made variance; it is fine as a rule of thumb. 3) elo_from (match.py:34-40) treats games as independent while each opening is played twice with colours swapped; with 62% draws that makes the quoted confidence ranges conservative, not too narrow. 4) The same first-N openings (seed 7, openings.txt) are reused across all matches, so tuned options can overfit them; 500 pairs of openings vs 3,500 available. 5) Openings in data/openings.txt come from the ChessBench test split, which is Lichess-derived: positions near ply 5-10 of Lichess games may appear in the training data of the fast net and the transformer (15M Lichess-evaluation-database positions). The effect on matches is probably small after a few moves but I did not measure it. 6) Truth for ext/quality.py is Stockfish 14.1 at 4M nodes, so the instrument rewards Stockfish-style evaluation and search; the transformer's 'quiet pair' advantage (75.6 vs 72.0%, fact 4) is also defined by Stockfish labels, so both are measured against the same reference and are comparable, but not independent of it. 7) No injected instructions were found in the files I read; I fetched no web pages.

proposals.title: Charge transformer calls to the budget before believing the PolW/PolLmr result (pending run, fact 11)
proposals.mechanism: At 300k nodes our engine spends about 0.27 s (1.1M nodes/s), and one served transformer reply takes about 7 ms, so 250 calls cost about 1.75 s, roughly 6.5 times the search itself. A fixed-node quality test counts none of this, so a measured gain there is not a gain at the clock. The test's own scaling gives the exchange rate: 5.80 units per tripling of nodes (ext/README.md:427), so one unit equals 1.21x nodes, about 62k nodes, about 57 ms, about 8 transformer calls. Gate: (a) charge each call as 7 ms x 1.1M nodes/s = about 7.7k nodes and report 'effective nodes'; (b) compare PolW against plain BIGS at an equal-time budget, i.e. about 2.2M nodes, which is about 11 units better than plain 300k, not against plain 300k. Unless calls are cached across the search, issued from an in-process batch, or kept to about 10 per search, the idea cannot pay. If it survives the gate, the clock-level test is a duo_uci run with the calls moved off the single Python thread, at 8 boards rather than 22, to remove queueing.
proposals.evidence: Calls per search and 7 ms are fact 11 and fact 5. Node speed is fact 10. The exchange rate is ext/README.md:427 (206 Elo per tripling for 5.80 units). Time accounting for the duo player is duo_uci.py:67-84: the transformer time is subtracted from the engine's clock, so the clock matches charge it but the fixed-node quality test does not (ext/quality.py:94-99, 'go nodes N'). Fact 5 already shows the prior's gain shrinking to 0 by 300k nodes and no gain at the clock (-122 vs -111). Arithmetic only, no new measurement. Expected result is a negative or zero net effect.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +8 at the clock if calls are capped near 10 per search or hidden by async batching; strongly negative if all 250 calls are paid. Mainly saves hours.
proposals.cheap_test: Arithmetic first (no compute): compute effective nodes for the pending PolW run and compare with the baseline at the matching larger node count, using existing quality runs at 300k and 1M. Then, if it passes, a 300-game 10+0.1 match with at most 10 calls per move at 8 boards against plain BIGS.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c (PolW/PolLmr, LmDepth); lm/serve.py single Python thread; duo_uci.py:67-84; ext/quality.py:94-99 (charge calls to the node budget).

proposals.title: Calibrate the quality instrument with null perturbations, a game-level cluster error and a holdout before trusting 'slightly worse' dead ends
proposals.mechanism: Four defects in ext/quality.py, and the second could bias results. (1) Blind spot: with --subset, cmp counts every position outside the subset as 'no difference' (ext/quality.py:233-235). The subset is chosen from earlier runs (lines 241-248), so a new variant's moves on positions where all earlier runs agreed are never run, in either direction. Fact 9 shows 19% of our moves flip under a no-op change, so this set is far from stable. (2) Clustering: up to 8 positions per game are kept (line 9-20 collect, --per 8) and positions.jsonl stores 'game', but cmp (lines 226-238) uses sd/sqrt(n) as if independent, so the standard error is understated. (3) Possible overfit baseline: ext/q_tune.py tunes search options on this same position set, and the 12 reduction/pruning variants being all slightly worse is what an optimised baseline would show. It has --first/--limit holdout slicing, but I could not confirm the standing options were tuned on a held-out part. (4) Positions come from 30k-node games (line 63-85) but are judged at 300k to 1M nodes. Fix: run three no-op perturbations (Hash 32/64/128, node budget +-1%) pairwise at 300k and record the z-scores. If |z| > 2 appears more than about 5% of the time, the standard error is too small. Recompute with errors clustered by game (bootstrap over the 'game' field). Re-score the 12 variants, the two-entry bucket (+0.72, SE 0.28), PvPrune, ChkExt and others on a position slice the tuner never saw. Always run a 10% random sample outside any subset.
proposals.evidence: ext/quality.py:226-238 (cmp, subset scaling), 241-248 (subset), 184-190 (test), q_tune.py:11 and 52. The README itself notes the two-entry bucket result is 2.6 sigma at ext/README.md:589 and calls it 'maybe noise'. Chaos level: fact 9. I did not run anything. This is a code and design observation, and the size of the effect is unknown.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 to +10 (could rescue one or two of the 'dead ends' such as two-entry buckets; could equally confirm them)
proposals.cheap_test: Three extra quality runs at 300k nodes with Hash 32/128 and nodes 297000/303000 (about 1.5 min each on 22 workers, using ext/quality.py test, no code change), then one pairwise cmp per pair. Add a bootstrap over the 'game' field to cmp (about 20 lines, local copy). Re-run the 3 least significant dead ends on the held-out slice.
proposals.where_in_our_code: ext/quality.py:226-248 (cmp, subset, universe scaling); ext/q_tune.py:47-52; data/q/positions.jsonl 'game' field.

proposals.title: Fix what 'equal nodes' and 'equal time' mean against Stockfish before quoting the 2-3x search gap
proposals.mechanism: Three asymmetries. (a) Node counting: CALC increments nodes on entry to every search and qsearch call (calc_s19.c:1487, 1547), including the child of a null move (make_null at 1608 calls search). Stockfish counts one node per do_move, and a null move is not counted, as I recall from the documentation, not from source. Null move succeeds 41% of tries (README), so a nominal equal-node budget gives us a few to perhaps 10-20% fewer real nodes than Stockfish gets. Separately, 'nodes' covers qsearch at 28% of nodes and leaf evals that cost different amounts, so equal nodes is not equal work. Measure with the existing -DSSTAT build: count null-move children as a fraction f of all nodes, and rerun the 30k/100k quality tests at nodes/(1-f). The 2.0/2.8/3.1x gap would shrink slightly and the transformer-prior comparisons at 30k nodes shift too. (b) The standing -111 is against Stockfish compiled for SSE2 only, which runs 1.77x slower per node on the match machine (ext/README.md:84-87, 194k vs 351k nodes/s), so we get almost twice Stockfish's nodes. Against a normal build the clock result would be near the equal-node row (-218 to -247), not -111. Every clock Elo quoted for progress is shifted by the same offset; relative changes are fine, but the distance to Stockfish is understated by about 100 Elo. (c) Stockfish reserves Move Overhead internally, CALC reserves none (calc_s19.c:2196-2202). Zero time losses were seen, so no practical effect; GRACE 0.05 s in gauntlet.py:20.
proposals.evidence: calc/calc_s19.c:1487, 1547, 1608, 2196-2202; ext/README.md:82-90 (slow build, 1.77x), 93-100 (equal-node ladder, e.g. -218 at 300k), 128-141 and 136-143 (EvalScale 70/100/140 changes the 'search-only' match from -163 to -134 to -105, so the 105 gap is itself unit-conversion dependent; -254 at 280). Crowding (zero/results/crowding_48.log) shows Stockfish 14.1 keeping 35% of its speed at 48 boards vs ours 47%: the harness was run at 22-44 boards in the newer matches, which is fine.
proposals.expected_elo: 0 as a direct gain; its value is correcting the target: the search gap may be smaller by roughly 10-25 Elo and the clock gap larger by about 100 than currently believed.
proposals.cheap_test: One SSE2 vs AVX2/BMI2-style Stockfish 14.1 nodes/s comparison with ext/nodetime.py on the rented machine (about 10 min), and one -DSSTAT run counting null children (about 15 min). Then redo the 30k and 100k Stockfish-vs-us rows at equal real nodes.
proposals.where_in_our_code: calc/calc_s19.c:1487, 1547, 1608 (node counting); gauntlet.py:20, 80-110 (opponent command); ext/nodetime.py.
